News.title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis found guilty of murdering rap legend Tupac Shakur in 1996 hit
News.content:
A VERDICT has been reached in the long-awaited trial of the only man ever charged over the murder of rap legend Tupac Shakur.

Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, was found guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon nearly three decades after the star was gunned down.



The decision was handed down at Clark County District Court in Las Vegas, bringing one of the most notorious unsolved killings in music history closer to a conclusion.

He was found guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote or assist a criminal gang.



Davis had pleaded not guilty and denied having any role in the September 1996 drive-by shooting.

He was accused of helping organize the revenge attack after Shakur and members of his entourage beat Davis’ nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, inside the MGM Grand earlier that night.

Prosecutors never alleged that Davis himself pulled the trigger.

Instead, they argued the former South Side Compton Crips leader helped set the killing in motion and supplied the gun used in the attack.

Under Nevada law, someone who aids or helps arrange a murder can be held responsible even if they did not fire the fatal shots.

Shakur, 25, was riding in a black BMW driven by Death Row Records boss Marion “Suge” Knight on September 7, 1996, when a white Cadillac pulled up alongside them near the Las Vegas Strip.



Gunfire erupted, leaving Shakur critically wounded and Knight injured.

The California Love rapper died in hospital six days later on September 13.

The killing stunned the music world and became one of hip-hop’s most enduring mysteries.

No one was charged for nearly 27 years.

The case eventually zeroed in on Davis after he repeatedly discussed the shooting in interviews, conversations with investigators and his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.



Jurors were played hours of recordings in which Davis described being inside the Cadillac on the night Shakur was shot.

In his earlier accounts, Davis said he and three other men went looking for Shakur and Knight after Anderson was beaten.

He said he obtained a gun and passed it toward the back of the Cadillac before shots were fired into Shakur’s BMW.



Davis previously named his nephew Anderson as the gunman, although other accounts have pointed to another passenger, Deandrae Smith.

Prosecutors did not ask jurors to decide who actually fired the weapon.

The other three men Davis said were inside the Cadillac have all since died, leaving him as the only surviving alleged occupant.

Prosecutors argued Davis’ descriptions of the shooting remained consistent on the crucial points and matched information investigators had developed about the case.

But defense attorney Michael Sanft told jurors his client had spent years exaggerating and telling sensational stories for attention and money.



The defense argued there was no physical evidence establishing Davis was even inside the Cadillac when Shakur was killed.

Davis did not testify in his own defense.

His lawyers instead called former investigators in an effort to show that key parts of his earlier accounts could never be independently confirmed.



Retired Las Vegas homicide detective Dan Long told jurors he had tried to verify details Davis gave police during an interview years after the killing.

“I wasn’t able to verify any of that,” Long testified.

Long said he could not independently establish that Davis had been inside the Cadillac and was unable to find records supporting some other parts of his story.

But prosecutors pointed out that Davis had identified the same four alleged occupants of the car that investigators had already focused on.

Long also testified that he believed there had been enough probable cause to seek an arrest warrant after interviewing Davis, although prosecutors at the time told investigators to hold off while the case was reviewed.



The trial also saw dramatic testimony from former Mob Piru member James “Mob James” McDonald, who openly told the courtroom he did not want his answers to help send Davis to prison.

“You’re asking me something that wouldn’t be good for [Davis],” McDonald told the defense during one tense exchange.

Jurors ultimately heard 24 prosecution witnesses and three defense witnesses across nine days of evidence before the case headed to closing arguments.

Prosecutors urged the panel to trust Davis’ own words, arguing his years of public comments had effectively placed him at the heart of the revenge plot.



The defense maintained those same statements could not be treated as a reliable confession when investigators lacked hard evidence to back them up.

Davis was arrested and indicted in September 2023, reviving a case that had remained without a prosecution for almost three decades.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shakur’s relatives attended the trial, which unfolded just weeks before the 30th anniversary of his death.

The rapper remains one of the most influential artists in hip-hop, with his killing continuing to fuel questions, investigations and theories for decades.

News.title: Brit, 31, stabbed to death at railway station in Germany named as popular pub landlady
News.content:
BRUTAL ATTACK Brit, 31, stabbed to death at railway station in Germany named as popular pub landlady

A BRITISH woman stabbed to death at a railway station in Germany was named as a popular pub landlady as tributes were paid yesterday.

The 31-year-old woman died of wounds suffered in a mystery knife attack in Rosenheim, Bavaria at 12.50 am on Sunday.



Bavarian police said she died in hospital of “severe” injuries and arrested a 27-year-old German man near the scene immediately after the horror.

The man appeared in court yesterday and was ordered to be taken to a secure psychiatric hospital as police probed the motive for the attack.



Social media posts paid tributes and named a woman described as a Buckinghamshire pub landlady, though Foreign Office officials have yet to confirm relatives have been informed.

But a friend posted on Facebook: “She (not mentioning her name out of respect to her family) was our local landlady who was on her way to support a friend at a funeral in Austria.

“This lady was an old soul and everyone in our local always felt safe and secure, and she turned the local around to modernise it but also keep it a welcoming safe space for our community.

“A true professional in hospitality with grace and dignity.

“She loved her dog so much and was so tolerant and non judgemental.

“We are absolutely devastated for her loss and for the loss her family. Her beautiful dog who was our dog’s best friend.



“Our whole community know and are processing slowly in shock and are in mourning.”

Police revealed the knifeman was a German citizen of no fixed address.

The attractive pub boss was also a keen runner who ran the 2022 London Marathon to raise money for the Spinal Injuries Association and finished gruelling Iron Man events.

Locals said she had turned around her historic 17th century pub, transforming the run-down boozer into a thriving community hub after modernisation work.

Another friend posted: “The lady was so lovely – knew her very well.



“Just can’t believe it, Only saw her Saturday lunchtime and then 12 hours later she (bless her) is no longer with us….”

Rosenheim is one of the largest cities in Upper Bavaria acting as a rail hub for passengers travelling to Austrian cities including Vienna, Salzburg and Innsbruck.

The Rosenheimer Herbstfest – an event similar to the Oktoberfest beer festival – is currently taking place in the area.

Rosenheim Mayor Abuzar Erdogan said “there are no indications of a security threat in our city or of any link to our Herbstfest”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The criminal investigation department is working closely with the public prosecutor’s office to investigate the circumstances.”



A Foreign Office spokesman said: “We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local authorities.”

News.title: Fury as major historic English cities could LOSE their prized status due to Rayner’s barmy local government reforms
News.content:
HISTORIC cities across England could lose their prized status because of Angela Rayner’s barmy local government reforms.

Winchester and even Canterbury have held city status by ancient prescriptive right for at least 837 predating English common law.



But plans stirred up by the Secretary for Housing, Communities and Local Government two-tier county and district councils are being abolished.

It means cities face being merged into unitary authorities, which require a new charter trustee to continue to use the city’s title and coat and arms.



Cities that fail to do this will lose their status.

Ancient Roman settlement Winchester – which served as the capital of England during Anglo-Saxon rule – risks being consumed by the creation of Mid Hampshire council.



Meanwhile, Canterbury – whose city council and mayor date from 1448 during Henry VI’s reign – risks being earmarked to become part of the East Kent authority.

Stoke-on-Trent, Chelmsford and Southend-on-Sea could also be affected.

Gareth Bacon, the shadow local government minister, said: “This is Labour’s constitutional wrecking ball.”

News.title: Teen, 16, set for court in Tyrone charged with murder of man, 61, two counts of attempted murder & threats to kill
News.content:
MURDER RAP Teen, 16, set for court in Tyrone charged with murder of man, 61, two counts of attempted murder & threats to kill

A 16-year old boy is set to appear in court charged with murder, two counts of attempted murder and threats to kill following the death of a 61-year-old man at a home in Co Tyrone.

The deceased’s wife and eight-year-old daughter were also found injured at the house in the Lisnahull Road area of Dungannon on Saturday.

Emergency services were dispatched to the scene at 10.55am on August 29 after police received a report of an ongoing “disturbance”.

The 61-year-old man was found deceased at the scene.





He was from Guinea-Bissau but had been living and working in the area for over 20 years.

His 48-year-old wife “had sustained non-life threatening injuries” but the couple’s daughter had been “severely injured”.

Both mother and daughter were airlifted to hospital and the girl’s condition remained “critical” over the weekend.

However, the PSNI confirmed this afternoon that the eight-year-old is now “stable” and her mother was discharged from hospital over the weekend.

Detectives from the Police Service of Northern Ireland’s Major Investigation Team said the teenager is due to appear before Omagh Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday, September 1.

The 16-year-old is charged with murder, two counts of attempted murder and threats to kill.

A spokesperson for the force said: “Detectives from the Police Service of Northern Ireland’s Major Investigation Team have charged a 16-year-old male to court following the death of a man in the Lisnahull Road area of Dungannon on Saturday, 29th August.

“The teenager is charged with murder, two counts of attempted murder and threats to kill.



“He is due to appear before Omagh Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday, 1st September.

“As is usual procedure, all charges will be reviewed by the Public Prosecution Service.”

News.title: Moment biker zooming down road crashes INSIDE open doors of bus before climbing back out
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a motorbike slams into a bus – but its open doors let the rider land safely inside.

Shocking footage shows how a bus’ open doors save the biker’s life.



The motorbike rider can be seen slamming into the bus at high speed at a junction in Buga, Colombia.

His bike is thrown in the air with the force of the crash.





It slams to the ground, with pieces breaking off at it does so.

But because the bus’s doors were open, the bike’s rider lands inside the bus.

CCTV from inside the vehicle shows the dramatic moment the biker flies into the bus.

He is flipped upside down, bouncing on his head on a seat.



The force breaks part of the bus door.

Miraculously, the rider remains conscious and can climb back out of the bus.

Just one passenger is seen inside the bus and the biker does not hit anyone else on his way in.



The driver stops the bus and the rider gets to his feet, seeming to escape without serious injury.

He was hospitalised to rule out any internal injuries, Infobae reported.

The terrifying crash took place at the crossing between seventh Street and 13th Avenue on Sunday.

The motorcyclist allegedly went through a red light before colliding with the bus.

It comes after a teen singer who starred on The Voice Kids was struck by a hit-and-run driver who fled the scene in Quindio, Colombia earlier this year.



Nicole Valeria Vargas Gomez, 19, died in the horror crash.

She appeared on Colombia’s edition of The Voice Kids in 2019 at just 12 years old.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

William Andres Paipa, 40, also died in the collision on the Circasia–Armenia road in western Colombia.

Cops said the pair were crossing the road when an unidentified vehicle smashed into them out of nowhere.

News.title: Putin prison ‘torturer’ blown up in suspected car bomb attack in occupied Ukraine
News.content:
A TORTURER of Ukrainian prisoners of war has been blown up in a suspected car bomb attack.

Dmitry Neyelov, deputy of the Olenivka camp in occupied Donetsk, is said to have tortured, beat and humiliated captured troops and civilians.



Reports suggested a bomb planted under the car exploded as Neyelov, 44, was getting into it.

Russian-led authorities have not disclosed the prison beast’s condition.



Two Ukrainian security service sources corroborated the car bombing.

In December 2024, the former head of Olenivka prison camp, Sergei Yevsyukov, 49, was killed in a car bombing in Donetsk.



He had faced a Ukrainian charge of mass murder over a 2022 explosion at Olenivka torture jail when at least 53 Ukrainian POWs were killed and 73 wounded.

Yevsyukov was also accused by the Ukrainian SBU intelligence service of involvement in the torture of more than 100 POWs.

Ukrainian agent have mounted sophisticated sabotage campaigns targeting Putin’s commanders, launching bomb and booby trap attacks in both Russian and occupied Ukraine.

News.title: SAS veterans of Troubles must be spared endless threat of legal repercussions, warns former Armed Forces minister
News.content:
SAS veterans who fought the IRA must not be left facing “endless legal jeopardy” decades after the Troubles, former Armed Forces Minister Al Carns has warned.

The ex-Royal Marine backed a new report warning ageing troops risk fresh investigations and possible prosecution under Labour’s Troubles Bill.



The Tories’ 2023 Legacy Act offered conditional immunity from prosecution to people accused of Troubles offences if they co-operated with the independent body investigating legacy cases.

Labour’s legislation would scrap that immunity and allow some civil claims and inquests to resume.



Mr Carns said: “No soldier should be above the law. Equally, no soldier should face endless legal jeopardy.

“Accountability is not the same as perpetual investigation. Justice is not served when the process itself becomes the punishment.



“That is why this paper matters. It gives voice to men who were there, making decisions almost impossible to recreate 40 or 50 years later.”

Policy Exchange is demanding ministers scrap the draft legislation, block new inquests and inquiries and be prepared to face down Strasbourg.

But speaking in Belfast last week, Andy Burnham said the Bill would be brought back to Parliament in the autumn.

A Government spokesperson said: “There was no equivalence between the lawful service of our veterans and the sickening deliberate actions of the terrorists.



“We will make that clear in the Bill, and introduce a package of new, effective and lawful protections for our former service personnel.”

News.title: Hospital ask schoolboy, 13, if he is PREGNANT before allowing X-ray as ‘ridiculous gender nonsense’ exposed
News.content:
'NONSENSE' Hospital ask schoolboy, 13, if he is PREGNANT before allowing X-ray as ‘ridiculous gender nonsense’ exposed

A BOY of 13 was asked if he was pregnant by an NHS nurse before being allowed to get an X-ray.

The lad had to sign a “nonsense” waiver confirming that he did not have a foetus growing inside him.

The teen was admitted to the Royal Hospital for Children in Edinburgh after getting injured playing rugby on Sunday.

His grandfather said: “He tried to laugh it off but seemed quite confused why anyone would need to ask if he was pregnant.





“It’s strange. Gender politics, particularly in Scotland just now, is creating quite a lot of division.

“The nurse threw her arms up as if to say ‘don’t blame me’.”

Posters state “all genders aged between 12 and 55” are to be asked if they are pregnant before an X-ray near the stomach.

Scottish Tory equalities spokeswoman Meghan Gallacher said: “John Swinney needs to tell NHS Lothian to stop this nonsense.”

Fiona McAnena of charity Sex Matters branded the situation “ridiculous”, adding: “Of course that clinician knew that the patient was a boy.”

The Scottish Government said it was a matter for NHS Lothian.

The health board was contacted for comment.

The outrage comes after revelations that a Scots charity has received hundreds of thousands of pounds to run sessions in Edinburgh teaching trans women to breastfeed babies.

LGBT Health and Wellbeing, which receives funding from the NHS, the Scottish government, and councils, says its “Queer Milk” group welcomes those “breastfeeding, chestfeeding or giving human milk to their baby in any amount … no matter what your feeding journey looks like.”



Its logo features a person with a beard, who is wrapped in a trans flag, holding a young baby to their bare chest.

Susan Smith, a director of For Women Scotland, told The Times: “To state the obvious, biological men cannot breastfeed babies.”

She added: “It is high time that the SNP government, NHS and Scottish councils stopped lavishing these activist groups with millions of pounds to promote such perverse ideas.”

News.title: Mel Stride and Priti Patel replaced in major Tory reshuffle
News.content:
Badenoch's reshuffle is intended to bring solutions to a number of problems.

First, she wants to retire those members of her top team that have had a relatively low profile, or who have not been delivering sufficient blows to both Labour and Reform UK.

Badenoch paid a warm tribute to Sir Mel but some recent polls suggested that Reform UK were more trusted on the economy than the Conservatives.

And that is something Kemi Badenoch felt needed to change.

Second, while familiar faces like Dame Priti were useful to have in the top team as they brought high-level government experience, they might also remind voters of the party they decisively rejected in 2024.

There has been a changing of the old guard, and Badenoch is now focusing on who can take the Conservatives into the next election - faced as she is by a new Labour leader and cabinet.

Third, she wants to focus on issues where Labour is perceived to be vulnerable.

One such area is defence spending and national security.

So as shadow foreign secretary she appointed Tom Tugendhat - a former security minister and current army reservist who served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He will work as part of a team with the shadow defence secretary.

Some opinion polls rate the economy as the most important issue for voters, above asylum and immigration, and again the Tory leader believes the government is vulnerable here, with sluggish growth.

So she has announced a new Conservative economic unit headed by Griffith, with his extensive business experience.

Coutinho as his deputy is seen as a rising Conservative star who has performed well in her previous role shadowing the former energy secretary Ed Miliband in the Commons, and as a potential future chancellor if the Conservatives were ever to recover electorally.

But the Tory leader has also included the former Conservative chairman and City Minister Richard Fuller in the unit, concentrating on fiscal responsibility and tax.

He will be deployed as an attack dog if - as she believes he will â the chancellor raises taxes in the Budget.

But the role will also underline that the Conservative leader is serious about making her sums add up, in contrast to her characterisation of Reform UK's plans as ill-thought out.

The question now though is whether Badenoch will change her own approach to political leadership.

While some of her top team may be seen as lacklustre, how much opportunity did they get to shine?

She tends to make the big announcements and is ubiquitous on the media.

If the Conservatives are to convince voters they are once again a government in waiting then the public will have to see that there is breadth and depth in the team that is shadowing current ministers.

News.title: Messi retires from international football with 'nothing left to give'
News.content:
In the race between athlete and time, there is only ever one winner.

Messi has pushed that defeat date back for a long, long time now. But I think maybe two things hastened it a little bit.

One is the recent death of his father and the other is - although it was 1-0 on the scoresheet - the World Cup final defeat by Spain. The distance between the two sides was so, so large.

You could see Messi, as he looked around the stadium almost thinking, "I don't think I can go through this again".

What memories he has given us. This little man has been a part of my life for 21 and a half years - but it had to end some time and that day is today.

Could Messi move back to Newell's Old Boys to finish his career? I think there are two problems there.

One is moving his family back to the city of Rosario. It is a little bit provincial, and there are problems with violence there. True, his old mate Angel di Maria has done it with Rosario Central without too many problems. But I think Messi would worry about taking his family back into a goldfish bowl.

The other is that the level of football might not attract him quite so much. It could happen for just a few games, as a kind of romantic end to his career. He has talked about it plenty of times in the past. But I imagine Inter Miami might be the end.

Who knows? He will stop playing when he feels like it. If he doesn't feel like going on until the end of 2028, he could knock it on the head before then.

We will have to see. Inter Miami fans are the lucky ones. They will get the last drops of this little man's genius.

News.title: Hundreds remember Heaton Park synagogue attack victims at memorial event
News.content:
The Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner were among about 800 people who attended a memorial event for the victims and survivors of last year's Heaton Park synagogue attack.

Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed, and three others injured, as they tried to defend their place of worship from attacker Jihad al-Shamie on 2 October 2025.

Relatives of the bereaved and some of the survivors were among the speakers at Monday's service of remembrance at the synagogue in Manchester.

Prior to the event, Rabbi Daniel Walker said the Jewish community feels less safe now than it did immediately after the attack.

He said rising antisemitism, combined with a lack of action to "deal with core problems", had left many members of Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation â and British Jews more widely â feeling increasingly vulnerable.

Two seats remained empty for the service, bearing the names of Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby.

News.title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Bank of England chief warns
News.content:
The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.

Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.

In an open letter to finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".

Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.

"The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more, but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration, in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers, in a way that could amplify a future market correction," he said.

Bailey has called on those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis".

Bailey, who was writing in his capacity as chairman of the Financial Stability Board international watchdog (FSB), expressed concern about the "volatility" prompted by the effect of energy supply shocks caused by the US-Iran war.

His warning comes several months after UK Chancellor John Healey announced a Â£100m fund aimed at backing British AI start-ups.

That is part of the government's efforts to grow the country's "sovereign AI" capacity, developing homegrown AI technology to ensure the UK is not dependent on services from abroad.

Ministers want to see companies compete for the funding to help tackle challenges like cutting waiting lists in the NHS and bolstering cybersecurity and defence.

A UK government spokesperson said its new AI economics institute was working with international partners to build "a stronger shared understanding of how AI is transforming economies around the world."

"The institute is the first government-backed body of its kind focused on AI's economic impact, helping policymakers understand what AI means for growth, productivity, jobs and public services as the technology develops at pace," the spokesperson said.

But there is growing concern that AI companies are increasingly developing models that can easily override the safeguarding systems of banks and financial centres.

News.title: Notting Hill Carnival revels in 60th anniversary celebrations
News.content:
Notting Hill Carnival has celebrated its 60th anniversary with three days of revelry fuelled by drummers, dancers and colourful costumes.

Europe's biggest street party continued on Monday with the adults' parade, live bands, more than 30 static sound systems and the scent of jerk chicken floating through the air.

The carnival, which celebrates Caribbean culture and history, was first held in west London in 1966.

"We are the greatest when we come together as people," said Jackie, from Jay Dee's Catering, who has been trading at the event for 15 years with her family business.

News.title: Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo
News.content:
A weak orangutan was found laying on the ground in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island.

Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from wildfires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands.

The wildfires have destroyed part of the habitat of hundreds of orangutans and risking the survival of the species.

"The situation is quite critical", said Karmele Llano Sanchez, CEO of the wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).

Sanchez said the fires are "leaving [the orangutans] without any food or water".

The orangutan found will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment and will be released back into the wild after recovery, according to YIARI.

News.title: Summer 2026 expected to be declared UK's hottest on record
News.content:
There is something striking about the way the UK's summer temperature record is being broken.

In a climate that isn't changing, new records should generally become progressively rarer, because every time a record falls, it raises the bar for the next one.

Instead, all five of the UK's hottest summers on record have occurred since 2000, external. And until last year, the margins between them were tiny: the four hottest were separated by just five hundredths of a degree.

Then came 2025. The record jumped by 0.34C. Now, just a year later, it looks like that record has gone too.

"Record-shattering" sounds like the kind of language we journalists would use. In fact, it is a term climate scientists use for records broken by unusually large margins. Research suggests, external these big jumps become more likely if the climate is warming rapidly.

So why is this happening so quickly here? The UK sits on the western edge of Europe, the fastest-warming continent on Earth - warming at roughly twice the global rate.

There are a few reasons for that. Land heats up faster than the oceans, parts of Europe stretch into the rapidly warming Arctic, and changes in weather patterns have favoured more frequent and intense summer heatwaves.

Scientists are still working out exactly how much each factor contributes, but the result is clear: the background climate in which British weather happens is getting warmer.

None of this means the UK will break its summer record every year. Weather will always give us cooler summers as well as hotter ones. But the pattern is becoming unmistakable: records that once marked the extreme edge of the UK's climate are being overtaken with remarkable speed.

So the question is not whether the UK will experience summers hotter than this one. It is how often they will come - and how much hotter they might be.

News.title: New super flu vaccine rollout begins as NHS regroups from 'busiest summer'
News.content:
Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual, external with the Super-K strain.

Super flu is not a medical term, and it does not mean the virus has become harder to treat, just that people are yet to build up immunity against it.

Flu vaccines are updated annually to ensure they are a good match for the type of flu circulating. Influenza viruses constantly mutate and experts have to predict these changes ahead of time.

This year's vaccine has had a few tweaks, including one to better match subclade K.

It is not clear when flu will hit this year, and whether it will be a bad season. But experts often look to southern hemisphere countries, like Australia and New Zealand, to gain a better understanding of how the UK could be affected.

Their flu season peaks in July or August, and these countries have so far had a relatively mild year in terms of cases.

Dr Amanda Doyle from NHS England said it was best to be cautious.

"Last year's flu season came early and was made worse by a new variant, which had a major impact for patients and put enormous pressure on urgent and emergency care services across the country," she said.

"With the NHS experiencing its busiest summer on record, staff have started preparing for this winter earlier than ever â and with services already under significant pressure, it is vital that everyone offered the vaccine comes forward."

News.title: More cells being built within prisons to help tackle overcrowding
News.content:
The government is spending Â£110m on creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

The money, which has been "fast-tracked from existing budgets", will be used to speed up the construction of hundreds of new prison places, the Ministry of Justice has said.

Existing space within prisons, such as unused office space, laundry rooms and storage areas, will be converted into cells.

The announcement comes at a time of crisis for the prison system, which is close to maximum capacity, with the government being criticised for its handling of an early release scheme.

Lord Chancellor and Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government would be "getting spades in the ground quicker to deliver thousands more places to lock up dangerous criminals and keep the public safe".

Norris said: "This government is serious about fixing the broken prison system we inherited, which is why we've already delivered more than 3,200 prison places in just two years.

"We're now investing to boost these efforts further."

Investment to create more prison spaces was announced as part of the government's 2025 spending review, which covered plans for the period from 2024â25 to 2029â30.

As part of this, it allocated a Â£7bn capital investment to create 14,000 prison places by 2031.

The Â£110m announced on Monday is not a new investment, and is being drawn from money previously announced.

The Lord Chancellor will update Parliament on Tuesday, setting out changes to upcoming sentencing reforms which will block hundreds more dangerous offenders from earlier release.

Measures also include plans to remove foreign national offenders more quickly, and ending the historic injustice of Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences in a way that balances fairness and public safety, the government has said.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "It is absurd for Labour to talk about a 'prison building boom' when there are 700 fewer prison places than a year ago.

"In a matter of weeks thousands of dangerous criminals will be released onto our streets thanks to Andy Burnham, including perpetrators of some of the most vile crimes."

An extra Â£18.9m investment into vital services for victims will also be announced to Parliament.

The services will provide the specialist emotional and practical support needed to help victims move on with their lives, according to the Ministry of Justice (MoJ).

This money will be reprioritised from existing budgets and will be on top of the Â£550m already announced by government for this support.

The MoJ also announced that it had signed a contract to start building a new jail for 1,700 hundred inmates in Lancashire.

News.title: Boy, 16, charged with murder and attempted murder
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been charged with the murder of a man in Dungannon, County Tyrone, and the attempted murder of two other people in the same incident.

The body of the dead man, who was 61, was found alongside his injured eight-year-old daughter at a house on Lisnahull Road on Saturday morning,

The man's 48-year-old wife sustained non-life threatening injuries during the attack.

The teenage boy, who has also been charged with making threats to kill, is due to appear before Omagh Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Man dies near Notting Hill Carnival after entering canal
News.content:
A man died near Notting Hill Carnival in London on Monday afternoon, the Metropolitan Police have confirmed.

Police officers had attempted to stop the man, believed to be in his 20s, as he approached the event. He fled on foot with officers in pursuit, and entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens a short time later, the force said.

Taken to hospital by ambulance the man was pronounced dead a short time later.

Cdr Claire Smart said: "This is a tragic incident and our thoughts are with the loved ones of the man who has lost his life."

The Met Police said officers had attempted to stop the man at about 15:19 BST near Harrow Road.

The man entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens, off Kensal Road.

Officers and members of the public went in after him and pulled him from the water, police said, and officers immediately started CPR.

Paramedics were called and continued treatment at the canal side before taking the man to a central London hospital. He was pronounced dead at 16:43.

The Met Police said on Monday night that urgent enquiries were ongoing to locate and inform his next of kin.

Smart, gold commander for the Notting Hill Festival, said: "Any death following contact with the police is passed to the Independent Office for Police Conduct so the circumstances can be fully investigated.

"I would encourage everyone to avoid speculation while this work takes place."

She added: "I acknowledge the efforts of the officers and members of the public who entered the canal to rescue this man. I know they will be devastated that his life couldn't ultimately be saved."

The Met Police said the two days of the festival had passed "largely without incident".

There were two assaults with knives - one stabbing and one slashing. Neither resulted in life-threatening injuries.

On Monday evening, police said there had been 315 arrests that day, bringing the total number of arrests to 560.

News.title: Holy Cross school dispute was 'hatred at its worst'
News.content:
The priest who helped shield schoolgirls during the 2001 Holy Cross dispute has said the "hurt" of that ordeal could happen again.

Speaking on the 25th anniversary of Holy Cross, Fr Aidan Troy said that possibility is what keeps him "devoted to dialogue, to conversation, to searching for justice and to caring about people".

Fr Aidan said the sectarian dispute was "hatred at its worst".

It happened in north Belfast when loyalist protesters tried to block the route taken by Holy Cross school pupils and their parents, who were from a Catholic background, on their walk to class.

Following the initial violence, the police and Army put up crash barriers to keep a corridor route open for the Holy Cross pupils.

The images of terrified schoolgirls having to run the gauntlet between lines of armoured police officers in order to get to their primary school were beamed around the world.

Protestants claimed that Catholics were attacking their homes and said the school protest was their way of highlighting their concerns.

Stones, bottles, fireworks and even a blast bomb were thrown during weeks of unrest.

Fr Aidan, who was parish priest in Ardoyne at the time, told BBC News NI that "none of us want to see hatred".

News.title: Nursery fined after baby boy burned by bleach
News.content:
Defence advocate Barry Smith KC said the first priority of a nursery was the safety and wellbeing of the children there.

He added: "It is of the utmost regret from all involved - from the director and all staff - that this accident occurred and injury was caused to a young child."

In a statement released via law firm Digby Brown, the family said: "We've had to wait five years for Little Dreams Nursery to admit what happened to our son was their fault but we don't feel the severity of his injuries have been acknowledged.

"We trusted them to take care of him and for such an injury to happen to a 10-month-old baby is indefensible.

"In the months and years that followed, we had to watch our boy deal with the consequences of something that was never his fault. No parent should have to experience that, but we are thankful what happened hasn't had a more serious or longer-lasting impact."

The statement concluded: "Today we close the most horrific chapter of our lives and we want to thank everyone who has supported us during this time and now request our privacy as we move forward."

Little Dreams said the safety, wellbeing and care of every child entrusted to them was of the "highest priority".

"We deeply regret that this incident was able to occur and are profoundly sorry for the distress and impact it has had on the child and their family," the nursery said.

News.title: Emergency measures needed to stop teachers quitting, say Lib Dems
News.content:
Burnt out teachers urgently need better working hours and more support to stop them leaving the profession, the Liberal Democrats say, as the new term approaches.

Nearly half of the teachers surveyed by the party in England said they were planning to quit the classroom in the next five years, with many saying they felt overworked and stressed.

The Lib Dems are urging new Education Secretary Lucy Powell to fully fund teachers' pay, rather than raiding school budgets to cover increases, and to bring in limits on overtime.

The Department for Education said last year saw the lowest rate of teachers leaving the profession since 2010 but acknowledged there was "more to do".

The survey asked more than 900 teachers, headteachers and Special Educational Needs Coordinators (SENCOs) across England how long they planned to stay in teaching.

Almost half of those in post said they were considering leaving teaching in the next five years, while one in ten were planning to spend less than a year in the job.

More than three quarters of those surveyed, which included former teachers, said they had felt "frequently or constantly burnt out" while at work.

Respondents cited high workloads on marking, lesson preparation and other tasks, which they said gave them less time in the classroom.

The Liberal Democrats' schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said this pointed to a government that is "not listening" to the profession.

"We rely on teachers to educate our children, the least we can do is make sure they want to come back after the summer," she said.

Teacher retention is a challenge successive governments have had to grapple with.

The National Education Union (NEU) reported that 4 in 10 teachers were planning to quit over "huge workloads and excessive accountability" in 2019.

This latest survey was also conducted with the help of the NEU, as well as the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL).

"After over a decade of austerity and chronic underfunding in our schools the system is on its knees" said the NEU's general secretary Daniel Kebede.

"The new academic year is the perfect time for Andy Burnham to signal a fresh start for our schools" he added.

"That means fully funding the pay award and properly funding all our schools and colleges to stem the recruitment and retention crisis and give children the education they deserve."

"As Lucy Powell enters her first term as education secretary the Liberal Democrats are calling for her first act to be to introduce an emergency package of 'back to school' measures to face this crisis head on," Voaden said.

The Lib Dem proposals include the government fully funding teacher's pay, which will increase in England by 3.5% from September, with an additional 3% the year after.

Currently, half of the pay increase will come from existing school budgets.

The party is also calling for proper enforcement of teacher's legally mandated working hours, the introduction of reasonable limits on overtime, and for all schools to be required to introduce flexible working policies.

The party did not identify where funding might come from to pay for the policies.

An education department spokesperson said: "We know teachers do an incredible job and we're determined to make sure that dedication is matched with the right support.

"Last year saw one of the lowest rates of teachers leaving the profession since 2010, and a record number of teachers returning to the classroom, but we know there's more to do.

"We're taking action by announcing pay awards of almost 17% over two years, funding schools to improve maternity pay and offering targeted support to normalise flexible working and manageable workloads so that more teachers stay in our classrooms and thrive."

News.title: Business groups urge Swinney to scrap 'ineffective' food price cap plan
News.content:
The SRC said the policy also risked forcing small shops which are not covered by the proposed legislation to be uncompetitive.

"Scottish consumers benefit from the most affordable food prices in western Europe," MacDonald-Russell added.

"We know food price inflation is a problem, but the best model to deal with it is the one we have right now and price caps are going to make that worse.

"It is giving a false promise that it is going to be able to help with something.

"In reality, there is as good a chance it is going to make the overall cost of a shopping basket higher, because the cost of the scheme as well as the cap have to be absorbed by businesses."

It is thought the proposals would require changes to the UK Internal Markets Act of 2020, which was brought in after Brexit to prevent trade barriers and regulatory divergence between England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland as powers returned from the EU.

The Scottish government said helping people with the cost of living was a "top priority".

A spokesperson added: "Ministers have welcomed engagement with stakeholders, including retailers, food producers and farmers on proposals for food price controls.

"A consultation will launch shortly for further views."

News.title: Twenty-seven people rescued from rollercoaster
News.content:
Firefighters have rescued 27 people who were stuck on a rollercoaster for up to three hours.

Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service said it was called to the Wipeout ride at Pleasurewood Hills in Lowestoft at 13:36 BST.

An eyewitness described what appeared to be a power cut affecting multiple rides at the attraction, and video footage showed the moment the carriages came to a stop about 15m (49ft) in the air.

Pleasurewood Hills said it was "incredibly grateful for the way [the riders] handled" the situation and to their families for their "understanding and patience".

"We appreciate that being stuck on a ride is not something anyone expects when visiting us."

News.title: Woman shot dead by police in Times Square after fatally stabbing one and injuring another
News.content:

A woman has been shot dead by police in the heart of Times Square in Manhattan after she allegedly killed a person and injured another in a stabbing attack that lasted mere seconds.

Pamela Cisneros, a 49-year-old Queens resident armed with two knives, stabbed a 68-year-old man and a 32-year-old woman just before 4:30 p.m. ET on Monday, as tourists filled the streets and New Yorkers were on their evening commute home, according to police.

Cisneros pulled the knives out, waved them around and then stabbed the man who had just exited a subway station with his wife, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a Monday night press conference.

The man was struck in the right side of his abdomen, Tisch said. The commissioner said Cisneros then approached a 32-year-old woman and stabbed her in the abdomen.

Both incidents, which happened 20 seconds apart from each other, appear to be “random and unprovoked” attacks, Tisch said.

open image in gallery A woman has been shot dead by police in the heart of Times Square in Manhattan after she allegedly killed a person and injured another in a stabbing attack that lasted mere seconds ( WABC-TV via AP )

open image in gallery Pamela Cisneros, a 49-year-old Queens resident armed with two knives, stabbed a 68-year-old man and a 32-year-old woman just before 4:30 p.m. ET on Monday, according to police ( AFP via Getty Images )

Witnesses flagged down NYPD officers who confronted the woman. For four minutes, officers talked with Cisneros, demanding she drop the two knives she was still holding, but she refused, Tisch said.

Cisneros told police, “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” according to Tisch.

As the suspect waved the knives at the officers, they deployed their tasers, but she continued to move toward them, Tisch said.

Two officers then pulled out their guns and opened fire at Cisneros, striking her, according to Tisch. She later died at the hospital.

The woman Cisneros allegedly stabbed also died at the hospital. The 68-year-old man was in stable condition as of Monday night. The identities of the victims have yet to be revealed.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at the press conference, “I ask New Yorkers to join me in holding the victim in our thoughts and wishing them a full recovery.”

open image in gallery When officers confronted Cisneros, she refused to put down the knives, allegedly telling them, ‘I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you’ ( AFP via Getty Images )

open image in gallery Officers have recovered the suspect’s knives ( NYPD )

A motive for the attack remains unclear at this time, but police do not believe it was terrorism-related. Officers have recovered the suspect’s knives.

“Cisneros has a documented mental health history with the NYPD with one incident in 2018 and one in 2019,” Tisch said, adding that officers have never arrested her.

Tisch defended the NYPD’s actions during the attack, telling reporters, “At any given moment, there are thousands of New Yorkers, commuters, tourists, families, workers moving through these streets.

“Our officers were confronted with a rapidly evolving threat with countless innocent people around them. In that moment, they did what we trained them to do.”

open image in gallery A motive for the stabbing remains unclear at this time, but Cisneros has a ‘documented mental health history,’ according to police ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Mamdani thanked the NYPD officers 'who stepped in and prevented a horrific attack from becoming even worse' ( Reuters )

Mamdani thanked the NYPD officers “who stepped in and prevented a horrific attack from becoming even worse.”

Tisch said there has already been an increased police presence in Times Square this summer with festivities surrounding America’s 250th birthday and the World Cup, “and we will continue to ensure that there is a heavy police footprint in this area.”

Authorities have closed off several city blocks as they continue to investigate the stabbing. Metal barricades and police tape have also cordoned off the crime scene.

The NYPD told travelers at around 4:50 p.m. to expect delays in the area.

Mamdani said there will also be an internal NYPD investigation, as part of standard protocol.

This is a developing story...

A summer when Arsenal targeted Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez seems set to end without them luring a Galactico of a forward but Mikel Arteta may have other ways of adding a new dimension to his attack. Perhaps typically, given the Arsenal manager’s obsession with accumulating defenders, it involves a man whose day job is at the back.

But Riccardo Calafiori got their season off to a flying start with a goal after 23 seconds in the Community Shield. And, when Arsenal seemed short of incision at Villa Park, it was their charismatic, compelling left-back who provided the element of unpredictability required. By surging forward to supply Bukayo Saka with a simple finish, Calafiori maintained Arsenal’s 100 percent start to the campaign. If part of the test is to improve upon last year, in one respect they already have: defeated at Villa Park in December, they were victorious now.

open image in gallery The buccaneering Calafiori provided the breakthrough with his low cross for Saka’s winner ( Reuters )

“That image when the players were on the floor, totally battered, it was a really difficult one to take and we used that,” said Arteta. This was cathartic and came from the collective. “It was a squad victory,” Arteta said.

It was forged more by perspiration than inspiration. If Arteta had seemed to take the handbrake off in eviscerating first Manchester City in Cardiff and then Coventry at home, this was a night when it was back on. Arsenal can win in different ways, but many of them involve a clean sheet and Aston Villa finished without a shot on target. The travelling Gunners’ eventual chorus of “1-0 to the champions” was a retort to their Villa counterparts chanting that they would never be able to call themselves champions of Europe.

Maybe, maybe not. But Saka’s second goal in as many league games showed Arsenal already had the potential to kick on; if Saka, Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard can stay fit, each could offer more goals than last year. And while they are yet to land a left winger, Gabriel Martinelli’s departure could afford Eberechi Eze the chance for more minutes on the flank.

He came on at half-time for Christos Tzolis who, after a fine start to his Arsenal career, was booked then hooked. Eze offered an indication of what he can offer to help set up the goal, releasing the underlapping Calafiori, who centred for Saka. “Ebs comes on and makes the difference to win the game,” said Arteta.

It was a personal comeback, with Eze culpable for Matty Cash’s goal at Villa Park last year, and a swift response to a collective disappointment. Five minutes earlier, Arsenal were initially awarded a penalty when Ian Maatsen’s nudge in the back sent Saka flying. A VAR review later and the offence was adjudged just outside the box. Odegaard dinked the resulting free kick just wide.

Until then, the goalmouth action consisted of Villa rattling the frame. Emi Buendia, the late match-winner last season, was almost an early scorer, his ferocious, first-time shot thudding into the Arsenal bar.

Buendia had begun Villa’s Premier League campaign as a false nine at Brighton. They had a genuine striker here, the £47.5m Nicolas Jackson parachuted in for a debut after his move from Chelsea. He showed flashes of pace without getting a chance.

open image in gallery Arsenal shut out new-look Aston Villa, who offered a debut to striker Nicolas Jackson ( Getty )

Perhaps the more auspicious bow came at the other end of the pitch, even if the statistics will not reflect it. Goalkeeper Zion Suzuki made fine saves from Declan Rice’s header and Havertz’s shot, when the German was clear on goal; he was not to know that, with the flag raised for different reasons, neither would have counted. The Japan international cut an authoritative figure and looked a worthy successor to the sold Emi Martinez.

The most notable bow, however, came in the closing stages. It was certainly the most audible introduction, with boos apparent when Ezri Konsa was on the ball. A stalwart of Villa’s best team of the 21st century had decamped to London amid the exodus. The fixture list may have been unkind to him, giving him an immediate return to Villa. Even with William Saliba and Jurrien Timber injured, Arteta had enough defenders to start without the £51m man.

open image in gallery Saka scored his second goal of the season to earn Arsenal victory ahead of next week’s showdown with Chelsea ( PA )

He also benefited from having players already accustomed to lining up alongside each other. This was change against continuity, with the upheaval at Villa versus Arsenal’s summer of stability and solidity. The stands at Villa Park contained Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye, perhaps the last arrivals in a recruitment drive that has cost a quarter of a billion pounds, all funded by sales.

“We are happy how we are closing the window,” said Unai Emery. “We are not regretting anything.” His Villa were far better than they were against Brighton, though that is not saying much. They made that rout look like an aberration. “We performed like we planned and we competed like we planned,” added Emery. “The result, of course, is painful.”

He is reconstructing his side. Villa Park can whip up an atmosphere for a night game even when the North Stand is a building site but Arsenal are sufficiently battle-hardened they could cope with it. This was not a statement performance but, in its own way, it may prove a statement result. "To lose in Villa Park is not normal," said Emery. It may have been a good time to face a team in transition but, thanks to Calafiori and Saka, Arsenal ensured it was as they pocketed the points.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader during the Trump administration.

Driscoll and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s working relationship had endured months of tension during his time in the job, reported Reuters and CNN.

No reason was given for the departure of Driscoll, who is a friend of Vice President JD Vance, but tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have been widely reported. It marks the latest in a series of shakeups of the military leadership, with the Army especially seeing major upheaval.

“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.

"The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

Dan Driscoll leaves after 18-months in the job with Iran conflict still dragging on ( Reuters )

A U.S. Army official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Driscoll spoke with President Donald Trump on the current state of the Army and submitted his resignation. The official did not provide additional details. The Pentagon referred questions to the Army. Driscoll's resignation was reported earlier Monday by The Wall Street Journal.

Hegseth suddenly ousted the service's top uniformed leader, Gen. Randy George, in April, while the Army’s commander in Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down in June.

Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who has made a meteoric rise under Hegseth, took George's place as the Army’s acting chief of staff. Under LaNeve, the service is pulling the plug on a drone modernization program that Driscoll had heralded. An Army unit based in Europe was building its own drones before LaNeve directed it to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion, officials said in August.

Driscoll was a George ally and lamented his departure, along with both Republican and Democratic lawmakers. He told Congress in April that he and his family drove to George's house following his resignation “and we all gave him a hug.”

“That being said, the civilian leadership, the design of our system, is that they get to pick the leaders that they want," Driscoll added.

Driscoll is an Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vance, whom Driscoll met at Yale Law School. When nominating Driscoll in 2024, Trump called him “a disruptor and change agent.”

As Army secretary, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. He was also a major force behind trying to cut the red tape for military contractors to quickly develop more drones and counter-drone capabilities as warfare rapidly changes around the world.

The Senate confirmed him in February 2025, voting 66-28, following an Armed Services Committee hearing that was largely unconfrontational and focused on how the Army could modernize its systems, improve recruiting and beef up the military industrial base.

Driscoll noted that his father and grandfather served in the Army and he vowed to be a secretary focused on the needs of soldiers. According to the Army, Driscoll served as an armor officer from August 2007 to March 2011, deploying to Iraq from October 2009 to July 2010.

He also ran unsuccessfully in the Republican primary for a North Carolina congressional seat in 2020, getting about 8% of the vote in a crowded field of candidates.

His departure comes after Hegseth ousted several other generals and admirals, including the head of the Navy.

The Pentagon abruptly announced in April that Navy Secretary John Phelan was leaving the job, becoming the first head of a military service to depart during Trump’s second term.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

President Donald Trump said he was reviewing the United States’ position on the British sovereignty over the Falkland islands, in a move that will raise alarm for Labour ministers.

It follows reports last week that the US administration was prepared to oppose British rule of the overseas territory as an incentive to encourage Andy Burnham to increase defence spending,

The islands are administered by the UK but are claimed by Argentina, whose president is an ally of Mr Trump.

"I always review every ⁠position,” Mr Trump told reporters on Monday, when asked about the islands' sovereignty. “That's just one of ​many,” he added.

A senior US official told The Telegraph that Pentagon officials were understood to be reviewing the commitments of Nato allies in a bid to ensure they commit 5 per cent to defence spending, with the UK to get “special attention” under the assessment.

They said that changing America’s stance on the UK’s claim to the Falklands was a possibility in incentivising the government.

Mr Trump’s comments from the Oval Office on Monday were his first publicly on the matter.

Shortly after, in a published interview with The Times, chancellor John Healey inisited he was “100 per cent” committed to delivering a defence spending target of 3 per cent of GDP, adding he would set out the plan at the spring review.

open image in gallery U.S. President Donald Trump spoke for the first time publicaly on the Falkland Islands ( Getty )

Mr Healey, who also told The Times he had not heard the suggestion the US could side with Argentina on the islands’ sovereignty, said: “The Falkland Islands are British. The Falkland Islands will remain British as long as the Falkland Islands want that to happen.”

Also in response to the report in The Telegraph, over the weekend the UK government reiterated its position by asserting its “long-standing and unwavering” commitment to ensure the islands remain a British Overseas Territory in line with the wishes of the Falkland islanders.

A spokesperson said: “The UK is playing a central role in Nato and strengthening collective defence across Europe. We are Nato's third largest cash spender on defence and the only European NATO member to commit our nuclear deterrent to the alliance.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham faces pressure from Mr Trump over defence spending ( PA Wire )

That report followed an earlier threat made in April, when a leaked internal Pentagon email suggested that the US could review Britain’s claim to the Falklands in retaliation for a lack of support in the Iran war.

Tensions have been building between Mr Trump and Europe for months as he has hit out at several countries for not pulling their weight in contributing to Nato and in supporting US military action against Iran.

Throughout the conflict Trump has alternately threatened to pull troops from Europe and to have the US quit the Nato alliance.

An Oklahoma man has been charged with murder following a large explosion at a marijuana extraction facility that killed two of his employees and damaged surrounding businesses, prosecutors said Monday.

Ryan Bassham, 35, turned himself in this weekend after being charged with two counts of first-degree murder in Thursday’s blast at Solos Extracts near Tulsa, authorities said. The explosion around 1 a.m. partially tore the roof from a building, crumpled doors and scattered debris around an industrial park.

Bassham was booked into a Tulsa jail and released after posting a $2 million bond. Court records did not list an attorney for Bassham, and phone numbers for him and the business could not immediately be found. The Associated Press left a message with a law firm that previously represented Bassham.

The two victims, Michael Newman and Stephen Scott, both worked for Bassham, said Adam Jones, spokesman for the Tulsa County district attorney's office. He said prosecutors believe the employees were unlawfully manufacturing hazardous chemicals that wound up creating an explosion.

A fire marshal told authorities the business was seeking an updated marijuana license and narcotics registration, according to court records. Medical marijuana is legal in Oklahoma.

According to court documents, Newman told a paramedic on the way to the hospital that the area had not been well ventilated and that the explosion happened after he unplugged something. He was conscious when paramedics arrived but later died at the hospital.

No one else was harmed in the explosion, but multiple nearby businesses were damaged, authorities said.

According to court records, investigators believe Bassham bought Solos Extracts earlier this year. A fire marshal who inspected the facility in January found an outdated fire suppression system and equipment commonly used in marijuana manufacturing. The marshal returned to the facility after the explosion and found large amounts of liquid propane and other hazardous material that were not there in January, according to court records.

The owner of a neighboring marijuana manufacturing business told police he spoke with Bassham earlier this year after noticing high levels of carbon dioxide on a building sensor. He described being lightheaded when he walked into the building.

News.title: Arsenal maintain perfect start but lack firepower of rivals
News.content:
Bukayo Saka maintained Arsenal’s perfect start to the season, but Mikel Arteta appeared to acknowledge that the Premier League champions are in danger of leaving themselves short in attack.

There is still time for Arteta to add another forward to his squad and whether he does so or not could be important, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday night.

Having sold Leandro Trossard and with Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus on the verge of moves away, Arsenal appear light of forward options.

Lyon winger Malick Fofana has been offered to the club, but he is an underwhelming target given Morgan Rogers and Vinícius Júnior were pursued earlier in the summer.

“We are trying to improve the squad,” said Arsenal head coach Arteta. “Until Tuesday night, we’re going to try to do that. I’ve been disconnected from the world for 24 hours because I think my energy and focus has to be on the match. I will give it (my energy) now.”

Asked if he currently has enough depth in forward positions, Arteta added: “It depends if everybody is fit or not. We know that the depth has to be really big when you are fighting for four competitions. So we’re going to try to do that.”

News.title: Despite ugly ending to his Argentina career, Messi redefined beautiful game
News.content:
To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely-scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pele’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

News.title: Manchester United’s attack may be their best form of defence this season
News.content:
Is attack going to be Manchester United’s best form of defence this season?

There was plenty to like going forward, particularly once United had nudged their way in front after their second lucky break of what had hitherto looked like being a tricky afternoon.

Give this team a little space and they have the attacking players to inflict some serious damage, none more so than Bruno Fernandes who, just five days after collecting the PFA Players’ Player of the Year award, scored a hat-trick in what was another inspired performance.

Ipswich Town will testify to that after a sobering second half when it felt like United were going to score with every raid forward and, for a time, even threaten to equal the nine goals they scored against the promoted side at this ground 31 years ago.

In the returning Marcus Rashford, whom manager Michael Carrick likened to a “new signing”, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and, of course, Fernandes, United have an intriguing blend of attacking players. Throw in Kobbie Mainoo who, on another day, would have stolen the headlines with an imperious display in central midfield, and one thing United are not lacking for is creativity.

News.title: Robinson’s Victorian-style bowling figures secure series victory over Pakistan
News.content:
The only missing aspect was a five-fer which would have brought a 100th Test wicket. Even so, his career average is now 19.53, the best for England since Frank Tyson of those with 50 or more wickets.

Mr Nude Nuts, as Matthew Hayden called him, could be devastating against Australia and, like Root the captain, deserves to be judged on what happens in his second incarnation rather than what went before.

Robinson’s pace has lingered around the 79mph mark and inevitably that throws up Rob Key’s assertion you cannot succeed in Test cricket bowling in the 70s with the keeper standing up. Key was referring to county bowlers pitching it up and relying on the Dukes ball to do the rest.

It was thrown in his face in Australia but Michael Neser and Scott Boland are not county trundlers: they extract more energy off the pitch than that.

Robinson is also no dobber. His high release point combined with a mastery of length means he is always threatening the top of off stump. He also knows which way the ball is going to nip, giving no clues to the batsmen due to his sleight of hand skills.

With Jamie Smith improving under the tutelage of Sarah Taylor, he can operate with the keeper standing up which pins batsmen in the crease, bringing all modes of dismissals into play. Robinson was as effective with the new ball as the old: his two seven-over spells were two for 13 and two for 11.

How snarling Robinson adds edge and precision

At 32, he has become a combination of Stuart Broad and James Anderson, although down on their pace with the height and bounce of the former, and tricks of the latter. He can move the new ball further either way than Anderson or Broad but the question is whether he has their durability and sheer competitiveness.

He has not been tested this summer by pitches or opponents. He has not bowled more than 18 overs in an innings and was injured when England played on the best batting pitch at the Oval. He was not trusted at Trent Bridge because the old management had burned their fingers before. That decision may well have cost the coach his job.

Like Broad and Anderson he has a snarl too, sending Abdullah Shafique on his way with a word or two. There was no need for that but maybe it was just a carried away reaction to bowling an absolute beauty that angled in, seamed away and hit the top of off.

News.title: Chelsea are great entertainers but possess clear weakness
News.content:
Xabi Alonso takes charge of his first home Premier League game in charge of Chelsea as they host Brighton at Stamford Bridge. Both sides were in action in two different competitions on Thursday night. Chelsea reached the League Cup third round as they beat Luton 2-0 at Stamford Bridge, with former Brighton man Danny Welbeck scoring on his debut. Brighton meanwhile confirmed their place in the Conference League group stages with a 4-0 aggregate win over Tromso.

Chelsea began their Premier League campaign last Monday in a west London derby against Fulham at Craven Cottage, winning 3-2 in Alonso’s first game as Chelsea boss. Enzo Fernandez was not involved in Chelsea’s squad against Luton on Thursday and has been heavily linked with a move to Manchester City. Alonso was asked about Enzo’s absence on Thursday and did not confirm whether the Argentine would be involved today.

“It was just because of the game today [on Thursday] and we have other players who need minutes,” Alonso said. “[On Wednesday], in the afternoon. It is a decision that I took. Enzo is a good professional. He is training well and I have nothing to say about this. It was just decisions that we have to take thinking about the game that we were playing tonight [Thursday]. We will see for Sunday [today].”

Brighton began their Premier League campaign in emphatic style as they thrashed Aston Villa 4-0 at home seven days ago. Jack Hinshelwood scored twice in that game but will now miss a number of weeks with an ankle injury. They are also without Yankuba Minteh, who has been linked with a move to Liverpool this summer but is unavailable due to injury.

“When the window is closed I demand from him [Minteh] that he is fully committed to this club,” Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler said. “There are dreams and wishes for players, but in the end we always need to figure out what is best for the club.

“We have had an exchange with him. At the moment he is definitely a Brighton player. It is very important to understand his thoughts but also our planning. As a club we try to develop players. The last few years have shown that the whole environment gave him a lot of trust and belief that he is capable of having this progress. It is always a give and take and he has gotten a lot from us.”

Brighton won both Premier League meetings last season, winning 3-1 in this fixture last September. Brighton have won five of their last eight top-flight meetings with Chelsea. Team news from Stamford Bridge to follow shortly.

News.title: Moses Itauma lifted out of ring after losing IBF title bout to Filip Hrgovic
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of the heavyweight clash between Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic.

Itauma is on the cusp of becoming a British boxing star, but for now there remain questions. It is not that people doubt his talents, more that he needs to prove them emphatically to the wider boxing world.

At just 21, Itauma has been creating rumblings since 2023. He has 10 straight knockouts. He is undefeated. His last two wins were against Dillian Whyte and Jermaine Franklin, but he is yet to beat a fighter you might regard as a gatekeeper to a title fight.

Hrgovic might normally be seen as that gatekeeper. At 34, the Croatian has plenty of experience in the ring, with 21 fights bringing 20 wins, 15 of them by knockout. His only loss was against Daniel Dubois in 2024, but his wins since then have been against Joe Joyce, David Adeleye and Dave Allen. Not the highest quality, by any means. Hrgovic, then, has something to prove to us too.

However, this is no eliminator, this is for the full IBF world heavyweight championship. A win for Itauma would see him become the second-youngest world heavyweight champion in boxing history.

As Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury circle one another, threatening to never fight at all, Itauma looks set to be Britain’s next heavyweight star. All he has to do is win at the O2 Arena tonight. If he does that, he could then be a fixture at the top of the sport for a decade, perhaps more.

Ringwalks are expected at around 10.30pm for the main event. So if men in dressing gowns is your thing, get ready.

News.title: £380m = zero points: Big-spending Spurs humbled by Newcastle
News.content:
“After the first goal we lost confidence,” said De Zerbi. “The reaction was not good enough, not what I want to see on the pitch. The solution is not to put the head down, but to react.”

To be clear, Spurs were not quite as bad as they had been against Brentford on the opening day. They did create chances here, taking 17 shots and forcing a few terrific saves from Lukas Hornicek, Newcastle’s impressive goalkeeper. But in the key moments they suffered from the same absence of clarity and execution as they did last season. Troublingly, this seemed to affect the new signings as much as it did the longer-serving players.

Of the five new arrivals who featured for Spurs, Tonali was the least effective. The Italian had been vigorously booed by the away fans before kick-off and the travelling Geordies waited with palpable excitement for his first mistake. Much to their delight, it arrived after only three minutes: an underhit pass, in his own half, which directly led to Micky van de Ven picking up a yellow card. Tonali was outshone by new Newcastle midfielder Nico Gonzalez, who excelled only a few days after completing his move from Manchester City.

News.title: Lawrence seizes his opportunity on rain-ruined day at Lord’s
News.content:
On a bleak day for batting, Dan Lawrence seized an opportunity that he must have feared had passed him by.

Lawrence was one of the victims of Bazball excess, shoved up to open in place of Zak Crawley two years ago in a punt that backfired and could have ended his Test career.

It took the sudden retirement of Ben Stokes and an injury to first-choice replacement Sam Curran to open up a position at No 6, Lawrence’s natural home, and it has come at just the right time.

At 29 he is a much more rounded cricketer than the one who debuted in Sri Lanka under Joe Root in 2021 and he showed it here with a hard-fought half-century on a gloomy, dank Saturday when only 25 overs were possible between the frequent drizzly showers, forcing MCC into a 50 per cent ticket refund.

It was a second fifty in three innings since his recall and he will not have faced many tougher conditions than this, with the ball seaming around on a spiteful pitch. With Mohammad Abbas teasing the ball off the surface and the athletic Mohammad Rizwan snaffling everything up to the stumps, this was a real challenge of mind and technique.

Lawrence will never win awards for aesthetic beauty but he chose the right balls to put away in a 66-ball unbeaten 50 that stretched England’s lead to 357 at 177 for seven in their second innings. Lawrence settled any wobbles about Pakistan pulling off a miracle recovery.
