Two days before Banxico published its revised growth forecasts, the federal Economy Ministry reported that Mexico received just under US $35 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first six months of 2026. While the amount is a record high, it represented annual growth of just 2.1%, much lower than the 10.4% year-over-year increase recorded in the first quarter. Less than 8% of the FDI was “new investment,” with “reinvestment of profits” accounting for almost 90% of the total.

According to the latest MND Economy Index™, Mexico’s economy has meaningful strengths, but there is ample room for improvement. The index score in June was 66.9 out of 100, a decrease of 1.7 points compared to May.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Belize mourns the passing of longtime children’s healthcare advocate Milagro Garel
World.content:
Belize mourns the passing of longtime children’s healthcare advocate Milagro Garel

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Milagro Garel, the woman behind two decades of children’s medical missions in Belize, has died.

Her family confirmed her passing in a statement, saying she went peacefully with her loved ones at her side.

“It is with broken hearts that we share that our beloved Milagro passed away peacefully this afternoon, surrounded by love.”

Garel collapsed on July 28 with a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. Doctors stabilised her here before an air ambulance took her to Guatemala, where surgeons operated and she remained in intensive care for weeks. Her husband Joe kept the country updated as she regained consciousness in stages.

Belizeans raised the money that made the treatment possible, covering transport, surgery and hospitalisation costs running between $95,000 and $140,000.

As country director for World Pediatrics, Garel spent more than twenty years getting Belizean children onto operating tables they would never otherwise have reached, working alongside Friends of Pediatrics and other groups.

“Your beautiful smile, your incredible spirit and the light you brought into so many lives will remain with us forever,” her family wrote.

World.title: Court orders psychiatric evaluation for accused thief after questions arise about identity, ability to understand proceedings
World.content:
Court orders psychiatric evaluation for accused thief after questions arise about identity, ability to understand proceedings

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 33-year-old man accused of stealing a cellphone was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Monday after a magistrate ordered that he undergo a psychiatric evaluation amid concerns about whether he understood the court proceedings.

The man, known to police and the court as Raymond Moody and also as Lavender Kendale, appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison on a single charge of theft.

Moody is accused of stealing a dark blue Samsung cellphone valued at $650, on Wednesday, August 26.

His arraignment was initially halted because he could not provide identification and questions again arose over his true identity. The matter was briefly stood down while prosecutors sought further information.

Later in the day, a woman identifying herself as his mother, Maria Moody, appeared in court and told the magistrate that the accused is her 33-year-old son, Raymond Moody, who was born at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital. She did not have documentary proof of his identity with her.

When the theft charge was read and Moody was asked to enter a plea, he reportedly responded, “I nuh know which is correct.”

Senior Magistrate Dennison subsequently ordered a psychiatric evaluation, with the court expressing concern that Moody may not be in a position to properly understand the proceedings or enter a plea. He was remanded until September 30, 2026.

Outside court, Maria Moody became emotional over her son’s remand. She said her son has experienced memory problems since suffering a blow to the head approximately three years ago.

“He is not crazy. Things come and go,” she said, explaining that he had previously been treated at the Port Loyola Clinic and KHMH following the injury.

Moody previously came before the court in 2025 after attorney Audrey Matura reported a burglary. During those proceedings, questions also arose over his identity after the man police knew as Raymond Moody told the court his name was Lavender Kendale.

That burglary case was eventually dismissed after the court was unable to establish with sufficient certainty the identity of the person before it.

Moody is scheduled to return to court on September 30.

World.title: Fear No Evil: American ex-soldier jailed after breaking Jesus statue, threatening to kill priest, attempting to strike priest with crucifix in church
World.content:
Fear No Evil: American ex-soldier jailed after breaking Jesus statue, threatening to kill priest, attempting to strike priest with crucifix in church

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 40-year-old American former soldier was sent to the Belize Central Prison on Monday after pleading guilty to damaging property at the Divine Mercy Church on the Philip Goldson Highway during an incident in which the church’s priest was allegedly threatened.

Nathan Thomas Mikesell, an American national residing in San Pedro, appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to one count of damage to property.

Mikesell was fined $2,000 plus $5 cost of court and ordered to pay the amount forthwith. In default, he was ordered to serve five months in prison. He was reportedly unable to pay the fine by the end of the day and was escorted to the Belize Central Prison.

The charge arose from an incident at Divine Mercy Church at around 5:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 29.

According to the facts presented, the church’s priest was preparing for Mass when he heard the church hand bell ringing and later encountered Mikesell inside the building. The pastor told police that Mikesell became aggressive and allegedly threatened to kill him.

Mikesell reportedly picked up a procession crucifix and attempted to strike the priest, but missed. He then allegedly repeatedly struck the crucifix against the ground, damaging it, before later using a pole to damage the Divine Mercy Jesus statue located in the church plaza.

The pastor estimated the damage to the statue at approximately $12,000. Three hymn books, the procession crucifix and a bathroom gate were also reportedly damaged. The pastor was not physically injured.

Police eventually arrived and detained Mikesell. He was later taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for an evaluation after police reported that he appeared unable to provide a meaningful account of what had occurred. Following treatment, he was released back into police custody and subsequently charged.

After pleading guilty, Mikesell also alleged in court that he had been beaten while in police custody. Senior Magistrate Dennison informed him that any complaint regarding alleged police misconduct would have to be taken up with the Police Professional Standards Branch, as the matter before the court concerned the damage-to-property charge.

World.title: Last day to apply: Warehouse Assistant position at WESTRAC Dangriga
World.content:
Last day to apply: Warehouse Assistant position at WESTRAC Dangriga

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Today is the deadline to apply for a Warehouse Assistant position at WESTRAC’s Dangriga branch.

The role involves labelling, sorting, organising and storing items, replenishing stock as needed, preparing orders for customer pickup and delivery, and inspecting goods for quality and quantity.

Applicants need a minimum of a high school diploma, strong verbal and written communication skills, attention to detail, and basic computer skills.

The company is looking for a team player who can work in a fast paced environment.

Warehouse roles like this offer a practical entry point into logistics and supply chain work, and Dangriga residents will not have to travel far for it.

The application deadline is today, August 31, 2026 and you can apply here: https://westrac.bz/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Westrac-Ltd-Employment-Application.pdf

Anyone interested should get their application in before the day closes.

World.title: BEL asks PUC to declare emergency over power shortfall
World.content:
BEL asks PUC to declare emergency over power shortfall

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Electricity Limited has formally notified the Public Utilities Commission of an anticipated material shortfall in generation services and is asking for an emergency to be declared.

The notice, dated August 26 and signed by Executive Chairman Ambassador Lynn Young, was sent to PUC Chairman Dean Molina.

BEL says its analysis shows that expected peak electricity demand within the next twelve months will exceed available generation capacity. That warrants procuring additional generation beyond what currently exists or will realistically exist within the next year.

The company is acting in its capacity as Single Buyer in the electricity market, under Section 19 of the Public Utilities Commission Request for Proposals Regulations, 2024.

That section allows the Commission, with government approval, to declare that an emergency situation has arisen beyond the reasonable control of Belize when the single buyer gives notice of a material shortfall within twelve months.

“BEL hereby requests the PUC to secure the approval of the Government of Belize to declare an emergency in relation to generation services in Belize to initiate the process for emergency generation procurement,” the letter reads.

The notice was copied to Minister of Public Utilities Michel Chebat.

World.title: Police investigate suspected drowning of Cesar ‘Koka’ Cruz in Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Police investigate suspected drowning of Cesar ‘Koka’ Cruz in Orange Walk Town

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the suspected drowning of a man identified as Cesar Cruz, also known as “Koka,” who died while swimming in a river in Orange Walk Town on Sunday afternoon.

According to police, officers responded at around 3:10 p.m. on Sunday, August 30, to a report of a drowning at a river near Riverside Street.

Upon arrival, officers were informed that Cruz had been swimming in the river when he went underwater and failed to resurface.

A search party was subsequently formed, and Cruz’s body was later recovered from the water.

Police say an examination of the body revealed no visible signs of physical injury.

Cruz’s body was transported to the Northern Regional Hospital morgue, where it awaits a post-mortem examination as police continue their investigation.

World.title: Man drowns in Orange Walk Town river
World.content:
Man drowns in Orange Walk Town river

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Cesar Valentin Samayoga, a 49 year old labourer of Sitee River Street, drowned in the river at Riverside Street, Orange Walk Town on Sunday afternoon.

Police received information of the drowning around 3:10pm and visited the area, where they found a group of people on the river bank.

A 14 year old student told police he was fishing at the river bank with friends when he saw Samayoga take off his clothing, remaining in his underwear, and enter the river to swim. He said Samayoga appeared to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

The teenager said he then saw him struggling to resurface and trying to swim out of the river before he sank and disappeared from sight.

Police found a green shirt, grey three quarter pants and a pair of black tennis shoes on the river bank.

A search party was formed and divers entered the water. Samayoga’s body was recovered by a diver.

No physical injuries were observed. He was pronounced dead at the Northern Regional Hospital at 4:49pm.

His body awaits a postmortem examination.

World.title: Jealousy accusation ends with woman beaten and locked in bathroom
World.content:
Jealousy accusation ends with woman beaten and locked in bathroom

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 30 year old labourer has been detained after allegedly beating his common law wife at their Orange Walk Town home on Sunday afternoon.

According to the report, a 25 year old call agent arrived home with her two children around 3:30pm after watching football at the Louisiana football field.

She told police her common law husband of 11 years began accusing her of having an affair with a neighbour. She said she tried to calm him down because their children were home, but he punched her twice to the left eye, then to the mouth and about her body.

She reached for a pair of scissors nearby, which he grabbed from her hand, cutting her right index finger. She said the bleeding was profuse and that he continued punching her despite her pleas.

She told police he then dragged her into the bathroom, told her to bathe and locked her inside.

Police arrived shortly after. She said the accused attempted to run but officers grabbed him.

Her injuries were certified as wounding. Court action has been requested.

World.title: Crackdown on care
World.content:
TUFTON...people must play their part...or they make way for someone else to do itPhoto: Garfield Robinson

SPURRED by more than 1,000 patient complaints in the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s Client Care Connect report, portfolio Minister Dr Christopher Tufton says efforts to expose system failures and hold negligent medical professionals accountable will intensify.

The move comes as the ministry prepares to publish its accountability data in September, which Tufton says highlighted various client complaints of poor communication, professional conduct, and overall patient experience.

“We’re looking to transform the health workforce. We are taking an inward look, recognising that a highly qualified health system cannot exist without sound governance, and that transformation requires effective leadership, which will be essential to managing the critical components of health.

“So when we speak about an accountability framework, it’s about delivering service with compassion, with empathy and, of course, ensuring that every patient is treated with dignity, respect, and fairness at every point of care,” said the minister as he delivered the keynote address at the Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston in St Andrew last Friday.

According to him, the report’s data aims to isolate departments and individuals responsible for poor patient experiences rather than allowing the failures of some to tarnish the reputation of the wider health-care system.

“Where there is a problem, we need to identify the institution, the department, and who is in charge. You have to start with all the names, because you can’t allow one bad apple to spoil the whole lot…Tell me where the worst experience takes place, the bad experience; tell me which department, and tell me who is in charge.

“And what leadership ought now to do is to address the specifics of a problem. Stop generalising the problem, because we’re letting down people who make sacrifices every day to do the work, and that’s a new modus operandi…People must play their part, and we must emphasise and insist on it, or they make way for someone else to do it,” charged Tufton.

The minister’s push for greater accountability comes amid heightened public scrutiny of the health-care system after the death of 33-year-old Kenise Dunn gained widespread media traction. The eight-month pregnant mother of three passed away at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days post-delivery.

When asked if his call for accountability extended to the contentious incident, Tufton told the Jamaica Observer that he cannot comment conclusively while the investigation is ongoing. Still, he emphasised that health-care professionals are always bound by a duty of care. “What I’ve heard, preliminary, is that, clinically, there was a diagnosis of the problem, but it appears, based on some of the feedback — including from persons who are on the ward — that maybe the management of the customer care and the empathy to the patient may have been less than desired. Now, I don’t have the final report, so I prefer not to conclude on that,” he said. “But the truth is drawn from what I said about the complaints report, the 1,000, which I spoke to, it’s quite clear that while we have excellent health workers, we have to work harder at delivering service with compassion and with empathy. And it’s not good enough to just have technical competence. If you treat people badly, if you don’t listen to them, if you don’t respond to them, if you don’t give them a sense of comfort when they’re in distress, then it hampers the healing process,” said the minister. In the meantime, Tufton urged the 141 recipients of the Barry Wint medical grant, valued at over $190 million, to be the difference once they enter their respective fields of practice. “I say this at the risk of offending some, that money is not the primary issue in health care, currently public health; the primary issue is how we conduct ourselves within the system. People who are in the system only for a pay cheque are not sufficiently willing to give the commitment and show care. You cannot afford to be like that. You have to show a better way, and that’s what Barry Wint is investing in. Not just in your capacity as a technical and competent person, but in moving the process forward,” the minister said. Pointing to what he identified as the major weaknesses of the system, Tufton noted that health care in Jamaica lacks a sufficient number of practitioners — specifically specialised individuals — and professionals with the capacity to show empathy to patients. He reiterated that that was not the type of behaviour that he expected from recipients of the Barry Wint scholarship, and challenged them to become “a catalyst for change”. “If you just want to be a nurse, a doctor, a biotech engineer because at the end of the month you’re going to get a fat pay cheque, and that’s the only driving motivation to apply and to pretty up the application for this money, do not accept it. There are too many people in the profession who see the profession only in financial terms, and not enough as a passion and commitment to enhance service delivery for those who need it, Jamaicans who are in distress,” he said firmly.

World.title: Jamaicans loud and proud!
World.content:
Trinidad and Tobago’s High Commissioner to Jamaica Deborah Thomas-Felix shares her admiration for the manner in which Jamaicans display pride in their country while speaking at the Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday. Photo: Naphtali Junior

FROM schoolchildren in the country’s colours to packed cultural events, Trinidad and Tobago’s new High Commissioner Deborah Thomas-Felix says the unapologetic pride Jamaicans display in their identity is one of the things that has impressed her most since taking up her post.

Having lived in several Caribbean countries, Thomas-Felix said Jamaica’s expression of national pride stands out to her because of how openly it is displayed in everyday life, from the workplace to sporting and cultural events.

She was particularly struck by the way Jamaicans embrace national occasions, including Jamaica Day, when people turn out in the country’s colours, adding that the celebration of national identity extends beyond the traditional observances of Independence and Emancipation.

“You all have a national day — schoolchildren, big people going to work in Jamaica colours. I was so struck by that when I experienced it… Don’t get me wrong, because Trinidad and Tobago has a deep sense of pride and love, but it’s the way, the open way in which it’s displayed in Jamaica,” she expressed during the a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s Beechwood Avenue, St Andrew, headquarters last Friday.

For Thomas-Felix, the pride is also visible in how Jamaica celebrates its culture, with Reggae Month — commemorated in February — providing an entire month of activities centred on one of the country’s most recognisable cultural exports.

She said that visible enthusiasm has helped her better understand Jamaicans in the Diaspora.

“Everywhere you go within the country, they say, ‘Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica,’ and I think that is so encouraging, and it gives me a better understanding of the Jamaicans I know who don’t live in Jamaica,” she said.

Thomas-Felix, whose parents are Grenadians and who has lived in St Vincent, Barbados, and Trinidad and Tobago, stressed that she was not suggesting that Trinbagonians lack national pride, but said she was particularly impressed by how visibly Jamaicans express theirs.

“There’s this open display of pride, and I think you all should keep that. I think that is just an excellent way to let [future] generations inherit that and continue with that, because I really, really like that,” she said.

Her comments come as Thomas-Felix seeks to strengthen ties between Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago across areas including trade, culture, and people-to-people relations.

She said the relationship between the two countries extends well beyond governments, pointing to Trinidadians who have built lives and careers in Jamaica and Jamaicans who have done the same in Trinidad and Tobago.

For Thomas-Felix, those personal connections are part of the Caribbean relationship that she wants to strengthen during her tenure.

“So the relationship is way beyond government to government, it’s really about people, and we interact through music, we interact in terms of culture, and so I want to really strengthen those bonds,” she said.

World.title: Slow movement on Spring Mount road repairs
World.content:
Residents of Spring Mount listen keenly as manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw (left) provides an update on plans to rehabilitate collapsed roads in the area.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — A soil test is among the items to be done before the State-run National Works Agency (NWA) can finalise a design to rebuild Spring Mount road in south St James. Last October’s Hurricane Melissa caused two major breakaways on the heavily trafficked route, leaving commuters with the choice of engaging in risky road use or a much longer, more costly journey.

With schools about to reopen, residents of Spring Mount and neighbouring areas have become increasingly anxious for an update on what is being done to fix the road. They were given the clearest signal, Thursday evening, that the road will likely be rebuilt in the same location; but there was no timeline on when work will start.

“We are looking to build back the road. We have looked at different possibilities and I can tell you straight up, one of the things that we are looking at is to take down the hillside and acquire [those] two houses on top of the hill,” manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw told residents during a meeting held at Spring Mount Basic School.

He said the goal is to rehabilitate the roadway as soon as possible, restoring the vital connection between the north and south of the parish. The damage has made safe passage by vehicular traffic impossible just beyond Spring Mount Police Station. Residents have established a pedestrian path which is sometimes utilised by motorcyclists.

Shaw made it clear that there will be challenges in executing the project, given its scope and magnitude.

“It is not the normal run of the mill [approach of] looking at it as a breakaway, put up a wall, backfill it, and move on. No. We are going to have to do what are called bore hole tests,” he warned, adding that this falls outside the technical capabilities of the NWA and a private sector firm would have to be engaged.

These tests, he explained, will provide laboratory-based information on the soil in the area that will guide the designs on which work has already started.

“That testing of the material beneath there will inform us as to what else, if required, needs to be done to ensure that… when we build up that road, you have it longer than all of us inside here will live,” Shaw told the audience.

“Based on the survey that was executed, a design is being worked on but that design will not be finalised until the boreholes are done,” he added.

He explained the importance of the soil tests.

“A crucial factor in this area is the springs. It’s called Spring Mount for a reason. We have to design with that in mind to ensure that we don’t see a situation where we build a big wall, costing a lot of money… and then, [as seen in other locations] rain came, and the entire retaining wall just moved like… it was plastic,” Shaw outlined.

“We have that kind of experience and historical knowledge on which to build or not to build. We are not taking anything lightly in ensuring that the design solutions that we come up with, they are adequate, they are appropriate, are sufficient, and necessary for the particular areas that we are going to be working,” he added.

Responding to residents’ questions about timelines, the NWA representative said he was unable to provide one as it depends on the soil testing which is being done outside of the agency. He did, however, promise to explore ways in which alternate routes — such as the journey through Kempshot, up the treacherous Charlie Mount — may be improved.

Councillor Uvel Graham (Jamaica Labour Party, Spring Mount Division) was at the meeting and while he acknowledged that the project is complex he expressed frustration that it is moving too slowly.

“To be honest, I was looking for more of a timeline and that these tests would be done already and people would be hearing that the next two to three months, the work would start,” he told the

Jamaica Observer after the meeting.

World.title: ‘I’ve run my leg’
World.content:
GREENE...I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

AFTER a brief but impactful two-year term as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Health and Wellness, Errol Greene is ready to pass the baton, proud of his legacy but acknowledging that critical work remains.

“As we gather to award students pursuing courses in public health, I am filled with mixed emotions. I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness,” said Greene, as he formally announced his retirement from the role — which takes effect Monday, August 31 — while delivering greetings at the Dr Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston last Friday.

Under the scholarship, named in honour of the former chief medical officer, recipients are awarded up to $1 million annually for health care-related studies in priority fields such as nursing, biomedical engineering, and medicine.

For this year’s staging, 141 awardees were selected from more than 700 applicants to benefit from over $190 million in scholarships, with the Government having spent approximately $900 million towards the initiative to date.

“While there’s a sense of nostalgia, there’s also a sense of tremendous pride and optimism as I look out at this room filled with talented, ambitious, enthusiastic, and determined persons who represent the future of health care in Jamaica,” said Greene, who noted that he would continue to watch their progress as professionals in the health field from the sidelines.

When asked by the Jamaica Observer if his retirement signalled a complete departure from public service, Greene offered a cryptic, “We’ll see how it goes.” However, he maintained that he is ready to hand over the reins to a capable professional who can drive the remaining work forward.

“We have done well, and we can do better. I certainly want to be a part of the journey because I know my minister is passionate about health, he’s passionate about service delivery, and I would have run my leg of the race and I have handed over the baton, so I’ll just go in the pavilion and watch the race finish,” he said.

Before his two-year stint as permanent secretary, Greene led a career spanning decades. His life as a public servant began when he assumed the role of town clerk of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) and also served at the St Thomas Municipal Corporation.

He then pivoted to begin service in the health sector, serving as regional director of the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), which oversees health services in Kingston and St Andrew, St Thomas, and St Catherine.

He was also a former regional director of Western Regional Health Authority and a former chief executive officer of the Kingston Public Hospital.

Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton, who delivered the keynote address at the scholarship event, used the opportunity to acknowledge Greene’s contributions and bid him farewell.

“Our permanent secretary, who is not riding off in the sunset, but is closing one chapter to start another, Mr Errol Greene…give him a round of applause, please. I believe he has done 50 years, thereabout. I don’t want to tell his age, because he is still young,” joked Tufton. “But he has done a whole heap of years, whole heap of decades to public service, and I just want to recognise him and thank him for his services.”

World.title: UWI Freshers’ Series delivers a hit, energises campus
World.content:
DJ Breeze in full flight at Freshers’ Fete.

Jermaine Francis, vice-president of properties and special initiatives at The University of the West Indies, Mona Guild of Students, has described this year’s Freshers’ Series as one of the most successful in the past five years, attracting one of the largest turnouts seen during that period.

The Freshers’ Series took place from August 26-28.

According to Francis, the strong participation and vibrant atmosphere throughout the week signals that “the vibes on campus are back.” He noted that the enthusiasm and engagement displayed by students demonstrates the immense value and potential of the university market.

“UWI, Mona provides corporate entities with a unique opportunity to connect with the next generation of leaders and consumers. The energy is back, the students are engaged, and the platform is growing. I am urging corporate Jamaica to tap in and become part of these experiences,” Francis told the Jamaica Observer on the weekend.

Francis is therefore encouraging corporate Jamaica to take greater interest in and tap into this unique and dynamic student market. With major events such as UWI Integration Thursday and UWI Carnival on the horizon, he believes there are significant opportunities for brands to engage directly with thousands of young, influential, and emerging consumers.

The first event in the Freshers’ Series was the Freshers’ Concert, which took place inside Students’ Union on the campus. Representatives from the various halls performed talented pieces including singing, drama and poetry.

“The idea behind the Freshers’ Concert is really to give our new students a proper welcome to UWI and allow them to experience the university beyond the classroom. We wanted each hall to come together, showcase their creativity and talents, and give the freshers an opportunity to build friendships and create memories from the very start of their university journey. We also ensured that the freshers got the opportunity to interact with their guild councillors.

The George Alleyne Hall emerged winner, with Mary Seacole Hall, Elsa Rynie Towers, Irvine Hall, and Taylor Hall finishing in second, third, fourth and fifth places, respectively.

“The halls showcased a range of talents, including singing, dancing, drama and other creative performances. What stood out to me was how each hall found its own way to tell a story and represent their identity through their performance. The Freshers’ Concert also gives the freshers an opportunity to get involved and feel like they are part of The UWI community from early. University is not only about academics; it is also about the relationships you build and the experiences you have along the way,” said Francis.

On Thursday, August 27, Freshers’ Cocktail took place under the theme “Port of Paradise”.

“The Freshers’ Cocktail, themed Port of Paradise, was a premium and elegant experience designed to give incoming students an opportunity to dress up, socialise, and enjoy an evening of entertainment, fine cuisine, and networking. The event created a sophisticated atmosphere within the Freshers’ Series, combining elements of Caribbean culture with exceptional food, performances, and meaningful social interaction. The objective was to create a welcoming environment where freshers could connect with one another outside of the traditional orientation setting. We wanted students from different faculties, halls of residence, and backgrounds to interact, build friendships, and develop a genuine sense of belonging within The UWI, Mona community,” Francis explained.

On Friday, August 28, Freshers’ Fete, under the theme “Island Fever”, closed the week in a major way, with popular university DJs playing hits that saw students partying until early Saturday morning.

“Freshers’ Fete was the perfect climax to an exciting and memorable week of activities. The energy was unmatched, the turnout was strong, and students came together to celebrate the beginning of their university journey in an atmosphere of unity, entertainment, and celebration. The experience was premium and exceptionally well supported. We would like to extend special recognition to our valued sponsors, including CPJ, which provided Str8 Vybz Rum and Angostura Chill, as well as Red Bull, Reggae Jammin’, JN Bank, LASCO Food Drink, and Wisynco, through brands such as Wata and Mpowa. We are also grateful to all the other sponsors and partners who came on board and contributed to making the Freshers’ Series a success,” said Francis.

DJs including Carlos A-Team, DJ Jubba and Breeze, and Kurt Riley provided the musical vibrations.

World.title: Young scholar rises above Riverton roots to pursue dreams
World.content:
Recipient of the Open Tertiary Male Bursary award Javon Gentles (left) embraces his sister Kadeen Fyffe at the Burger King National Scholarship Programme Awards held last Tuesday at AC Hotel Kingston. Photo: Naphtali Junior

BORN and raised in one of Kingston’s inner-city communities, Javon Gentles knows what it is like to lose opportunities due to his Riverton City address rather than his credentials. But when he took the stage at the Burger King National Scholarship Awards last Tuesday, he showed up as a testament to perseverance and being able to rise above the limitations placed on him.

“I grew up in a community where potential is everywhere, but opportunities are often scarce. Growing up there taught me resilience and resourcefulness. It also taught me the hard truth: Sometimes people will see your address before they see your character, your abilities, or your potential.

“But I learned that I could not control the assumptions others made. What I could control was what I believed, the opportunities that were brought to me, and the place in which I wanted to go — the direction in which I wanted to choose to take. And I choose greatness,” declared Gentles, as he spoke on behalf of the 2026 cohort of scholars at the AC Hotel Kingston.

The scholarships — valued at more than $14 million and awarded to 34 high achievers and are granted by Restaurant Associates Limited, franchise operator of Burger King in Jamaica — provide funding to students who sat the Primary Exit Profile (PEP) exam and are entering secondary schools, as well as students heading into accredited local universities.

Standing proudly as the recipient of the ‘Open Tertiary Male Bursary’ award, Gentles shared that he learnt from an early age that success did not happen by chance, but by sacrifice, determination, and resilience.

On his quest for greatness, Gentles did not squander his time as a student at St George’s College, serving in various leadership roles and amassing 10 grade ones at the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) level, and four distinctions across both units of the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE).

Yet, even with an exemplary academic record, his dreams of advancing to the tertiary education level remained uncertain.

“A dream that I have carried for years, [is] becoming a neurosurgeon. But, of course, with my background, eventually my dream, you know, it’s a difficult reality. I had the hope, I had the motivation, I had the grace and the feeling of experience, yet the financial reality of pursuing my career at The UWI [University of the West Indies] forced me to ask a difficult question: Can I actually afford to become a doctor? I had to consider whether to place the burden [of me getting higher education] on my family or to enter the workforce sooner, you know, choosing a path that might offer faster financial security, but not the fulfilment I was seeking,” said Gentles, adding that it was the hardest decision he ever had to make.

But, as he faced his darkest hour, navigating derailed dreams, Gentles shared that his reality changed instantly when he became one of the recipients of the Burger King scholarship and bursaries awards.

“To the Burger King family, thank you. Thank you not only for the financial support that makes this opportunity possible, but for believing in the potential of young Jamaicans and choosing to invest into our futures. This award is more than financial. It is an opportunity. It is motivation. It is a powerful reminder that the path we have chosen, no matter how difficult, is worth continuing,” he said triumphantly.

In an invigorating message to his fellow awardees, Gentles encouraged the scholars to make the most of the opportunity by tackling the future with confidence and a responsibility to become the best version of themselves.

“Fellow scholars, the trail ahead will not always be easy. There will be challenges, uncertainty and moments of doubt. But, we are prepared. So let us move with courage, let us work with discipline, and let us lead with integrity and let us serve with purpose. And when we reach the places we are working toward, let us turn around and make the trail wider, brighter for those coming behind us, because our success should become a bridge for those who are coming after us. The trail is before us, my dear scholars. Let us go and set it ablaze,” he charged.

Watching after her brother with sheer pride as he commanded the stage, Kadeen Fyffe told the Jamaica Observer that Gentles had always been exceptional.

“I’m very much delighted and happy for him. He’s been doing well academically, so this is well deserved. But this [scholarship] wasn’t expected because we tried other places for scholarships before, but Burger King came through. So we big up Burger King for giving the youth hope to pursue their dreams, and we thank God for giving us this grace and the privilege to watch him reach as far as he has…we thank our mother, Juliette Sital, who is the backbone for both of us. So, as he starts this new journey, we’ll continue to trust God,” said Fyffe.

For her part, minister of state in the Ministry of Education Rhoda Moy Crawford highlighted the ceremony’s theme, ‘Blazing a trail to success’, encouraging the scholars to continue on their path of excellence and to rise again when faced with challenges.

“To blaze a trail is to create a path where there may have been none before. It means pursuing your goals, even when the road is unclear. It means being brave enough to explore your abilities, to challenge yourself, and sometimes to go further than where anyone else in your family has gone before. Use this opportunity to develop the knowledge, skills, character, and confidence to make the most of your journey,” charged Crawford.

World.title: GIVE US A HAND!
World.content:
Justin Greaves (second right) celebrates with teammates after dismissing Australia’s Alex Carey during the day/night third Test at Sabina Park in Kingston, Jamaica, on July 12, 2025. Photo: Naphtali Junior

With India and England set to tour the Caribbean next year, Jamaica Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says the Government must make a serious effort to ensure the two cricketing powerhouses play at Sabina Park.

Although not officially announced by the ICC or the respective cricket boards, the West Indies are expected to host the Indians next June where they will play two tests, three One-Day Internationals (ODIs) and five T20s. England are scheduled to arrive next December to battle the Caribbean men in five T20s in preparation of the 2028 Twenty20 (T20) World Cup.

India’s last visit to the region was in the summer of 2023 while England last toured in the final quarter of 2024.

Bennett, who also serves as a CWI board director, told the Jamaica Observer that unlike other touring nations, territories have to make official bids to CWI to host the Indians and the English because of the significant commercial value the two teams bring.

“The bid documents should be out in another four weeks. I’ve already written to the Ministry of Sports outlining and sensitising them to the fact that England and India will be here next year,” he said. “As soon as that document comes out then we’re going to have to engage the Ministry of Sports, and probably the Ministry of Tourism too, in a serious way to ensure that we do bid for those games because they do have serious economic impact.”

Bennett says he’s optimistic the Government will follow through and see the value of the tours, particularly with India.

“Jamaica is just three hours away from the eastern seaboard of the United States and about three million Indians and cricket-loving or cricket-crazy people live on the eastern seaboard of the US so it can be a huge tourism opportunity,” he said. “So we’ll have to sit down with the Government and engage them and see how we go. The initial response that I’ve had is that there is a deep interest [within] the Government in these tours so, like I said before, we will see how it goes.”

Over the last two years, Sabina Park has seen an uptick in international matches, hosting South Africa, Bangladesh, Australia, and most recently Sri Lanka in June.

The steady turnout for those matches caught the eye of CWI President Dr Kishore Shallow who, according to reports, was impressed with Jamaica’s recent hosting stints.

However, Bennett says the Government will have to be more proactive this time around, given the number of bids CWI is expected to receive from around the region.

“There are other countries that have tourism as their main industry and they’re going to be wanting the tours too, and they’re going to be competitive too,” he said. “So we have to be on the ball and to do what we’re doing, and not only do what we should do, but we need to do it on a timely basis. We need to get in there as early as possible to see what we can get from those tours.”

Bennett, though, says Jamaica should gain an added advantage after the crowd support witnessed during the Sabina Park leg of the Caribbean Premier League earlier this month.

“It must be a factor because it’s not about just allocating to territories based on a wide basis. Cricket West Indies is not going to allocate matches just because you’re a territory and you haven’t had a game for one season or a game should go here and a game should go there. Clearly, there must be a consideration for crowd support, crowd support is an economic thing,” he said.

“The West Indies is out there to make money also and if territories support the game and come out in large numbers, clearly, we’ll have an advantage as far as the allocation of the game is concerned. I asked the cricket-loving public in Jamaica to come out and strengthen my hand and they certainly did. We can look forward to the India and the English tour with some sort of positivity. I’m sure that the crowd has put us into a place where we can barter and express our desire in a more forceful way.”

Bennett also hasn’t ruled out the possibility of hosting matches when visitors Afghanistan take on the Windies in February in both a red-ball and white-ball series.

However, the series could be postponed due to the Windies’ participation in the 50 over World Cup Qualifier which also starts in February.

World.title: Hundreds benefit from dental health fair in Mandeville
World.content:
Dental students McKenna Doyle (left) and Brianna Lopez (right) pose for a photo with 10-year-old Davere Lawrence after his dental procedure on Friday in Mandeville. Kasey Williams

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Hundreds of children and their parents benefited from free dental services during a back-to-school health fair dubbed 1000 Smiles, thanks to a partnership between overseas mission group Great Shape! Inc and businesses here.

The one-week fair, hosted at the Mandeville Baptist Church and supported by Golf View Hotel, Garden Hotel, Lial Global, QVC Financial Solutions, Allied Real Estate, Manchester Chamber of Commerce, and Ultimate Dining, attracted people from south-central Jamaica and as far north as Trelawny.

Dr Harvey Arnce, a board member of Great Shape! Inc, said 20 volunteers — including a mixed group of final-year dental students and retired doctors — participated in the mission.

“I have been doing this with the team for 22 years across the Caribbean. I have been to most of the islands. We also partnered with the Sandals Foundation,” he said in reference to missions, including a recently concluded health fair in St Ann.

Students from five dental schools participated in the health fair in Mandeville.

“The University of Western Ontario, Mid-Western University Illinois, Mid-Western University in Phoenix, University of the Pacific in San Francisco, and University of Southern California; the students typically come on these missions when they are not in school, so that is in August/September,” Dr Arnce told the Jamaica Observer last Friday.

Among the dental services offered were teeth filling, cleaning and extractions

“We have to limit the volume of what we do on each patient, because 500 people who showed up for this week’s treatment and if we did a full mouth’s restoration, 400 [would] get to be seen. We are trying to just do a quadrant on each person,” said Dr Arnce.

He is encouraging Jamaicans to pay greater attention to their dental health.

“The diet here has high carbs and people get tooth decay. They don’t have check-ups on a regular basis. The decay gets bigger from inside the tooth and by the time it hurts, it is already too late for that tooth to be fixed and they end up with extractions. You almost have to be serviced on a yearly basis to fix a problem while it is in the early stages.

“If not, you would require a root canal treatment or an expensive crown. People would rather have it out, it is an economic and cultural issue as well as an availability issue of help. We are trying to solve the availability and affordability issue,” he added.

The Great Shape! Inc team will now turn its focus to the western end in Negril, to continue its mission.

“We typically do about two weeks in each location and then we move. In each location we [stay] at a hotel and we go out to say two or three clinics,” explained Dr Arnce.

Among the beneficiaries of the dental clinic was Lorrimers, Trelawny resident Daegia Isaacs and her four children — ages 10, 16, 12, and five.

“I was scrolling through

TikTok and I saw someone talking about it and I did some checks and found that it was legitimate. I travelled all the way from Trelawny to be here, it is a huge help, especially that all four of my children [benefited]. I saved over $100,000 for all four of them and I was able to utilise the service for myself. Being that my children are not on any health insurance right now, this is a huge help,” said Isaacs.

General manager at Golf View Hotel Keitho Nembhard lauded the sponsors of the fair.

“We are in the centre of the island with small hotels. We don’t have a lot of rooms, so we partnered with Garden Hotel and they were able to accommodate the team and we gave up a lot of our rooms as well to accommodate the team. Meals were provided through the hotels and Ultimate Dining. QVC Financial Solutions was our transportation provider for the team. Allied Real Estate provided logistics and support… The Mandeville Baptist Church hall was used and the church was more than happy to accommodate the dental clinic,” said Nembhard.

World.title: Modi implores tense Putin to end Ukraine war
World.content:
Calling for a peace settlement and invoking Gandhi and Mother Theresa, Modi said India supports all peace efforts, and this is the direction that must be pursued.

“Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path,” Putin responded.

Russia insists that ending the war in Ukraine can only be done on its own terms, something Kyiv has continually rejected. Meanwhile, attacks on Ukraine have intensified in recent days, along with rumors that Moscow is set to mobilize hundreds of thousands of fresh troops and step up ground offensives.

Ukraine has also scaled up its drone strikes, attacking energy infrastructure within Russia, as well as the warehouses of online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.

While Modi’s call is one of the most direct, particularly to the face of the Russian president, India continues to be a significant trading partner of Russia.

India is one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil and has also recently stepped up to provide gasoline to Moscow following Ukraine’s attacks on its refineries.

World.title: Poland suspects foreign involvement in drone-plant arson attack
World.content:
Workers perform their tasks in the production line of small caliber ammunition during the opening of Mesko SA's New Ammunition Production Hall on June 13, 2025 in Skarzysko-Kamienna, Poland. | Omar Marques/Getty Images

The incident comes amid a range of suspected Russian-linked sabotage attacks across Europe.

Poland suspects a fire at a factory operated by a drone component maker was an arson attack involving foreign intelligence services, according to a statement issued by the prosecutors.

WB Electronics, whose factory caught fire shortly in the early hours of Monday, is one of Poland’s largest private defense companies. It produces reconnaissance drones and loitering munitions, including FlyEye and Warmate, used by Ukraine against Russian forces.

Polish prosecutors issued a press release Monday afternoon saying they were investigating the “terrorist crime” involving the “deliberate setting of a fire” at a WB Electronics plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna, in south-eastern Poland.

World.title: Von der Leyen set to deliver major speech on Europe’s space policy
World.content:
Von der Leyen's participation in the event has not been previously reported.

The Commission president's focus on space reflects mounting concern over Russian hybrid actions that appear to be taking aim at Europe's reliance on satellites for everything from military communications to civilian navigation. GPS jamming and spoofing, for example, have surged recently around the Baltic Sea, disrupting thousands of flights, according to Sweden's public broadcaster SVT. Von der Leyen herself got a taste of the potential risks last year when the private jet she was taking to Bulgaria experienced GPS interference.

The space policy address also comes as von der Leyen continues to build up the Commission's defense and security apparatus — including a new top recruitment of a senior official poached from the EU's diplomatic service.

Benedikta von Seherr-Thoss, currently the European External Action Service's managing director for peace, security and defense, is expected to join the Commission's Directorate-General for Defence Industry and Space (DG DEFIS). POLITICO previously reported she is expected to be appointed director for a new unit on Ukraine.

Von Seherr-Thoss did not respond to several requests for comment. The European Commission's spokesperson service declined to comment on senior appointments.

The expected move comes at a sensitive moment for the EEAS and its chief, former Estonian Prime Minister Kaja Kallas. Von der Leyen has increasingly sought to expand the Commission's footprint in areas traditionally associated with the EU's diplomatic service, from defense and foreign policy to intelligence, adding to tensions over where the Commission's remit ends and the EEAS' begins.

World.title: Belgian judge strikes down pre-trial detention appeal for alleged NATO spy
World.content:
The Belgian Federal Prosecutor’s Office announced on Monday that an individual accused of spying for a third country — a Canadian national of Chinese origin — would remain in pre-trial detention.

 

The Belgian Indictments Chamber rejected the woman's appeal during a closed-door hearing and extended her pre-trial detention by one month, a spokesperson for the Federal Prosecutor’s Office told Euronews.

Belgian authorities announced in July that they had arrested an individual accused of spying for a third country and belonging to a criminal organisation, ordering that she remain behind bars ahead of a trial.

It followed a police raid on her apartment in the Belgian city of Mons and her office at NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE).

It has not been confirmed which country she was allegedly spying for or what information she is accused of obtaining, but questions remain over the impact the incident will have on NATO's operations as well as on European security.

The spokesperson for the Federal Prosecutor’s Office said the investigation was ongoing, with no trial date set.

The individual — identified by Reuters as a woman in her thirties called Claire Z — is alleged to have carried out the espionage activities while completing a six-month internship at SHAPE.

SHAPE is where political decisions made in Brussels by NATO ambassadors and other officials are translated into military action by the Alliance’s military leadership.

A SHAPE spokesperson previously told Euronews in a statement that there was “no indication” the alleged activity had disrupted NATO’s military operations.

Candidates for the internship programme are generally required to obtain an appropriate security clearance from their national authorities before they can take part.

Euronews previously contacted the office of Canada’s foreign affairs minister to clarify whether their authorities had cooperated with their Belgian counterparts in the investigation. No response was received.

Canada's Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said when the initial news broke that they were committed to "get to the bottom" of the arrest and to ensure it does not occur again.

“As a country, we will continue to investigate the processes we have and the security screening," he said.

World.title: Tributes pour in for former French PM Edouard Balladur following his death aged 97
World.content:
Former French Prime Minister Edouard Balladur has died at the age of 97, his family told the AFP news agency.

 

A private mass service is now planned for Balladur, who died in Paris on Monday, the family said, without giving further details.

Balladur served as PM from March 1993 to May 1995 under the presidency of Francois Mitterrand, in the so-called "second cohabitation" government.

French President Emmanuel Macron has paid tribute to Balladur on social media following the news of his death, calling him a "demanding, level-headed, and devoted public servant" who had "dedicated his life to the Fifth Republic."

"I honor his memory and extend my thoughts to his family and loved ones," Macron wrote.

France's current prime minister, Sebastien Lecornu, described Balladur as a "statesman with a reformist spirit," adding that he "will remain a role model for many men and women in his political circle."

In a post on X, Marine Le Pen also shared her condolences to Balladur's family and former colleagues.

"Setting aside the political disagreements we had with the man who served as Prime Minister from 1993 to 1995, today we should pay tribute to a statesman who left his mark on French public life, who consistently upheld his convictions and his vision of service to the Republic, and who always demonstrated respect for democratic debate," she wrote.

Born in 1929 in Turkey to a family of Armenian origin, Balladur moved to Marseille in 1934. He eventually made his way to Paris, where he studied at the prestigious Sciences Po and Ecole Nationale d'Administration.

He later became a close adviser to Georges Pompidou, the former French president and prime minister, before running for president himself in 1995. He would go out in the first round of the elections after losing out to Lionel Jospin and Jacques Chirac, the latter of whom went on to claim victory.

World.title: Naomi Watts to receive Donostia Award at 2026 San Sebastian Film Festival
World.content:
Winter 1999. During the shooting of one of the most memorable scenes in 'Mulholland Drive', ranked the second-best film of the century so far by the 'New York Times' and widely praised by specialist critics, a then-unknown Naomi Watts manages to draw an unusual round of applause from everyone on set, including its director, the late David Lynch, whom the actress has recalled for how he kick-started her career with this unforgettable, dreamlike drama.

 

More than 20 years later, the English actress will receive the Donostia Award at the San Sebastián Film Festival, the Zinemaldia, after a career that has taken in horror classics ('The Ring'), major box-office hits ('The Impossible' by Juan Antonio Bayona) and even Ryan Murphy's televisual camp ('Feud').

Watts, twice nominated for the Oscars and the Golden Globes, as well as once for the British BAFTAs, Spain's Goya awards and television's Emmy, has been recognised by the historic San Sebastián festival as "one of the most talented and recognisable actresses of her generation". Among the other renowned directors she has worked with are Alejandro Iñárritu, both on '21 Grams' and 'Birdman', Michael Haneke, Woody Allen and Noah Baumbach.

The Zinemaldia jury has confirmed that Watts will receive the prize on 19 September at a gala after which the film 'La esposa perfecta', by Ben Shirinian, in which the actress appears in the cast, will be screened. It is a drama in which a young New York Times journalist uncovers a possible Nazi officer living in Queens while striking up a friendship with the suspect's wife.

The festival had already announced in August that the first of the Donostia Awards would go to director, screenwriter, producer and actor Werner Herzog. The list of previous honourees at the Basque festival includes Gregory Peck, Bette Davis, Lauren Bacall, Francis Ford Coppola, Agnes Vardà, Catherine Deneuve and Pedro Almodóvar.

World.title: Eurasian nations gather in Bishkek to forge stronger ties, new alliances
World.content:
The annual Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit is gathering a diverse group of world leaders from 21 countries in Kyrgyzstan’s capital Bishkek, as they pursue new alliances, ambitions and opportunities with the rise of regional powers in the rapidly evolving multipolar Eurasia.

 

The two-day summit kicked off on Monday, focusing on political, economic and security engagements and cooperation, a long-promised development bank, connectivity, energy and trade routes strained by wars and conflicts, and the defining challenges of the Global South.

The SCO’s 10 members — China, India, Pakistan, Russia, Belarus, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan — speak for more than 40% of the world's population.

The bloc increasingly bills itself as an alternative to a Western-led order, as it is joined by leaders of at least 15 states as “dialogue partners,” spanning Central Asia and the rest of the continent, the South Caucasus, as well as the Middle East, including Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Vietnam, as well as Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

The bloc, which marked its 25th anniversary, was formed to address regional security issues after the collapse of the Soviet Union, but over time it has evolved into a powerhouse of multi-layered trade, security and political cooperation.

The theme of the summit, “25 years of the SCO: together for sustainable peace, development and prosperity”, is a message in itself to the world as the 21 leaders convene to formulate answers, build influence — and possibly new alliances to the rapidly changing world.

China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, together with other presidents and prime ministers, including Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian as well as UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, arrived in Bishkek on Monday to hold a series of bilateral meetings and later attending the opening of the World Nomad Games, a traditional Central Asian sports and culture event.

The SCO announced that Russia’s war in Ukraine, the Iran war with its far-reaching global economic consequences, as well as the push of the major and middle powers in the SCO for wider global influence, are among the main topics of this year’s gathering, while the host country Kyrgyzstan is aiming to advance the establishment of a SCO Development Fund and an Investment Fund for major projects.

Developing economic connectivity opportunities, including new energy and transport corridors, is also a key objective as the Iran war reshapes the world’s transit and supply chains.

'Golden period' of ties

Host of the summit Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi on his arrival in Bishkek, and the two leaders signed a treaty on “eternal good-neighbourliness, friendship and cooperation,” which, the Kyrgyz presidency said in a statement, acts as a comprehensive strategic partnership in the new era.

Xi described the China-Kyrgyzstan ties as a “golden period” of development.

Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov also held a flurry of bilateral talks on Monday with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith, Togolese President Faure Gnassingbe and Vietnamese Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan as well as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

As the US and the EU are actively increasing their presence in Central Asia, China is also pushing for a rapid economic engagement across Central Asia, with major transport and infrastructure projects being developed to connect China and the West through Central Asia, such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which is expected to shorten transport routes between Asia, the Middle East and southern Europe.

As industrial cooperation and transport connectivity are major priorities for Tashkent, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev arrived in Bishkek to also promote the Trans-Afghan Corridor connecting the rapidly developing infrastructure projects of Central Asia’s countries to Afghanistan and ports on the Indian Ocean.

Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan held a new round of peace talks in Bishkek on Monday to discuss the former rivals’ next steps in their historic peace process.

The two leaders also discussed new trade and energy cooperation as well as the key Middle Corridor projects through the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev also met his Azerbaijani counterpart to discuss trade and investments through joint regional projects.

Putin also arrived in Bishkek on Monday to make his mark on the regional summit and will meet Xi amid Moscow's faltering economy.

The Russian president is scheduled to meet Erdoğan to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine and Black Sea security, as well as Iran's Pezeshkian, as Moscow has been a strong supporter of Iran during its military confrontation with the United States and Israel.

Putin is also expected to meet Pashinyan following Moscow’s warnings against Yerevan’s newly announced intention to apply for EU membership.

World.title: Polish prosecutors launch terrorism investigation following fire at drone maker's factory
World.content:
Prosecutors in Poland have launched a terrorism investigation into a fire at a drone factory in the city of Skarżysko-Kamienna.

 

In a statement, prosecutors said the fire, which broke out at a WB Electronics factory, was started deliberately "by planting an explosive device containing flammable materials."

CCTV footage had reportedly captured an unidentified person in a balaclava who allegedly entered the premises after climbing a fence. A backpack and a sweatshirt were also found near the site.

WB Electronics is the largest private arms company in Poland. Its reconnaissance and attack drones are used by the Ukrainian armed forces.

Prosecutors said in their statement that an investigation had been launched into "participation in the activities of a foreign intelligence service against the Republic of Poland and the commission of a terrorist offense, consisting of the deliberate setting of a fire on August 31, 2026, on the premises of WB Electronics S.A. in Skarżysko-Kamienna."

It added: "As a result of the fire, warehouse facilities were destroyed, and the value of the damage caused amounts to at least 15 million PLN."

Investigation

The local fire service said the fire at the facility "was not large" and that firefighters took just under two hours to tackle it.

After the blaze had been put out, police officers secured the scene and began a detailed investigation.

A fire investigation expert is also working at the scene.

WB Group responds

The plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna produces components for unmanned systems destined for the Polish army.

Remigiusz Wilk of WB Group told TVN24 that the company has enjoyed the trust of the Polish military and other armies for years.

"We are, in a sense, part of Poland's security system as a major entity that cooperates with thousands of enterprises across the country – from very small firms to giants such as the Polish Armaments Group, which is a subcontractor in some of our projects," Wilk said.

"When it comes to unmanned systems worldwide, we are one of the largest manufacturers. These are not single platforms; they are systems linked together into one large 'ecosystem,'" he said.

Speaking about the fire, Wilk said the facility would be ready to resume production as soon as authorities completed their work. He added that he did not expect the incident to cause delays in deliveries to the Polish armed forces.

Second similar fire within 24 hours

The incident marked the second similar fire in 24 hours.

On Sunday, firefighters were called to a blaze at a warehouse in Lublin belonging to a company that produces aircraft parts.

Asked about a possible link between the two incidents, Karolina Galecka, a spokeswoman for the Polish Ministry of the Interior and Administration, said authorities would investigate every possible lead.

British newspaper "The Telegraph," citing western intelligence sources, recently reported on a series of suspected Russian sabotage operations in Europe targeting arms factories and companies supplying weapons to Ukraine.

According to those reports, the operations are being carried out in a way designed to stay below the threshold that could trigger NATO's Article 5, which commits allies to collective defence should one of them come under attack.

World.title: Magyar says EU must decide whether to 'survive or win' and slams Brussels' lack of leadership
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said the European Union is facing a leadership crisis and needs to make crucial decisions about its future not only to survive, but to win.

 

Magyar made the remarks at the Bled Strategic Forum, where he spoke alongside Slovenia's Janez Janša, Croatia's Andrej Plenković and Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš about regional cooperation and competitiveness.

"There is a lack of political leadership, to be honest, in the European Union," Magyar said, pointing to the EU's bureaucracy, which he said stifled action.

"I was told by a member of the European Council not to deal at all with the bureaucracy, not to reply to them, because they will kill initiatives. They will eat them. And it's not a good sign. I think we should concentrate again on the reality."

Magyar said that while the EU was focused on institutional questions, China is preparing to fund nuclear plants and car factories in Europe.

"There is a feeling already in Brussels as well that we should change, and in my view we should decide whether the European Union would only like to survive or to win," Magyar said.

The prime minister, who belongs to the same centre-right European People's Party as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, also criticised the EU's daily migration fine against Hungary.

Brussels fined Hungary a lump sum of €200 million, plus a daily penalty, in 2024, after Viktor Orbán's government failed to implement a 2020 European Court of Justice ruling on migration. The court had found that Hungary breached EU law by failing to guarantee asylum seekers the right to fair treatment.

"It's quite difficult to explain to Hungarians why Hungary is treated so unfairly in Brussels on these issues," Magyar said. "We have a court ruling; we have to pay €1 million a day just for defending the common European borders. It's not fair, and nobody is ready to resolve this issue."

Under Orbán's government, Hungary built a border fence with Serbia to prevent migrants from entering the country. Asylum applications were required to be lodged at Hungary's consulate in Belgrade, and the vast majority were rejected. Hungary has been hit with almost €1 billion in EU fines as a result.

During the election campaign, Magyar promised a complete reset in relations between Budapest and its Western allies in the EU and NATO.

After forming a government, he struck a deal with the European Commission to release €16.4 billion in previously frozen funds for Hungary. His government announced on Monday that it had delivered on all the milestones related to the €10 billion Recovery Fund by amending anti-corruption and justice laws.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”

World.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis guilty
World.content:
The jury reached a verdict in less than three hours in a case that had been unsolved for nearly 30 years.

A Las Vegas jury has found former gang leader, Duane "Keffe D" Davis, guilty of orchestrating the killing of hip hop artist Tupac Shakur.

Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25. He was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

More to follow…
