World.title: Montenegro Opposition Seeks Parliament Speaker’s Dismissal Over Mladic Condolences
World.content:
Parliament speaker Andrija Mandic addresses parliament in Podgorica, October 2023. Photo: EPA/BORIS PEJOVIC.

Montenegro’s main opposition party, the Democratic Party of Socialists, said on Monday it will seek the dismissal of parliamentary speaker Andrija Mandic over his decision to express condolences to the family of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb wartime commander convicted of genocide and other war crimes.

Danijel Zivkovic, the leader of the Democratic Party of Socialists, DPS, said the party would send an initiative to all parliamentary groups and independent lawmakers before formally submitting it to parliament.

Zivkovic said Mandic “had crossed a line that could no longer be ignored by expressing condolences following Mladic’s death”.

“For a long time we have been told that a distinction should be made between his personal political views and the office he holds, that we should show understanding for the stability of the government and that difficult issues should not be raised because of the European path,” Zivkovic told reporters in parliament.

“But there are moments when silence ceases to be political wisdom and becomes acquiescence. This is one of those moments,” he said.

Zivkovic said the initiative was not simply about Mandic, but a test for the other lawmakers in the ruling majority.

“We are not asking them to support the DPS, change the government or change their political relationship with Andrija Mandic,” he said.

“We are asking only one question – can a man who, from the position of parliament speaker, expresses such an attitude toward a legally convicted war criminal and a man responsible for genocide have their confidence to represent the parliament of a country that wants to become the next member of the EU?”

The initiative comes amid renewed controversy and divisions in Montenegro following Mladic’s death.

Mandic, the leader of the ruling pro-Serb New Serb Democracy party, said last week that he had sent condolences to Mladic’s son, Darko, “in his own name and in the name of New Serb Democracy”.

President Jakov Milatovic sharply criticised the move, saying that respect for Mladic’s family could not be used to play down war crimes.

His office said Mladic had been convicted of genocide in Srebrenica and other serious crimes by an international court and that this “must not be subject to political relativisation”.

Several other pro-Serb politicians also praised Mladic. Milan Knezevic, leader of the opposition Democratic People’s Party, posted a photograph of Mladic saying that “every Serbian household has one Ratko.”

The Serbian Orthodox Church’s Metropolitan Metodije of the Budimlje-Niksic Eparchy also praised Mladic, saying that Serbs had recognised in him “not only a great Serb and a man worthy of respect, but all the beautiful and holy qualities of the holy Serbian warriors and knights”.

Metodije said Mladic had “stoically” borne his conviction and that his death should serve as a lesson to Serbs not to abandon the path of their “holy ancestors”.

Montenegro’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic, who leads the Bosniak Party, another coalition member, took a sharply different position, saying a convicted war criminal, “both alive and dead, deserves only contempt”.

The Bosniak Party later said Ibrahimovic had received death threats and calls for his expulsion from Montenegro, torture and violence on social media. It urged the police and National Security Agency to assess and strengthen security for Ibrahimovic and his family.

Islamic Community leader Rifat Fejzic said Montenegro “cannot move forward while some officials glorify Mladic”, urging the government to “decisively put its house in order”.

Human Rights Action, a prominent Montenegrin rights group, meanwhile warned that there was no “military or human honour” in war crimes, and recalled that Montenegro’s criminal code punishes certain forms of public approval, denial or minimisation of genocide and war crimes established by final court judgments when they can incite violence or hatred.

Zivkovic said the DPS would proceed with the initiative regardless of whether it secures enough votes to remove Mandic, arguing that the vote itself would show where each lawmaker stands on the issue.

The positions of the Europe Now Movement and the Democrats, allies of Mandic’s party in the governing majority, are not yet known, but the motion is unlikely to pass in the 81-member parliament, as the three groups hold a majority even without the Bosniak Party.

“If there are 41 votes for his dismissal, Montenegro will say that, regardless of political differences, there are lines that must not be crossed,” he said. “If there are not, citizens will at least receive a clear answer about who considers preserving the majority more important than those lines.”

Political analyst Stefan Djukic told BIRN that a similar initiative had previously been launched over similar actions by the parliament’s speaker in 2014, but failed to result in his dismissal.

“I do not expect that to happen this time either,” Djukic said briefly.

The European Commission last Friday told Vijesti, responding to Mandic’s condolences to Mladic’s son, that “glorification of war criminals was contrary to fundamental European values and had no place either in the European Union or in candidate countries seeking membership.”

The Commission also recalled that Mladic was serving a life sentence for crimes against humanity and genocide in Srebrenica. “He was a war criminal,” the Commission said.

World.title: Kosovo’s Vetevendosje, LDK Agree on Ex-Judge as Joint Presidential Candidate
World.content:
Kosovo presidential candidate Bekim Sejdiu (C) at a joint press conference with (L-R) former President Vjosa Osmani, LDK leader Lumir Adbixhiku, LDK MP Lutfi Haziri, and Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti in Pristina on August 31, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Vetevendosje and the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK party agreed on Monday on a joint presidential candidate – a move that could end the country’s long-running political crisis.

Following a meeting between the respective party leaders, Albin Kurti and Lumir Abdixhiku, the latter announced Bekim Sejdiu, a former judge at the Constitutional Court and a former diplomat, as their pick for the vacant post.

“The talks were not easy, but they were exhaustive; we held long meetings and engaged in continuous, quite intense discussions. Both sides were committed to finding a consensus candidate for the president of Kosovo,” LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku told media at a joint press conference with acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti and MPs from the LDK and Vetevendosje.

“Various names were considered during the discussions. Ultimately, we agreed on one name: Professor Doctor Bekim Sejdiu,” Abdixhiku said.

“It is a great mark of trust and a great honour,” 51-year-old Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court and ambassador, who currently lectures in law, told the press conference.

“Although my ambitions have always leaned more towards the academic and professional spheres, I have – fully aware of the burden and responsibility entailed by the office of the president, and mindful of the current political context in the Republic of Kosovo – placed myself at the service of the republic, its citizens, and our state,” he added.

The agreement is a move towards ending the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June. Parliament has yet to be inaugurated since then, as political parties disagreed over who should be the next president – a position whose incumbent is elected by MPs. Without an agreement, new elections seemed inevitable.

Amid the institutional logjam, the provisional parliament speaker, Avni Dehari from election-winning party Vetevendosje, refused to resume the inaugural session that started on August 6. Vetevendosje also refused to submit a name for the new parliament’s speaker, as it first demanded an agreement with other parties on the election of a new president.

When announcing the deal on Monday, Abdixhiku called for the inauguration of parliament “without delays” and a vote for a new government before the vote for the new president.

In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting it well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats.

Kurti is likely to obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

In the presidential election, Sejdiu must receive at least 80 MPs’ votes in the first two rounds of voting to be confirmed in the role. In a potential third round, he would need a simple majority of 61 votes.

Sejdiu is a former judge of the Kosovo Constitutional Court and served as as ambassador to Turkey from 2008 to 2012, and as Kosovo’s consul general in New York from 2012 to 2014.

Since 2002, he has worked as an assistant professor in the Department of International Law at the University of Pristina’s Faculty of Law.

Sejdiu was also the rapporteur judge in the December 2020 Constitutional Court ruling that the government led by the LDK’s Avdullah Hoti was illegitimate because it was voted in with an invalid vote from a MP who had been convicted of a crime.

Most recently, he served as an adviser to then President Vjosa Osmani. Osmani returned to political activity with the LDK after her presidential mandate ended.

World.title: Two Kosovo Serbs Plead Guilty to Participating in 2022 Unrest
World.content:
Dusan Dobrac (R) and Milos Radosavlevic (L) at the Pristina Basic Court on August 31, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Dusan Dobrac and Milos Radosavlevic were given prison sentences of one year and nine months respectively at Pristina Basic Court on Monday after pleading guilty to violating the constitutional order by participating in setting up roadblocks in the north of Kosovo in December 2022.

Dobrac was convicted of activity that breaches the constitutional order and obstruction of an official in the performance of their duties, and Radosavlevic of violating the constitutional order.

The indictment charged six Kosovo Serb men – Dusan Maksimovic, Dusan Drobac, Milos Radosavljevic, Nemanja Jolovic, Nenad Orlovic and Srdjan Vucinic – with staging organised, coordinated and violent activity to subvert the constitutional order by blocking public roads to two border crossings with Serbia: Jarinje and Bernjak.

While Dobrac and Radosavlevic have been sentenced, the trial of Maksimovic, Jolovic, and Vucinic will continue, as they have not pleaded guilty. The sixth defendant, Orlovic has not been arrested yet and the judge announced that Kosovo will seek his arrest internationally as he has failed to appear in court for two hearings in a row.

The charges relate to unrest in December 2022, when Serbs in northern Kosovo were setting up barricades at the two border crossings with Serbia, parking trucks, ambulances, diggers and other vehicles across access roads in what was cast as a ‘spontaneous’ outpouring of popular anger. It began after the arrest of a Kosovo Serb on suspicion of attacking election facilities.

The prosecution file, seen by BIRN, claims the unrest endangered the lives of police and customs officers. Those involved also allegedly participated in creating “a tense security situation through the opening of fortified positions and the presence of uniformed and armed persons”, according to the prosecution.

During questioning, Maksimovic, Jolovic, and Vucinic denied any role in organising the barricades, saying they were only part of a protest by local residents. Orlovic refused to answer the prosecutors during questioning.

However, the police discovered a Viber group named ‘Barricades December 2022’ on Maksimovic’s phone, suggesting the incidents were organised and coordinated.

They acquired the phone in September 2023, after Maksimovic was arrested over his involvement in an armed attack on Kosovo police in the northern village of Banjska, in which one Kosovo Albanian officer was killed and a cache of military-grade weaponry was seized. He was sentenced in the first instance to 30 years in prison over the Banjska incident,

The contents of his phone helped prosecutors investigating the unrest in Serb-majority municipalities and the setting up of the barricades of December 2022. The messages it contained included “Today we’ll all receive ammunition” and “In the afternoon we could try the weapons in Suvi Dol [local village] with two or three bullets each.”

Prosecutors stated that the phone evidence undermined claims that local Serbs had spontaneously set up the barricades and sparked the unrest.

World.title: Warsaw’s Political Fight with Kyiv Is Being Settled on Polish Streets
World.content:
Anti-Ukrainian card

In June, Polish-Ukrainian relations made international headlines after President Volodymyr Zelensky was stripped of Poland’s highest order, and returned it by post. But the hostility did not begin with a single political dispute.

Last year, BIRN documented how during Poland’s presidential race candidates across the political spectrum reached for the “anti-Ukrainian card”, pushing the boundaries of what is acceptable to say in public.

“The campaign was the real turning point, because that was when Ukrainians living in Poland – and, more broadly, Ukraine and support for it – became a domestic political issue,” says Iwaniuk.

It was much easier to blame “failing public services” on Ukrainian ‘privileges’ than to fix the system itself, she says: “Populists need an enemy, and after other groups, including the LGBTQ community, it became the Ukrainians’ turn – because there were enough of them to turn resentment into political capital.”

Ideas that had once largely been confined to the political right moved into the mainstream. After taking office, President Karol Nawrocki vetoed an extension of the Ukrainian assistance law, arguing that the 800+ child benefit should be reserved for Ukrainians working in Poland. Revised legislation tied access to some benefits more closely to employment and school attendance. In March, Poland also began winding down much of the exceptional system created after the invasion.

For Bartlomiej Pejo, an MP from the right-wing Confederation party, measures limiting exceptional treatment are not evidence of hostility but a correction to policies he believes privileged Ukrainians over other foreigners. “The Polish state should treat all foreigners equally, without granting special privileges,” he tells BIRN.

Pejo condemns attacks against Ukrainians but rejects the idea that Poland is experiencing an extraordinary wave of hostility. He argues that crimes by Ukrainian citizens against Poles receive less attention, and that Polish anger over Ukrainian attitudes to the massacres committed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, or UPA, during World War II is too readily dismissed as prejudice.

That historical dispute has become impossible to separate from the deterioration in relations.

The latest escalation began in May, when President Zelensky granted a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title of “Heroes of the UPA”. The UPA tis celebrated by many Ukrainians for fighting for Ukrainian independence during World War II, but its members were also responsible for wartime massacres of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia. Responding to Zelensky’s decision, President Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest state decoration in June, which Zelensky famously returned by courier.

By July, for the first time since this question was asked in polling, 52 per cent of Poles opposed accepting Ukrainian refugees, against 42 per cent who supported it.

“In Poland, the feeling was roughly: ‘We helped them so much, we opened our homes to them, and in return they honour people responsible for the genocide of Poles’,” Dr Adamski explains. “In Ukraine, it was: ‘For four and a half years we’ve been fighting, suffering and, in doing so, defending Poland too from Russian aggression – and now they’re trying to tell us who we can and cannot regard as our national heroes.’

Russia has inevitably sought to amplify those tensions. An analysis by the Polish Institute of International Affairs found that between May 26 and July 13 the number of Polish-language social-media posts containing extreme anti-Ukrainian hate speech rose by 171 per cent, while engagement with them increased by 345 per cent. Russian fingerprints were visible throughout the surge: VKontakte (VK), Russia’s largest social network, was the most prominent forum, while coordinated pro-Kremlin networks such as Operation Pravda also featured prominently. The institute concluded that, while Moscow did not create the crisis, Russia has become its main beneficiary.

The deeper problem, Adamski argues, is cumulative. Older prejudices met Russian disinformation, social media and a coarsening political debate, while journalists and intellectuals lost some of their traditional role as gatekeepers. Resentments that might once have been moderated increasingly reach voters directly – and can be rewarded politically.

But carelessness has not been one-sided.

History itself is understood very differently in the two societies. Growing up in Kyiv, Iwaniuk says she was barely taught about Volhynia: “Poles are immersed in history. They talk about history in magazines, on television, at the dinner table.” In Soviet and post-Soviet Ukraine, by contrast, people were taught not to ask too many questions about the past. She remembers asking her father about the UPA and Volhynia when she was still a schoolgirl. He answered: “I don’t know – I think they were the ones who fought against everyone.”

That gap, she argues, helped produce remarkably hapless political gestures. For example, the former Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko knelt at a memorial to Polish victims of Volhynia a day after Kyiv renamed Moscow Avenue after UPA leader Stepan Bandera; Ukraine’s parliament recognised UPA members as independence fighters on the same day that former Polish president Bronislaw Komorowski was visiting Kyiv.

“President Zelensky certainly knew that Poland had a different view of the UPA than Ukraine, but I doubt the decision to name one of the units after the ‘Heroes of the UPA’ was meant as a deliberate provocation,” Adamski says. “My impression is that no one in Kyiv fully anticipated the fallout.”

There is also an economic asymmetry.

“Poland’s post-Communist transformation succeeded, while Ukraine is still fighting for survival as a state,” Iwaniuk argues. “While Poles have the luxury of looking back and debating the past, for Ukrainians the reaction is often: ‘Are you kidding? You want to talk about this now, when we don’t even know if our country will exist?’”

That does not make anti-Ukrainian violence an inevitable or legitimate consequence. But it helps explain how a relationship built on extraordinary solidarity became politically combustible.

The distinction is visible in another paradox that Iwaniuk points to: Ukrainians are becoming more integrated into Polish society just as the imagined collective “Ukrainian” is becoming more threatening in political discourse.

“They are your neighbour, the father of your child’s classmate, a colleague, the woman working in the local shop, someone running a business down the street,” she says. Yet the abstract Ukrainian is increasingly portrayed as a criminal, competitor or security threat.

Vladimir Medvedev, a Belarusian-born Polish citizen who founded the Glos Migranta (The Migrant’s Voice) initiative this summer, encountered another consequence when organising a recent migrants’ rights demonstration: people with legal status worried about far-right activists, provocations and deportation. Even a German acquaintance of his, married to a Polish woman and fluent in Polish, had been told to “fuck off to Ukraine” after somebody heard his accent.

Both governments now appear to understand the danger. Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk has publicly urged Warsaw and Kyiv to de-escalate, and recent bilateral talks have stressed the importance of “responsible communication” and a balanced tone in public debate.

On August 24, Warsaw hosted an event marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s declaration of independence at Castle Square, where blue and yellow flags flew next to the white and red ones.

But the political temperature does not fall on command. On August 14, a 14-year-old Ukrainian girl and her 12-year-old brother were allegedly abused and physically attacked near the railway station in Bydgoszcz after speaking Ukrainian. A woman was later charged with insulting them and violating their bodily integrity because of their nationality. She has denied the allegations.

World.title: Author Lea Ypi Explores Albanians’ Struggles for Dignity Under Communism
World.content:
Throughout her childhood, Lea Ypi knew her parents were “talking in secret”.

“My childhood was full of mysteries about my family,” she recalled.

Ypi, author of the acclaimed 2021 memoir Free: Coming of Age at the End of History and, more recently, Indignity: A Life Reimagined, was 11 when communism in Albania crumbled and only later came to learn of the suffering her grandparents endured under the Stalinist regime of Enver Hoxha.

“I grew up as a girl in a communist system, a child who believed in the truths of that system, while I understood that there was something in my family that was not exactly the way I saw it,” Ypi said in an interview with BIRN during a visit to Pristina as a guest lecturer at the annual International Seminar on Albanian Language, Literature, and Culture.

World.title: From Zvornik to Visegrad, Bosnian Serbs Keep Cult of Mladic Alive
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Hundreds of people marched through the streets of the eastern Bosnian city of Zvornik on Thursday night, clapping and chanting the name of the man convicted of some of the worst atrocities in Europe since World War II, glorifying his name as they paid tribute after his death in custody.

“Ratko Mladic!” they shouted in unison. “Ratko Mladic!”

In the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity, the cult of Mladic lives on. Significantly, many of the participants in the Zvornik march were young men who may not have even been born when the Bosnian Serb Army chief waged his bloody campaigns during the 1992-95 war.

“This is Zvornik, the city of the mass graves of my people,” Bosniak politician Camil Durakovic, vice president of Republika Srpska, wrote in a shocked reaction to the video footage.

World.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.

“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.

He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.

On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.

Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.

“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.

“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.

Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.

Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

World.title: Janika Lõiv 17th as gears fail at mountain bike worlds
World.content:
Reigning Estonian women's mountain biking champion Janika Lõiv finished 17th at the Mountain Bike World Championships in Val di Sole, Italy in particularly gruelling style.

Lõiv finished 5:44 behind the winner in the elite women's Olympic cross‑country race, Switzerland's Sina Frei, who won the gold in 1:27:50.

Lõiv said she had a strong start and felt good in the early laps. "The start went very well and I came out of the starting lap just 20 seconds behind the leader. During the first laps I tried to hold back a little because it was hot and I knew it would be a long race," she said.

However, her race took a technical turn for the worse on the third lap. "During the third lap I felt that the gears were sluggish — sometimes shifting, sometimes not. Until they stopped shifting altogether," explained the rider, who represented Estonia at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

This meant having to continue up slopes stuck in too high of a gear.

"Having to ride those 15‑20 percent climbs in one gear was a nightmare. Tears came to my eyes as I pushed myself up the hill through the pain."

Lõiv said while she managed to reset her gear system at a technical point, the damage was done. "Several riders passed me at once and my morale fell. I realised my legs were tired from that one crazy lap. From then on I rode at my own pace. My legs were cramping and I couldn't focus or think positive thoughts. I just wanted the finish to come quicker."

Of other Estonians competing, Mairit Kaarjärv finished 51st and Maribel Rannala 53rd in the women's under‑23 race, and Matthias Mõttus finished 58th in the men's equivalent.

World.title: Starting school in Estonia: Top tips for supporting your first grader
World.content:
For thousands of kids in Estonia, starting first grade on September 1 also means starting school. One psychologist offers tips to help families navigate this new chapter.

Children in Estonia generally start school at around seven years old, but Viktoriia Tkachuk, a psychologist at the Tartu Rajaleidja Center, explained in a video guide for "Let's Learn Together" that school readiness involves more than just a child knowing their letters and numbers.

Other factors include a child's emotional, social, cognitive, language and physical development, including their ability to focus, follow instructions, communicate and handle everyday tasks independently.

What matters most, Tkachuk said, is a child's overall, well-rounded development. A child who is curious, active, interested in learning, able to community and responsive to rules and requests is generally ready to start school.

"Other skills will develop along the way," she added.

Tkachuk said children should gradually learn to manage everyday tasks themselves, as independence can build confidence and reduce anxiety. Parents can help by involving kids in simple routines such as getting their school things ready in the morning.

The psychologist also advised encouraging a genuine interest in learning rather than drilling children on skills they'll need in school, including writing letters and numbers.

"The most important thing is to spark the child's interest," she said, warning that forced practice can ultimately backfire, leaving them tired and frustrated.

First graders starting school in Tallinn. September 1, 2022. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Starting school in a new language

Children starting school in a different language than those spoken at home face an entire extra layer of challenges, which Tkachuk said can leave even capable children feeling anxious, helpless or simply like an outsider.

Practicing communication skills at home can help, however, including learning basic Estonian phrases and roleplaying teacher-and-student situations in Estonian. Families can also make their own "My First 50 Estonian Words" dictionaries, and even watching cartoons and listening to music in Estonian can help.

At the same time, parents should also continue speaking their home language. Tkachuk said parents often worry this could cause their child to mix up languages or struggle to learn another one, but a strong first language can actually help children learn a second one.

"Your native language isn't an obstacle; it's a support," she emphasized.

As new first graders adjust to attending school, parents can help by talking about school positively, maintaining a predictable daily routine and making time each night to discuss how the day went.

A family in Tallinn on September 1. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

"Children are very sensitive to their parents' emotions, and when parents are calm and confident, kids feel that support," Tkachuk said, suggesting encouraging messages like "Your teacher will help you if you have trouble understanding something."

A lot to handle

If a child says they don't want to go to school, she recommends responding with curiosity rather than jumping straight to arguing. Kids starting school have to navigate new relationships, social skills and a much bigger workload, all while adults can sometimes forget just how young they still really are.

Above all, the psychologist stressed, parents should avoid comparing them with others, as all children are different.

"Talk with your kid about their day," she said. "Ask what surprised them today, and who they played with at recess. Hold space for all their emotions."

If something has put your child off of school, ask what happened or what exactly they don't like.

"Let them be sad, angry or tired, and support them without criticism," Tkachuk said, stressing the importance of maintaining home as a safe environment for your child to be themselves. "Remind them that mistakes are normal and that we're all learning."

When it comes to homework, parents should support their child without taking over. They can explain instructions and check work together, but should let their child solve problems themselves, and praise effort rather than just results.

Families on the first day of school in Estonia. Source: Anna Aurelia Minev/ERR

"Kids can quickly lose motivation when they feel there's no point in trying because their parent can just do it better anyway," Tkachuk explained.

A child refusing to do their homework should also be taken as a sign — and an opportunity to talk to them.

"Tell them, 'I can see this is hard for you,'" she suggested. "'Let's figure out together what to do. Do as much as you can; it doesn't have to be perfect.'"

Helping kids make friends

Social skills develop through practice, Tkachuk said, and simply playing with other children provides valuable opportunities to learn how to communicate, resolve conflicts and cooperate.

"It can also help to talk through social situations together," she said. "If your child has a conflict with someone, talk about what happened without judging. Ask what they think about why the other kid acted the way they did, or how things could have gone differently."

Families should also talk to their kids about how various classmates may speak different languages at home and may need extra time to feel comfortable.

"They may avoid talking to other children even if they really want to because they are afraid of making linguistic mistakes," the psychologist explained.

Student on their first day of school in Estonia. Source: Anna Aurelia Minev/ERR

"But sometimes," she added, "just one friend is all it takes for a child who speaks a different language to feel more comfortable in a new environment."

Ask for help too

While adjusting to starting school can take several months, if your child continues to struggle, Tkachuk said it's worth seeking extra help.

"You can reach out to a psychologist, as well as contact a Rajaleidja center for educational advice and support," she said, adding that families can also talk to their child's teachers or school specialists.

"School is a big step toward independence, but the journey should be shared by the child, their parents and their teachers," Tkachuk said. "You are not alone in this process."

"Let's Learn Together" is a new online resource offering families practical guidance on navigating education in Estonia, from how the kindergarten and school system works to information on what additional help and resources are available.

Available in English, Estonian, Russian and Ukrainian, the site features articles, personal stories, podcasts and videos in which parents, young people and experts share their experiences with adapting to multilingual and multicultural life and education in Estonia.

All "Let's Learn Together" video guides include subtitle options on YouTube.

World.title: Association: While mistrust of AI still high, 3 out of 4 firms still use it
World.content:
The the Estonian Marketing Association (Eesti turundajate liit) noted cost savings is not always the main driver, but whatever the reasoning, AI should remain a tool and not an end in itself.

Supermarket Maxima runs around 300 campaigns a year which make use of AI. Its sales and marketing manager Jaanika Terasmaa said the technology allows ad agencies to bring hot ideas to meetings. "The agency comes to every meeting with a live idea, because it has been able to make quick clips of what a new advertising campaign could look like," Terasmaa told "Aktuaalne kaamera".

In any case, if agencies have been using AI, this has not been detrimental to campaigns, she went on.

"Unfortunately, or fortunately, an advertising agency is made up of people, so we don't recognize that from the price list, but we have been seeing better and more interesting quality in the content," Terasmaa added.

AI-created Ad on a billboard. Source: ERR

Kent Raju, creative director at Kala Ruudus, an advertising agency, said AI should remain a tool, not a final product. "We don't start by writing a command, but rather come up with an idea which is right for the brand," he said.

He criticised the use of AI for more simple tasks, such as restaurant menus, and which can be quite obvious. "I feel bad looking at the waste of artificial intelligence – material where restaurant menu pictures are taken with AI – for what purpose? You can take a real picture of real food, but it came with AI and it seems like the wrong choice."

Musician Mikk Saar said AI has created ads for events he has been a part of which have had defects, such as distorted faces or incorrect text, and he now wants to be consulted before ads get run. "A party won't be canceled, but if the poster is made with AI and everything is distorted, I won't be sharing it on social media – which means the organizer loses out. It doesn't match my brand image."

In any case, old‑fashioned advertising seems to be making a comeback. "It's become very popular to put out an ad and show that you actually made it," said Anniken Haldna, CEO of the marketing Association. This fact can get as many views as the ad itself, she added

The growing use of AI in advertising has also raised concerns about authenticity and trust. Studies cited by the association suggest that consumers are nowadays generally sceptical of AI‑generated ads, while experts warn that overuse could lead to a greater spread misinformation, as well as damaging companies' credibility. Creative professionals say the human perspective remains essential, with AI best employed as an aid rather than a replacement for human creativity.

World.title: School year opens with hundreds of students still waiting for placement
World.content:
As of Monday, 575 young people who finished basic school this spring still do not have a new school place registered in the Estonian Education Information System. The lists continue to change constantly, as some students decline the places offered to them, after which those places are offered to the next candidates.

The situation is especially tense in the capital. "There really aren't many free places in Tallinn," said Krista Keedus, head of education management at the Tallinn Education Department. "Estonian‑language high schools have completed their admissions and all places are filled," she added.

Tallinn's municipal high schools currently do not have the capacity to add more places, due to both space limitations and a shortage of teachers, Keedus said.

"There is no immediate plan to create additional places," she noted, pointing to the need to wait for the final data on needs and available places on 10 September.

The filling of school places is also strongly affected by the influx of residents from neighboring municipalities, as nearly 27 percent of students admitted to Tallinn's 10th grades for the new school year are not residents of the capital.

Tallinn's municipal high schools currently do not have the capacity to add more places. Source: Anna Aurelia Minev/ERR

Although high school places in Tallinn are full, there are still available study places at Tallinn Applied College and the technology college Tehno Tallinn. Keedus encouraged students without a place to consider vocational education: "Our vocational education is not only vocational training — it is also vocational secondary education." "They could at least try continuing their studies there first, and if it truly doesn't suit them, then look again for a gymnasium place," she said.

Places in preparatory studies — intended for students with weaker final results — were also filled already in the summer. Discussions are currently underway with the Ministry of Education about creating additional places based on need.

The final deadline for local governments to offer solutions to students in need is 1 November, but officials are already trying to contact young people now to understand why they have ended up without a school place.

"It is of course sad if young people haven't managed to secure a school place by 1 September and cannot start their school year," Keedus said. "But that doesn't mean starting later — a few days or even weeks — would be impossible. Their learning opportunities are certainly not locked," she added.

Keedus also pointed out that in previous years, the number of young people who ended their education after basic school was similar or slightly smaller, although monitoring was incomplete before the study obligation was introduced.

"The ministry has monitored each year how many young people do not reach the next level of education, and that number has usually been around 400–500," Keedus said.

"Previously, this was not a legal problem. It was, however, a problem for the young people and for Estonia as a whole, because those who continue their education have better chances of coping in life — which is why the study obligation was established. Until now, this issue wasn't directly on the table, because young people had the freedom to go to work, for example, and therefore we did not conduct this kind of ongoing monitoring at the start of the school year," Keedus explained.

World.title: 'Even If...' campaign assures sexual assault survivors help is available
World.content:
A new Estonian campaign is reminding survivors of sexual violence that they can seek free, 24/7 help even if they lack the words or don't remember everything.

The Social Insurance Board's (SKA) "Even If..." campaign highlights the free, round-the-clock assistance and care available at dedicated sexual violence crisis centers (SAKs) across Estonia.

It addresses three common reasons survivors may hesitate to seek help: "Even if no one saw," "Even if you don't remember everything," and "Even if you can't find the right words."

"After experiencing sexual violence, your memories may be patchy, and you may feel confused, angry, ashamed or guilty," said Kai Part, a gynecologist at the Tartu University Hospital (TÜK) center. "These are normal trauma responses to an abnormal event."

No police report or referral needed

Estonia's sexual violence crisis support centers are free and open 24/7 to anyone who has experienced sexual violence or suspects they may have, regardless of age or gender.

The sooner someone seeks help, the better, but it's still worth coming to a crisis center even after changing clothes, showering or waiting some time before deciding to seek help.

No referral or police report is required, and minors can also seek help independently.

Sexual violence crisis centers offer medical examinations, evidence collection, pregnancy prevention, STI testing and treatment, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and counseling.

The centers will also help people access further psychological and other help, and provide support if a victim chooses to contact the police.

"People can decide for themselves what help they want to receive," Part said. "That can also be the beginning of healing — when they can once again decide what happens to them."

Patient at a psychiatrist appointment. Photo is illustrative. Source: Sigmund/Unsplash

Five centers across the country

Annika Silde, head of violence victims services at SKA, emphasized that anyone can become a victim of sexual violence, regardless of age, gender or background.

"You don't have to prove what happened or explain why you reacted a particular way in order to seek help at a SAK," she said. "The responsibility always lies with the perpetrator."

Sexual violence crisis centers operate at five hospitals across Estonia: West Tallinn Central Hospital (LTK), Tartu University Hospital (TÜK), Pärnu Hospital, Ida-Viru Central Hospital (IVKH) in Kohtla-Järve and Kuressaare Hospital in Saaremaa.

In 2025, 268 people sought help at the centers, including 106 minors. Women accounted for 95 percent of those seeking help.

SKA's "Even If..." campaign runs in public and online through September 13.

More help available

If you have experienced, are experiencing or think you may be experiencing domestic abuse, domestic violence or sexual violence, or are otherwise in crisis, help is available.

In case of emergency, call 112. Estonia's five sexual violence crisis centers (SAKs) are open 24/7 in Tallinn, Tartu, Pärnu, Kohtla-Järve and Kuressaare. On-call psychiatric care can also be reached by phone 24/7 in Tallinn at +372 617 2650, in Tartu at +372 731 8764 and in Pärnu at +372 447 3281. The Eluliin emotional support hotline is open daily from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. in Estonian (+372 655 8088) and in Russian (+372 655 5688). Another emotional support hotline is available every day from 10 a.m. to midnight in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 123. The Ohvriabi victim support hotline is available 24/7 in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 006. The child helpline is also open 24/7 in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 111.

World.title: Pioneering Estonian curling duo Kaldvee and Lill split after 11 years
World.content:
The duo, who won silver at the 2024 World Championships and were named Estonian Team of the Year the same year, made history as the first Estonians to compete in mixed doubles curling at the Olympics, which they did in February this year at the at the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics.

"We played together for 11 years — it's a very long and successful collaboration. We are both very proud of what we achieved," Lill told ERR. "The decision didn't come easily. We met several times and discussed what to do, as we always do after an Olympic cycle. This time we decided to go our separate ways, but we are both staying in curling."

Lill outlined just how extraordinary their sporting journey had been, starting from training in a Soviet-era munitions plant. "What we did is quite impossible — you come from an old Soviet rocket factory and make it to the Olympics," he said with emotion. "Against all the odds, we made it happen. I'm deeply proud of that."

Asked if he had any regrets, Lill said: "Every athlete feels they could have done better. We are ambitious people and always aimed high. We gave our maximum and achieved great results."

Lill will continue in the mixed doubles, partnering with Karoliine Kaare, his life partner. Kaldvee is to captain an all-new new Estonian women's team. "There were options — not too many, we are in Estonia after all," Lill joked. "With Karoliine, we decided it was worth trying. You never know how a new team will work, so we'll give our best and see what happens."

Kaldvee is at the helm of a young and talented women's team with Czech coach Jakub Bareš already on board. Lill was buoyant about the team's prospects. "Marie is Estonia's most experienced curler," he said. "She has captained the national team before. She will lead a young and talented team, preparing for the European Championships and the B‑division World Championships."

Lill and Karoliine Kaare. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"If I ever leave curling, I want the sport to be in a better place than when I started. It would be sad if we just walked away and didn't pass on what we've learned," he reflected.

The Lill-Kaare new sporting pairing's immediate goal is to qualify for the World Championships in January. "First we need to qualify from Estonia," Lill said. "November will see who gets to represent Estonia."

In an Instagram post, the duo wrote: "One chapter ends but the journey continues! From an old Soviet missile factory to the Olympics. Against all the odds, we made Estonian curling history."

Kaldvee and Lill placed 10th at the 2026 Winter Olympics.

World.title: Population of major forest pest drops for second straight year
World.content:
Three to four years ago, the population of spruce bark beetles in Estonian forests was still increasing, but in recent years it has been trending downward.

The spruce bark beetle is a small insect, growing only 4–5 millimeters long. During mass reproduction, however, they are capable of killing large spruce trees and entire spruce stands.

Cooler and wetter summer weather has helped reduce their numbers, and the number of the beetle's natural enemies has also grown.

The spruce bark beetle is monitored across Estonia by the Environmental Agency in cooperation with the State Forest Management Center (RMK). In some counties in South Estonia, the Estonian University of Life Sciences also operates its own monitoring stations. Both the university's data and nationwide monitoring results show that the beetle's population has been declining over the past two years.

The beetle's population was very high in 2022 based on RMK and agency monitoring data, said Merit Ehrpais, senior specialist at the Environmental Agency.

A patch of forest with bark beetle damage in Ida-Viru County. Source: Dmitri Fedotkin/ERR

In 2023, the population remained high, but a downward trend began to appear in some counties. In 2024, the decline became clearer, and the 2025 results were even lower than those of 2024.

Kristjan Ait, junior researcher in forest management and forest ecology at the Estonian University of Life Sciences, added that based on this year's available data, the catch numbers are relatively modest. One direct factor influencing beetle numbers is Estonia's summer weather.

"Last summer was generally cool and rainy, which kept the population lower. This year's spring was also extremely unfavorable for the beetles: their flight began quite late, in early May," he said. Typically, the beetles begin flying in mid‑April. This year's spring dragged on, remaining cool and rainy, which further affected beetle numbers.

Ehrpais confirmed that results from pheromone traps show a clear link between weather and beetle activity. During cooler, wetter, and windier weeks, beetle spread is lower, while warmer periods bring higher numbers again.

In addition, the number of the beetle's natural enemies — such as bark beetle flies, ant beetles, and birds — has increased over the years. Their numbers have reached a level where they can now limit the beetle population more effectively.

Meelis Matkamäe Autor/allikas: Erlend Štaub

Meelis Matkamäe, chairman of the Estonian Private Forest Union and CEO of Rakvere Forest Cooperative, has also noticed that there have been fewer beetle outbreaks in the past two years.

"The last two years have been quite good, especially in managed stands. The spruce bark beetle mostly infests weakened trees, and in a properly managed forest it is generally difficult for the beetle to establish a colony. But in unmanaged stands — for example those with storm damage or weakened trees — it can operate more freely, and conditions for reproduction are much better," Matkamäe said.

Ait added that managed forests offer better opportunities to limit beetle numbers, and mixed stands also provide poorer breeding conditions for them.

What will happen to the beetle population in the future is impossible to predict. "Right now the situation is fairly normal, but nature is constantly changing. What will happen in a couple of years, we don't know. Many influencing factors are things you can't directly see. For example, how root rot develops and affects spruce health, or whether new drought periods or storm damage occur — any of these could turn this calm period upside down," Ait said.

World.title: Photos: Kaido Ole's exhibition "Krt" opens at Temnikova & Kasela gallery
World.content:
On 28 August, Kaido Ole's new solo exhibition "Krt" opened at the Temnikova & Kasela gallery in Tallinn.

Ole's new exhibition focuses on the artist's recent paintings, where a recurring motif of burning becomes a tool for giving shape to something difficult to define — an all‑encompassing "bad."

Ole describes the exhibition as an attempt to "move the bad out of oneself and into the pictures." "Through art, the bad can find a place, and the world can at least momentarily return to balance," the artist explained.

"Krt" is Kaido Ole's third exhibition this year. At the beginning of the year, he opened the show "Müüa maja Raplas" in Rapla, and in February he presented examples from his art collection at Vaal Gallery.

The exhibition "Krt" will remain open at Temnikova & Kasela gallery until 10 October.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate increases against Iraqi dinar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar experienced an increase on Monday in both Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,541.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,540 Iraqi dinars on Sunday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,545 Iraqi dinars and 1,535 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate increased, fluctuating between 1,541.5 and 1,541 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars to every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraqi judiciary sentences kidnapper of US journalist to 15 years in prison
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Central Criminal Court sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim, a member of the Iran-backed group Kataeb Hezbollah, to 15 years in prison under the country’s anti-terrorism law for kidnapping US journalist Shelly Kittleson on March 31.

Kittleson was kidnapped during the daytime on Saadoun Street in central Baghdad. Armed gunmen pushed her into a silver vehicle, while another getaway car crashed during the escape. Iraqi security forces intercepted the crashed car and arrested Lazim.

The US journalist was kept hostage for more than a week when Kataeb Hezbollah freed her in early April ahead of a US-Iran ceasefire.

Kittleson, who has extensively covered the Middle East for publications like the BBC and Politico, expressed her gratitude to the Iraqi justice system on X and affirmed her right to seek compensation.

This decision marks a rare court step against a major, Tehran-aligned armed group in Iraq.

The verdict comes at a critical time for Iraq’s new government, led by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, which is under intense pressure from Washington to disarm pro-Iran militias and place all weapons under strict state control.

The effort to disarm Kataeb Hezbollah has pushed Iraq into a severe security and political crisis, as the group has rejected the government’s disarmament mandates and vowed to expand its military arsenal.

World.title: Iraq discusses oil and gas development with BP, ConocoPhillips
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair and representatives from British Petroleum (BP) and Texas-based ConocoPhillips discussed on Monday the development of Iraq’s oil and gas industry.

The meeting held in Baghdad included BP’s Iraq director Zaid al-Yasiri, Nader Zaki, Ariel Flores, and ConocoPhillips representative William Arnold, as well as senior Iraqi officials in the oil sector.

The discussions addressed strategic advancements to maximize the utilization of Iraq’s hydrocarbon resources, optimize field development, and upgrade extraction technologies, according to a statement cited by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The Iraqi Oil Ministry activated in early August its Kirkuk oilfield contract with BP, a project aiming to elevate crude oil production from its current capacity of 320,000 barrels per day to a peak target of 420,000 barrels per day.

The deal expands crude extraction while capturing associated gas to eliminate gas flaring and provide fuel for power plants.

The activation of the Kirkuk project represents a major step in Iraq’s broader energy strategy to achieve natural gas self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on imported fuel.

ConocoPhillips has agreed to purchase a 42 percent share in BP’s Kirkuk project, boosting its position in Iraq by redeveloping four key oil resources in the northern Iraqi province.

ConocoPhillips Chairman Ryan Lance said that the investment aligns with the company’s conservative approach by offering access to a big, high-quality, and long-life resource base while needing very little expenditure.

The agreement represents another initiative by Iraq to attract foreign investments and boost production from its aging oil assets, as well as to strengthen partnerships with prominent global energy companies.

World.title: India to receive first Iraqi oil shipment in five months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – India is preparing to receive its first shipment of Iraqi oil in five months, a development reflecting the return of Iraq’s crude oil flows to one of Asia’s largest oil markets, despite ongoing shipping challenges across the Strait of Hormuz.

India’s Bharat Petroleum expects to receive the shipment within the next few days. The tanker carrying Iraqi oil has already passed through the Strait of Hormuz and arrived in Fujairah, UAE, for a ship-to-ship transfer, according to Reuters.

Bharat Petroleum’s Chief Financial Officer, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, said that the company secured a vessel to load the Iraqi shipment and transport it to Fujairah. There, the oil will be transferred from ship to ship before reaching the company’s refineries.

These arrangements reflect the efforts of Asian refiners to find flexible logistical solutions for securing crude oil at a time when transportation cost, insurance, and tanker availability have become crucial factors in determining the viability of purchasing shipments from the Gulf region.

The Indian company typically requires around two million barrels of Iraqi oil per month, making a consistent supply from Baghdad crucial to meeting its refinery’s crude oil needs.

Bharat Petroleum has not disclosed the name of the vessel used to transport the shipment but stated that the ship’s owner agreed to load the crude and proceed to Fujairah for a ship-to-ship transfer.

Iraq is one of the countries most affected by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, given that a significant portion of its oil exports depend on ports located on the Arabian Gulf.

World.title: Iraq exports 21 million barrels of fuel oil through Syria
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s fuel oil exports through Syria have seen a significant increase since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28.

Iraqi oil flows via neighboring Syria are part of alternative routes for the country’s oil shipments to global markets following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Total Iraqi fuel oil exports transported via Syria reached 21.4 million barrels between March and the end of August 2026.

This step is part of Baghdad’s continuous efforts to establish alternate export channels amid shipping disruptions via the Strait of Hormuz, the country’s primary maritime trade artery, which led to unprecedented challenges to the oil industry.

Iraqi fuel oil began flowing overland through Syrian territory after the Iraqi state-owned oil marketing company (SOMO) reached deals to transport approximately 650,000 tons per month (approximately 4.7 million barrels) to be stored at the Baniyas port before being shipped to global markets.

Iraqi fuel oil shipments via Syria increased rapidly between March and the end of August 2026.

Iraq’s fuel oil exports through Syria were 254,000 barrels in March, 686,000 barrels in April, 3.86 million barrels in May, five million barrels in June, 5.65 million barrels in July, and 5.91 million barrels in August.

World.title: Iraq imported $52.4M in potatoes in 2025: Expert urges supply chain reforms
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq imported approximately 90,000 tonnes of potatoes valued at $52.4 million in 2025, according to specialized agricultural market data from IndexBox, highlighting a structural gap in domestic agricultural supply chains and food security planning.

Economic researcher Ali Karim Idheeb stated on Monday, August 31, 2026, that trade volumes across core vegetable crops demonstrate that domestic output remains vulnerable to seasonal volatility, regional price shocks, and supply disruptions.

Trade Figures and Regional Sourcing

2025 Potato Import Totals: ~90,000 tonnes with an aggregate import value of $52.4 million.

Primary Source Markets: The Iraqi market relies predominantly on regional agricultural exporters, led by Iran, Egypt, and Turkey.

Price Transmission Factors: Consumer prices in Iraqi wholesale markets are directly influenced by freight logistics, climate shocks affecting export yields, and input pricing within supplier countries.

Economic Opportunity: The $52.4 million import bill represents capital that could be retained within the domestic economy through targeted investments in post-harvest cold storage, yield optimization, and certified seed propagation.

World.title: CBI: Iraq’s domestic public debt reaches 106T dinars in H1 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s domestic public debt surged to 106.072 trillion IQD (approximately $80.97 billion) by the end of June 2026, up from 103.179 trillion IQD at the end of May, according to official financial data published by the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) on Monday, August 31, 2026.

The monthly jump of 2.893 trillion IQD caps a broader upward trajectory over the first half of the year, with total domestic liabilities expanding by 15.557 trillion IQD from 90.515 trillion IQD recorded at year-end 2025.

World.title: Integrity Commission halts 550-dunam land auction in Anbar, saving 19B dinars
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Federal Commission of Integrity announced on Monday, August 31, 2026, that it has successfully halted the fraudulent sale and auction procedures of a prime 550-dunam state-owned real estate parcel in Anbar Governorate, preventing the squandering of over 19.25 billion IQD (approximately $14.7 million) in public funds.

According to an official statement received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the operation was executed by a field investigation unit from the Commission’s Anbar Investigation Office as part of its ongoing oversight of state-owned properties nationwide.

Field investigators conducted comprehensive on-site audits and cross-referenced documentation across the State Real Estate Department in Anbar, the Urban Planning Directorate, and the City Organization Division at the Ramadi Municipality Directorate:

Location & Unauthorized Sale: The 550-dunam plot is situated within the master plan designated for the future urban expansion of Ramadi. It had been auctioned and sold to an individual buyer without obtaining statutory municipal approvals from the Ramadi Municipality Directorate.

Severe Undervaluation: The official appraisal committee at the Anbar State Real Estate Department had valued the property at just 25.09 million IQD per dunam, resulting in a total sale price of 13.75 billion IQD.

Market Discrepancy: The Commission’s field investigators analyzed land coordinates and comparable market pricing, referencing the General Commission for Taxes’ benchmark guidelines. They determined that the actual market value stands at 60 million IQD per dunam, bringing the true aggregate value to 33.00 billion IQD.

Total Prevented Loss: The fraudulent undervaluation represented a direct financial deficit of 19,250,000,000 IQD against the state treasury.

Comparison of Real Estate Valuations

World.title: Bihar, Jharkhand settle 25-year Sone water row
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Bihar and Jharkhand Monday signed a water-sharing agreement for Sone river, resolving a 25-year-old dispute over sharing of water between the two states.

The agreement, signed here in the presence of union home minister Amit Shah and CMs of Bihar and Jharkhand â Samrat Choudhary and Hemant Soren respectively â will provide irrigation water to millions of farmers across vast rural areas of the states, while also ensuring access to drinking water for the people in both the states.

Shah said the agreement is an excellent example of the âTeam Bharatâ vision and cooperative federalism championed by PM Modi. âWhile all states possess their own distinct identities, if they move forward as âTeam Bharatâ within the national context, there is no problem which cannot be resolved,â he said after the signing of the agreement.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

He said that issues concerning vast geographical areas, farmers, rural regions, and drinking water supplies in both states have been âpermanently resolvedâ with the agreement.

Sharing details, the home minister said the agreement would ensure the availability of adequate water for drinking and irrigation to a large population across the districts of Bhojpur, Buxar, Rohtas, Kaimur, Aurangabad, Arwal, Gaya, and Patna in Bihar. âMoreover, water would become available for irrigation and drinking purposes in Palamu, Garhwa, and other regions of Jharkhand,â he said.

Though an agreement was reached among Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and undivided Bihar on the water sharing of Sone river and the cost of Bansagar dam in Madhya Pradesh in 1973, a dispute started in 2000 when Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar as a new state and it demanded a bigger share of water in Bansagar project as a large chunk of the catchment area came under it. Bihar, on the other hand, cited the 1973 agreement to claim water from the project.

NEW DELHI: The National Cybercrime Threat Analytics unit (NCTAU), under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), has warned users of financial fraud through sideloaded malicious Android apps masquerading as porn apps which, when downloaded, take control of usersâ devices by abusing accessibility permissions.NCTAU said misleading Facebook and Instagram ads under the names Night Play, Reloop, Kyss, Riva, Vima, Nexo and Vixa were redirecting users to phishing websites featuring pornographic content, with a prompt to download the APK file from outside the Google Play Store. World.title: IMD predicts below-normal rainfall over country in September
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Monthly rainfall over the country as a whole is most likely to be below normal in Sept, the last month of the monsoon season, said IMD Monday - an indication that the four-month rainy season is likely to end with overall deficient cumulative rainfall, as was predicted earlier due to the impact of El Nino.

IMD said Aug, which reported a deficit of more than 16% in monthly rainfall in the country despite good rains in certain parts, was the warmest Aug in India since 1901, recording a mean temperature of 28.010Â°C.

Region-wise, South peninsular India recorded its second-warmest Aug since 1901. East and northeast India recorded their third-warmest, while northwest India saw its fifth-warmest, Aug in 126 years.

So far, the country as a whole has reported a deficit of 14% in cumulative (June 1-Aug 31) rainfall, despite ânormalâ rainfall in July.

In June, the deficit was as high as 35%. Out of a total of 741 districts assessed for monsoon rainfall distribution, 312 (42%) received âbelow-normalâ rainfall and 38 districts (5%) reported large deficient rainfall till Aug 31.

A forecast of âbelow-normalâ rainfall in Sept may lead to a deficit in overall kharif acreage. Though the sowing of most seasonal crops is almost complete, with a decline in acreage of nearly 2% compared with the corresponding period last year, low rainfall in Sept implies an increase in input cost due to farmersâ spending on irrigation of standing crops.





âSpatially, many parts of the country are likely to receive below-normal rainfall, but some areas of northwest, northeast, east, east-central and south-east peninsular India are likely to receive ânormal to above-normalâ rainfall,â said IMD chief Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

He said âstrong El NiÃ±o conditionsâ are currently prevailing over the equatorial Pacific Ocean, with sea surface temperature remaining above normal across central and eastern equatorial Pacific.

âThese conditions are expected to strengthen further in the coming months,â said Mohapatra, hinting at its negative impact on Sept rainfall.

El NiÃ±o is invariably associated with a weak monsoon and a harsh summer in India.

At present, neutral Indian Ocean Dipole conditions prevail over Indian Ocean, which are likely to persist through Sept.This means that monsoon may not benefit from this climatic phenomenon as only positive IOD helps increase rainfall activities.

World.title: U.S. Supreme Court allows Trump's ballroom project to proceed
World.content:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday (August 31, 2026) allowed President Donald Trump to continue construction of his White House ballroom, granting him a major victory against opponents of the project.

The conservative-dominated court voted 5-4 to lift a lower order demanding construction be halted, with Chief Justice John Roberts notably joining the court's three liberals in dissent.

Mr. Roberts earlier this month issued a temporary order to allow construction while the full court weighed the matter.

The project has roiled Washington, with critics saying Trump acted unlawfully by unilaterally ordering the demolition of the entire White House East Wing.

The court decision means construction will advance, while a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation will play out in lower courts — a process that could take months or years.

The National Trust did not immediately return AFP's request for comment.

In its decision the court said that the government was likely to eventually win the ongoing lawsuit because the National Trust probably did not have the right to bring the claim in the first place.

The organization's case is grounded by one of its members, Washington resident Alison Hoagland, who claims that seeing the finished ballroom would result in damage to her "aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests," due to its size.

"This Court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury," under the US constitution, the five justices wrote in their ruling.

"Perhaps nearly any government action or project offends someone's sensibilities," they added.

However, those justices made clear that they were not making a final ruling on the legality of the ballroom project, just that construction could continue while the case is argued and decided in lower courts.

The dissenting justices wrote that the project was "likely unlawful," because "Congress has not passed any law resembling 'express authority'" for the administration to undertake it — despite a law requiring it to do so.

They also argued that Hoagland's claims "suffices for standing."

While the ballroom has drawn headlines, the project also includes a military bunker.

A district court and, later, an appellate court, halted work on the ballroom while allowing construction on the military facility to continue.

The president has trumpeted the ballroom as necessary for hosting galas and state dinners, while also stressing the national security need for the bunker.

World.title: After Supreme Court judge’s letters, Collegium recommends new Chief Justice for Rajasthan HC
World.content:
The Supreme Court Collegium on Monday (August 31, 2026) recommended Chhattisgarh High Court judge, Justice Sanjay K. Agrawal, for appointment as the Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court.

The resolution by the Collegium headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant came days after letters written by serving top court judge Justice Sandeep Mehta, complaining of the conduct of Rajasthan Acting Chief Justice S.P. Sharma, became public.

Justice Mehta, in a series of three letters in August, had accused Justice Sharma of “favouritism” and misconduct. The Supreme Court judge highlighted that his entreaties to Chief Justice Kant to transfer Justice Sharma out of Rajasthan failed to evoke any response.

Justice Mehta had sought a regular Chief Justice for the Rajasthan High Court. Justice Sharma had been the Acting Chief Justice for the past 10 months.

Chief Justice Kant had issued a press statement the same day the letters came into the public domain.

In his statement, the CJI had said the Collegium would consider Justice Mehta’s allegations through an institutional mechanism.

The Collegium has also recommended new Chief Justices for two other High Courts – Madhya Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

Justices Alpesh Yeshvant Kogje of Gujarat and Dr. Pushpinder Singh Bhati of Rajasthan have been suggested for appointment as Chief Justices of Madhya Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Courts, respectively.

In a separate resolution, the Supreme Court Collegium said it had recommended, in a meeting held on August 6, to appoint Justice Krushna Ram Mohapatra, a judge of the High Court of Orissa, as Chief Justice of the Chhattisgarh High Court on the retirement of the incumbent on September 4, 2026.

The Collegium has, in a separate resolution, recommended the immediate transfer of Justice Agrawal to the Rajasthan High Court, pending his appointment as its Chief Justice.

World.title: NCLT's first-ever 5-member Bench to decide on Subhash Chandra repayment plan
World.content:
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) on Monday (August 31, 2026) formed a five-member Bench to decide on media baron Subhash Chandra's repayment plan in a personal insolvency case involving claims of more than ₹22,000 crore after a Division Bench failed to reach a majority verdict.

The Division Bench had referred the personal insolvency case against the Essel Group chairman to the tribunal's president for fresh adjudication after failing to reach majority consensus on a proposed ₹6.5 crore repayment plan despite referring the matter to a third judge.

The five-member Bench, formed for the first time in the NCLT's history, will be led by president Justice Anupinder Singh Grewal. The other members are Bachu Venkat Balaram Das, Mahendra Khandelwal, Atul Chaturvedi and Ravindra Chaturvedi. The Bench will start hearing at 10.15 a.m. on Tuesday in the Principal Bench of NCLT.

Earlier, the matter had been referred to the third member, as the two-member Division Bench of Ashok Kumar Bhardwaj (Member Judicial), and Reena Sinha Puri (Member Technical), gave a split verdict on the repayment plan.

Third member’s order

The third member's order, dated August 26, backing the ₹6.5 crore repayment plan, was sent back to the original Division Bench for a formal order in line with the majority opinion, as required under Section 419 (5) of the Companies Act, 2013.

However, the Division Bench on Monday said no majority view has emerged despite reconsidering the matter, following a differing opinion from a third member of the tribunal, and referred the matter back to the NCLT president. The Bench said the "Third Member consciously passed an independent order. Thus, no majority view emerges" and hence "no order can be passed at this stage".

"While Member (Technical) rejected the plan, the Member (Judicial) confined the plan to those who accepted and approved it and accorded liberty to dissenting creditors to recover their debt. He did not extinguish the claim of banks/financial institutions/dissenting creditors qua principal debtor/debtor/PG. The Third Member approved the plan but extinguished the right of all the creditors by applying Section 115(1) of the Code uniformly," it said.

Lenders’ move

Earlier in the day, in a precautionary move, dissenting lenders of Mr. Chandra moved the insolvency appellate tribunal NCLAT, on the basis of the order/opinion by the third member, who approved a ₹6.5 crore payment by the Essel Group chairman over creditor claims of about ₹22,006.57 crore in his personal insolvency resolution process.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for LIC Housing Finance, mentioned it in the morning before an NCLAT Bench, comprising Officiating Chairperson Justice Yogesh Khanna, and sought an urgent hearing in the second half of the day.

Mr. Mehta, who also represented Canara Bank and Union Bank, said that if the order is allowed to continue, it will "defeat the very purpose of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code" and requested that the Bench hear it at 2 p.m.

However, NCLAT agreed to list the matter for hearing on Tuesday at 10.30 a.m.

The dispute has arisen over the interpretation of Section 79(2)(g) of the IBC and its interplay with the procedural provisions of Section 115(1), which deals with approval of a repayment plan by creditors.

Different interpretations

In the original order, Mr. Bhardwaj had confined the approval of the repayment plan only to creditors who voted in its favour — about 80.8% of creditors — while granting liberty to dissenting financial institutions and banks, comprising roughly 19.2%, to independently pursue debt recovery against Mr. Chandra outside the plan.

However, the third member of the tribunal, in an independent order, took a different view, applying Section 115(1) uniformly to all creditors. This approved the plan but extinguished the claims of all creditors, including dissenting banks and financial institutions, against the personal guarantor.

The Bench noted that the third member also disagreed with both members on the scope of the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction to question the Section 112 report submitted by the Resolution Professional on creditors' meetings.

World.title: Green-blue infrastructure and heritage: building a resilient and timeless Delhi
World.content:
A city’s greatness is measured as much by what it safeguards as by what it builds. On that count, Delhi has few equals. Its ecological wealth spans the Yamuna and its floodplains, the Ridge, urban forests and biodiversity parks, while its cultural wealth lives on in monuments, historic precincts, and archaeological sites that span centuries.

With the country working towards the Prime Minister’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, Delhi carries the responsibility of showing how a fast-growing metropolis can pursue development alongside environmental restoration and heritage conservation. The Master Plan for Delhi (MPD) 2047 gives the national capital a framework to put both at the centre of its future.

Nature as core infrastructure

Urban planning today operates under rules that climate change has rewritten. Higher temperatures, extreme rainfall, water stress, worsening air quality, and shrinking biodiversity all bear directly on residents’ health and daily lives. Rivers, forests, wetlands, lakes, and parks have moved beyond the status of amenities: they now function as core urban infrastructure.

At the heart of MPD-2047 is a connected green-blue network that draws the Yamuna, the Ridge, forests, biodiversity parks, water bodies, drains, and neighbourhood parks into one ecological system.

Urban forests and green corridors filter the air, cool heat-trapped neighbourhoods, and give native species a place to thrive. Revived water bodies, wetlands, and floodplains recharge groundwater and help the city cope with intense rainfall. Parks, trails, and cycling routes support active living and give communities spaces they can reach. The aim is straightforward: nature should run through daily urban life, not sit apart from it in scattered green patches.

Reviving the Yamuna and the Ridge

Any picture of Delhi’s future is incomplete without the Yamuna. The river has shaped the city’s geography and civilisation for centuries, though rapid urbanisation has left its floodplains under unprecedented strain. MPD-2047 puts the Yamuna at the heart of this ecological renewal, proposing to protect, conserve, and ecologically restore close to 1,700 hectares of floodplain.
