World.title: ‘Kocharyan’s arrest is driven by geopolitical motives’: Former Armenian president’s team speaks out
World.content:
Former president Robert Kocharyan’s team on his arrest

“President Kocharyan should be released because his detention is illegal, not at the request of President Putin,” opposition Armenia faction leader Anna Grigoryan said. In Armenia, people have spent recent days discussing whether the Russian president will ask for the release of Armenia’s former president, with whom he has friendly ties. Today, on Robert Kocharyan’s birthday, his allies and lawyer held a news conference. They said there were no legal grounds for his detention. Putin also congratulated Kocharyan, wishing him “strength in the face of adversity”.

Meanwhile, Russian officials have announced that Putin will meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan in Bishkek on 1 September. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the meeting would take place at a time “when opposition leaders are being arrested en masse in Armenia”.

Anna Grigoryan, who represents the faction led by Armenia’s former president, does not believe that Kocharyan’s detention should dominate the Pashinyan-Putin talks. She says the two sides should first resolve the crisis in bilateral relations to “avoid an economic collapse”. She hopes Russia will lift its restrictions on imports on Armenian food and goods, or at least refrain from introducing new restrictions.

At the same time, the opposition MP considers it natural and logical for Russia to discuss Kocharyan’s detention alongside other issues on the bilateral agenda. She notes that he is a “rational politician who supports maintaining good-neighbourly relations with Moscow”.

Former president’s lawyer Aram Orbelyan said both the criminal case against Kocharyan and the detention order were illegal.

“We have not yet received the detention order. As soon as we receive it, we will begin the appeal process,” he said.

Prosecutors have charged Kocharyan with abuse of office, accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. A court ordered the former president to spend two months in detention.

The lawyer argues that the alleged actions do not fall under the Criminal Code article cited in the detention order. He says the charges concern Kocharyan’s approval of certain government decisions while he served as president. According to Kocharyan’s defence, he had no choice but to approve them. The lawyer says the president’s office had no “tools, procedures or powers” to act otherwise.

Police detained Robert Kocharyan on 25 August. On the same day, law-enforcement officers searched companies belonging to the Kocharyan family and carried out other investigative measures. On 27 August, the Anti-Corruption Court granted the investigator’s request to detain Kocharyan. On 26 August, authorities also detained his eldest son, Sedrak Kocharyan, in the same case.

“Pashinyan is trying to minimise resistance”

Anna Grigoryan, head of the Armenia faction, believes that the case against Robert Kocharyan is not economic but political and even geopolitical. She says the fact that the issue will also come up at the Pashinyan-Putin meeting during the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit supports this view:

“If Kocharyan’s arrest were purely an economic and domestic issue for our country, would it be discussed at such an important forum? We are indeed facing a serious political and geopolitical arrest.”

She does not believe Robert Kocharyan’s “neutralisation” is accidental. She has put forward her own explanation for what prompted his arrest. In particular, she believes the Armenian authorities are preparing to amend Armenia’s Constitution and intend to “hand over territories to Azerbaijan”. She believes Pashinyan is trying to achieve “minimal resistance” in this context.

The MP says the case should also be viewed in a broader context. She believes Armenia will eventually find itself at the centre of a “clash of interests between geopolitical centres”. She says a similar process in Ukraine led to territorial losses and a mass exodus:

“But in the end, Ukraine achieved nothing. The country is still neither an EU nor a NATO member. And it remains unclear whether it will join the EU in the future. The Armenian authorities talk about diversification and reducing dependence on Russia, but they are leading the country towards Turkish domination and hostile relations with Russia.”

Lawyer says there are no grounds for arrest

Lawyer Aram Orbelyan says neither the former president nor his son committed any unlawful acts:

“They cannot fully understand what they are being accused of or what role specific individuals played in the whole process. All the processes were lawful. There were no fictitious processes carried out in the names of other people.”

According to him, the actions described in the indictment relate to the former president only through the phrase “persons associated with him”.

The lawyer stresses that the law prohibits accusing one person of another person’s actions, especially restricting someone’s freedom when “the other person’s actions are lawful in themselves”.

Orbelyan also announced that the statute of limitations for the charges had expired. In such cases, he explained, a court does not order detention, except in exceptional circumstances.

“If they saw a need to detain him, why could they not impose house arrest? It is unclear who the former president could have influenced, and what influence he could have had, if he had remained free,” he said.

Details of the case presented by the Anti-Corruption Committee

According to the Anti-Corruption Committee, Kocharyan, while serving as president, acquired several valuable public assets together with a group of people linked to him. They bought the assets at prices significantly below market value. Investigators also found that he received large bribes in some of the deals.

“According to evidence gathered during the preliminary investigation, the property was registered in the names of affiliated companies to conceal the actual ownership and the criminal origin of the assets. The acquired property was later transferred through development and sales, transfers to third parties, and the transfer of company shares, including as gifts,” the Anti-Corruption Committee said.

Investigators are also examining transactions made in the former president’s son’s name between 2001 and 2019. The investigation covers money transfers totalling around 144 billion drams (more than $397 million at the current exchange rate), $309 million, €77 million and 18 million Russian roubles during that period. It also covers the acquisition of more than three dozen properties in Armenia and abroad.

The same investigation has also opened criminal cases against nine other people. They include former Defence Minister Serzh Sargsyan, former Prime Minister Andranik Margaryan and former Yerevan Mayor Gagik Beglaryan.

In addition, the Prosecutor General’s Office has brought criminal cases against current and former directors of several local companies linked to Kocharyan. Authorities accuse them of failing to pay taxes on a particularly large scale. The total unpaid tax bill amounts to around 2.567 billion drams (more than $7 million).

Context

Opposition figures say Kocharyan’s arrest was politically motivated. They argue that the law-enforcement system is acting at the whim of a single person – the prime minister.

They also point to the heated parliamentary exchange between Nikol Pashinyan and Kocharyan’s son, Levon Kocharyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, which preceded Robert Kocharyan’s arrest.

“If the country’s prime minister says that this or that person should be sent to prison, or that this or that person should have their property confiscated, that is a political order. It is abnormal and goes against European standards, democracy and everything you fought for,” Kocharyan told Pashinyan.

The prime minister replied:

“Explain why you are a millionaire. Where did you get this property? And are you saying that you should remain a millionaire in Armenia? Are you saying that your millions should pass to your children and then from your children to their children? I’m sorry, but I’m telling you directly: that will not happen. For me, this is not a personal issue but a political one.”

Pashinyan said he had pledged to return to the people, “piece by piece”, all property that had been illegally plundered.

“In a democratic country, the court, not the country’s leader, should decide what should be returned to whom,” Levon Kocharyan replied.

Later, speaking to journalists, Pashinyan returned to the issue. He said that if Armenian citizens considered the government’s actions unlawful, they could stage a revolution.

“Let them remove us from power through a revolution. Let them bring their beloved and most honourable Robert Kocharyan, [former president] Serzh Sargsyan, [Russian businessman under house arrest on charges of calling for the seizure of power] Samvel Karapetyan, [major businessman arrested on charges of fraud, money laundering and extortion] Gagik Tsarukyan into government buildings. Let them take us to Republic Square and hang us. I’m fine with that scenario. If that is what they want, the people’s decision is not open to discussion for me,” the prime minister said.

Former president Robert Kocharyan’s team on his arrest

World.title: 1,795 applicants in Georgia to get second chance to enrol
World.content:
University admissions in Georgia in 2026

A total of 1,795 applicants in Georgia who passed the minimum threshold in the Unified National Examinations but failed to secure a place at a university will be given a second chance to enrol.

This year, the number of applicants who passed the minimum threshold but were unable to gain admission to a university increased 2.5 times compared with the previous year.

Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the decision, saying it had been made as a one-off exception this year because it is the first year of the higher education reform introduced by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Mikanadze said that registration for vacant places at public and private higher and vocational education institutions would open in the first half of September for applicants who had not previously secured a university place.

“As we have embarked on nationwide higher education reform, and this year is something of a transitional period, we are making an exception. Only this year, at the initiative of Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, we are giving 1,795 applicants who passed the minimum competency threshold in the Unified National Examinations the opportunity for so-called second-round admission,” Mikanadze said.

The Georgian government has radically changed the higher education system. Under the new reform, admission to public universities is organised around strict specialisation, with specific academic fields assigned to individual cities and universities.

The authorities say the measures are aimed at aligning the education system with labour market needs and concentrating resources. However, the changes have already raised questions about academic freedom, regional development and university autonomy.

More on the higher education reform can be found here.

World.title: Salaries rise 7% while house prices climb 12.4%: Is it worth buying home in Azerbaijan?
World.content:
Buying a home in Azerbaijan

The average price of a 65-square-metre flat in Baku is now around 178,000 manats (about $105,000). Someone earning the country’s average monthly salary of 1,174 manats (about $690) would have to save their entire income for 12 and a half years to afford it. But once the cost of food, rent, transport and other everyday expenses is taken into account, this calculation is purely theoretical.

According to an August review by the Central Bank, house prices rose by 8.6% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. Prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%, while those on the secondary market rose by 8.6%. Rents increased by 7.4%. Over the same period, average nominal wages rose by 7%.

Wage growth is failing to keep pace with house prices

In Azerbaijan, the average nominal wage rose by 7% over the year, or about 77 manats (around $45), reaching 1,174.4 manats. At the same time, prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%. This means new homes became 5.4 percentage points more expensive than the rate at which average wages increased.

The gap shows that housing affordability for potential buyers has not improved. The rise in wages increased a worker’s annual pre-tax income by around 920 manats (about $541). Meanwhile, a 12.4% increase in house prices means that a flat costing 170,000–180,000 manats would have become roughly 19,000–20,000 manats (about $11,200–11,700) more expensive over the year.

It should also be noted that 1,174 manats is the average nominal wage across the economy as a whole. The figure is calculated before taxes and social contributions and does not reflect the actual income of most workers.

How many years would it take to buy a 65-square-metre flat?

The m2map platform, which analysed more than 82,000 active listings in August, estimated the median asking price in Baku at 2,735 manats (about $1,609) per square metre. At that price, a 65-square-metre flat would cost 177,775 manats.

According to July data from the Azerbaijan Chamber of Appraisers, the median price per square metre for newly built homes was 2,812.5 manats (about $1,655), compared with 2,616.7 manats (about $1,540) on the secondary market. This puts the price of a flat of this size at roughly 170,000 to 183,000 manats (about $100,000–108,000), depending on the segment.

At the national average monthly wage of 1,174.4 manats, 177,775 manats is slightly more than 12 and a half years of a worker’s total earnings. Using Baku’s average wage of 1,487 manats (about $875), the period falls to around 10 years. But this is only a theoretical calculation, assuming a person spends none of their salary on anything else. In reality, someone on an average income would need considerably longer to save the full price of a flat.

If a buyer can save 20% of their salary, it would take around 50 years to accumulate the full cost of the property. To save the down payment required under a standard mortgage, which in this case would be around 28,000 manats (about $16,500), would take almost eight years.

The average wage also does not reflect the incomes of all workers. According to data from the State Statistics Committee, during the first five months of the year, average monthly wages were 763 manats (about $449) in retail, 825 manats (about $485) in education, and 800 manats (about $470.50) in tourism and catering. For workers in these sectors, a mid-range flat in Baku is equivalent to around 18–19 years of their combined earnings.

Does a mortgage make housing more affordable – or more expensive?

The maximum amount available under a standard mortgage from the Mortgage and Credit Guarantee Fund is 150,000 manats (about $88,235), with a loan term of up to 25 years, an annual interest rate of 8% and a minimum down payment of 15%. However, 85% of the 177,775-manat price of the flat exceeds the loan limit, meaning the buyer would have to provide at least 27,775 manats from their own funds.

If the remaining 150,000 manats were borrowed for 25 years at 8% interest, the monthly payment would be around 1,158 manats (about $681.20). Over the full term, the borrower would repay more than 347,000 manats (about $204,000) to the bank. Including the down payment, the total cost would exceed 375,000 manats (about $220,600). Insurance, property valuation, notary fees and other associated costs are not included.

A monthly payment of 1,158 manats is almost equal to the average salary across the country and represents 78% of the average salary in Baku. Under the Fund’s rules, mortgage payments must not exceed 70% of borrowers’ combined income after tax. This means that a Baku resident earning a single average salary would find it practically impossible to service such a mortgage alone.

In a household where two people earn the average Baku salary, the monthly mortgage payment would account for 39% of their combined nominal income. After tax, the share would exceed 40%. According to OECD and Eurostat methodology, housing costs exceeding 40% of disposable income are considered an excessive housing burden.

Under the subsidised mortgage scheme, the annual interest rate is 4%, the loan term can be up to 30 years, and the maximum loan amount is 100,000 manats (about $58,820). Although the monthly payment would be around 477 manats (about $280.60), buying a 65-square-metre flat at Baku’s average price would require around 78,000 manats (about $45,882) in the buyer’s own funds. The lower interest rate therefore does not solve the main problem for families without substantial savings.

Is renting cheaper?

The median advertised rent in Baku is 11 manats (about $6.50) per square metre per month. Renting a 65-square-metre flat would therefore cost around 715 manats (about $420.60) a month – 443 manats (about $260.60) less than the monthly payment on a standard mortgage. However, this still amounts to around 48% of the average salary in Baku, excluding utility bills.

If an investor bought such a flat for 178,000 manats and rented it out for 715 manats a month, the gross annual rental yield would be around 4.8%. After accounting for maintenance, periods when the property is vacant and other associated costs, the actual return would be even lower. Buying a flat with a mortgage and then renting it out therefore generally does not allow the owner to cover the full cost through rental income alone. The model may make sense primarily for investors with substantial capital who are betting on further increases in property prices.

What is driving prices higher?

The Chamber of Appraisers attributes the rise in new-build prices to strong demand in the mid-to-upper and premium segments, the availability of mortgage financing and the perception of housing as an investment asset. The Chamber’s land price index also points to rising prices and limited supply in premium areas. This may put additional pressure on the cost of newly built homes.

At the same time, according to the State Statistics Committee, investment in residential construction fell by 2.7% in real terms in the first half of the year. These figures strengthen the suggestion that demand, growing faster than household incomes, is running up against limited supply.

State-backed mortgages make housing more affordable for some families: in the first half of the year, 2,242 families received mortgage loans worth a total of 226.3 million manats (about $133.1 million). Since 2019, just over 10,000 families have used the rent-to-own scheme. However, it remains unclear whether these programmes are large enough to curb the overall rise in property prices.

Buying a home in Baku today is therefore more affordable for a household with two stable official incomes, substantial savings for a down payment or another property that can be sold than for someone living on a single average salary. Those who qualify for subsidised mortgages and have tens of thousands of manats in savings are also in a stronger position.

For everyone else, the choice is essentially between increasingly expensive rent and taking on long-term, substantial debt.

Buying a home in Azerbaijan

World.title: ‘Occupation is off’: Russian state media RIA Novosti on Georgian PM Kobakhidze’s remarks
World.content:
RIA Novosti on Russia-Georgia relations

Russia’s state-run news agency RIA Novosti has responded to remarks by Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, saying that Tbilisi had decided to reassess the history of its relations with Moscow.

The article, published on 24 August 2026 under the headline “Occupation is off”: Another country refuses to consider Russia an enemy, focused on Kobakhidze’s remarks about the Treaty of Georgievsk.

Background

On 18 August 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said that Georgia’s decision to sign the Treaty of Georgievsk had been a “civilisational choice”.

His main argument was that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation. According to Kobakhidze, Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose to align itself with Orthodox Russia.

Kobakhidze argued that the decision was not only justified but also “the only correct and only possible” choice at the time. He said Russia honoured the terms of the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end, and almost 20 years passed between the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country effectively survived.”

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement between the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and the Russian Empire, signed on 24 July 1783. Under the treaty, King Erekle II accepted the protection of Russian Empress Catherine II, while Russia pledged to defend the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and preserve its territorial integrity. The treaty formally preserved the internal independence of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and did not declare it part of the Russian Empire. However, in 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and incorporated it into its territory.

What RIA Novosti says in its article

The Russian state-run news agency says Kobakhidze presented Georgia’s decision to accept the Russian Empire’s protection as the only way for the Georgian people to survive Ottoman and Persian aggression.

The article quotes the views of several political experts, including Nino Skvortsova, whom the agency describes as a “Tbilisi-based political analyst”.

According to Skvortsova, Kobakhidze’s focus on the reign of Erekle II serves not only to reinterpret history but also to justify the government’s current policies.

“Kobakhidze is trying to place Erekle II back in his historical context. For him, the king is important as a ruler forced to choose between major powers while his country’s existence was under threat,” the expert says.

In her view, this approach allows parallels to be drawn with the current policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party:

“Modern Georgia is also caught in competition between major powers, while the authorities justify their actions by the need to preserve peace, sovereignty, traditional identity and freedom of foreign policy manoeuvre.”

RIA Novosti also quotes another expert, Artur Ataev, who says that Georgian Dream is trying to raise a new generation free from old stereotypes. Ataev argues that the opposition, in turn, wants Georgia to follow the example of Ukraine, the Baltic states and other former Soviet republics.

“Today, this is one of the main topics of debate in Georgian society. There are even calls to recognise the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia,” Ataev says.

He argues that Georgian society and the political elite are gradually changing, but that the restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia is unlikely in the near future.

“After all, most Georgians still see Russia as an occupier,” the expert concludes.

RIA Novosti on Russia-Georgia relations

World.title: Saturday March in Tbilisi: growing emigration. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Abkhaz blogger who spoke of ‘shared future’: Who was late Daur Buava?
World.content:
Abkhaz blogger found dead in Georgia

Young Abkhaz blogger Daur Buava has been found dead in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi. According to neighbours, they raised the alarm after Buava had not been seen for several days. Emergency services called to his rented flat found his body inside.

The cause of his death has not yet been established, and an initial examination of the body found no signs of violence. Georgia’s Interior Ministry has opened an investigation under the article covering “incitement to suicide”.

Who was Daur Buava?

Daur Buava, 32, was an Abkhaz blogger who attracted public attention for his open and unconventional views on Georgian-Abkhaz relations. On social media, particularly TikTok, he regularly posted videos advocating peaceful coexistence, dialogue and the rebuilding of trust between Georgians and Abkhaz.

Buava was born in Abkhazia in 1994. The Georgian-Abkhaz war had ended a year before he was born, meaning his understanding of the conflict was largely shaped by what he had been told by those around him. In 2021, Buava travelled to Tbilisi in an attempt to examine that version of events for himself.

“Later, I realised that it was the truth as seen by only one side. I learned the other side’s truth here,” he told Georgian media outlet Netgazeti that same year.

Within months, Buava had become one of the most recognisable Abkhaz bloggers on TikTok. His videos focused primarily on relations between Georgians and Abkhaz, the war, peace and Abkhazia’s future. He had tens of thousands of followers, including young people in Abkhazia.

Buava’s public activities were not confined to social media. He gradually became one of the few Abkhaz voices openly advocating dialogue with Georgians. It was this position that made him a target of persecution in Abkhazia.

Meeting the “enemy”

Buava said that before travelling to Tbilisi, his views of Georgia had been based largely on the information he received in Abkhazia.

One of the reasons he decided to visit Georgia was a TikTok livestream in which Georgians and Abkhaz called each other enemies and exchanged insults. For Buava, this became another reason to see for himself the place he had been taught since childhood to regard as hostile.

He said that in both societies there was a small group of people fuelling hatred, while most people wanted to communicate with one another.

Daur Buava

Persecution in Abkhazia

Buava’s activities did not receive unequivocal support in Abkhazia from the outset. In late 2021, he said that many people criticised his presence and activities in Tbilisi, although he also received messages of support from Abkhazia. Over time, however, criticism was followed by threats.

According to Buava, his supporters also faced pressure. He said that people who posted positive comments during his livestreams were identified and, in some cases, people even went to their homes. Buava also said that several of his supporters had been beaten.

In June 2022, Abkhazia’s de facto security service opened a criminal case against Buava on charges of “high treason”.

The agency said that videos posted by Buava on TikTok contained appeals that undermined Abkhazia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity, state security and defence capabilities”. It also accused him of promoting the idea of Abkhazia existing as an autonomous republic within Georgia.

The case against Buava was opened in absentia. He remained in Tbilisi and no longer planned to return to Abkhazia.

‘Amra’ and idea of shared future

In Tbilisi, Buava and his Georgian friend Mikheil Kvatashidze founded the Amra youth movement. The name means “Sun” in Abkhaz. The organisation aimed to create opportunities for young Georgians and Abkhaz to communicate with one another.

In December 2022, Buava obtained Georgian citizenship, which he said was granted under a simplified procedure. This became another source of criticism against him within Abkhaz society.

In 2023, Buava was invited to the European Parliament, where he spoke about relations between young Georgians and Abkhaz, the free exchange of information and overcoming the conflict.

“We must move forward and build a shared future,” he said.

At the European Parliament, Buava also addressed Russia’s role. In his view, Moscow had contributed to the escalation of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict and was continuing to obstruct dialogue between Georgians and Abkhaz.

That same year, Buava opposed the adoption of the so-called “apartments law” in Abkhazia, saying he did not want Russians to buy property and settle in Abkhazia in large numbers. He regarded the main threat to Abkhazia as not the restoration of relations with Georgians, but the loss of its own demographic and cultural identity.

World.title: Georgian president pardons nine activists, one may face deportation to Russia
World.content:
Georgian president pardons nine activists

On the occasion of the Orthodox feast of Mariamoba (the Dormition of the Mother of God), Georgian President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned 226 prisoners. They included nine people detained during various protests. Georgian civil society groups and several organisations consider them political prisoners.

According to pro-government media, those pardoned include Denis Kulanin, a Russian citizen who, according to his lawyer, faces possible deportation.

List of pardoned activists:

Fridon Bubuteishvili — sentenced to five years in prison on 20 January 2025 on charges of injuring a firefighter-rescuer and damaging the gates of the parliament building. On 8 May 2026, it was reported that he had petitioned the president for a pardon.

— sentenced to five years in prison on 20 January 2025 on charges of injuring a firefighter-rescuer and damaging the gates of the parliament building. On 8 May 2026, it was reported that he had petitioned the president for a pardon. Simon Makharadze — detained in connection with the storming of the presidential palace in October 2025. Several months ago, he reached a plea agreement and was sentenced to one year in prison and a further three years suspended.

— detained in connection with the storming of the presidential palace in October 2025. Several months ago, he reached a plea agreement and was sentenced to one year in prison and a further three years suspended. Davit Khomeriki — sentenced to four years and six months in prison on 15 August 2025 on charges of preparing to commit a crime and transporting or placing explosives or other devices or substances posing a danger to life and health.

— sentenced to four years and six months in prison on 15 August 2025 on charges of preparing to commit a crime and transporting or placing explosives or other devices or substances posing a danger to life and health. Saba Jikia — sentenced to four years and six months in prison on 10 July 2025 on charges of assaulting a police officer.

— sentenced to four years and six months in prison on 10 July 2025 on charges of assaulting a police officer. Daniel Mumladze — sentenced to three years in prison on 2 June 2025 on charges of damaging a CCTV camera.

— sentenced to three years in prison on 2 June 2025 on charges of damaging a CCTV camera. Guram Khutashvili — sentenced to three years in prison on 2 June 2025 on similar charges of damaging a CCTV camera.

— sentenced to three years in prison on 2 June 2025 on similar charges of damaging a CCTV camera. Tornike Mchedlishvili — detained in connection with the storming of the presidential palace and sentenced to five years in prison.

— detained in connection with the storming of the presidential palace and sentenced to five years in prison. Avtandil Topchishvili — also detained in connection with the storming of the presidential palace. Several months ago, he reached a plea agreement and was sentenced to one year in prison and a further three years suspended.

Сase of Denis Kulanin

Pro-government Georgian media report that those pardoned also include Denis Kulanin, a Russian citizen who lived in Georgia and took part in pro-European protests. He was detained on 28 March 2025 during a protest outside parliament on charges of breaking the window of a police vehicle and was sentenced to two years in prison.

However, according to his lawyer, Dimitri Nozadze, Kulanin has not been released. The lawyer believes that Kulanin is being held by the immigration authorities and is being prepared for deportation to Russia.

Nozadze says deporting Kulanin to Russia would be unacceptable and dangerous because, while in prison, he published a letter in which he wished Ukraine glory and peace. The lawyer says the letter could give the Russian authorities grounds to bring criminal charges against him.

Адвокат поясняет, что недавно был принят закон, наделяющий силовые ведомства полномочиями выдворять из страны иностранцев, совершивших преступление в Грузии.

На вопрос о том, обращался ли Денис Куланин к президенту Михеилу Кавелашвили с прошением о помиловании, адвокат ответил, что ничего об этом не знает.

World.title: Moscow posters: Are radical nationalists acting independently of Kremlin in Azerbaijan row?
World.content:
Protest at Azerbaijani embassy in Russia

On 27 August, at a time when independent political protests have become rare in Russia, a group of radical nationalists staged a protest outside Azerbaijan‘s diplomatic mission in Moscow. Participants put up three posters, filmed the action and posted the video on the group’s Telegram channel, which has tens of thousands of subscribers.

Azərbaycanın Rusiya səfirliyinin qonaq evi qarşısında naməlum şəxslər tərəfindən Azərbaycan əleyhinə təxribatın videosu pic.twitter.com/3CkEXuYacp — Unikal.az (@UnikalOrgPortal) August 27, 2026

Although the protest was small, it raises a question: can radical nationalists in Russia, where public expressions of opposition are tightly restricted, intervene in relations between Baku and Moscow without the Kremlin’s knowledge?

There is no clear answer so far. The issue is not whether the Kremlin learned about the protest after the event, but what boundaries the authorities set for the activities of such groups.

There is no evidence that the protest was organised at the request of the Russian authorities. However, the fact that the same group has now targeted Azerbaijan for a second time, coupled with the authorities’ differing treatment of public expressions of political views, raises questions about whether such groups may receive preferential treatment.

What accusations appeared on the three posters?

According to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry, the posters were placed not outside the main embassy building but in front of its guest house. The protest was covered by the Telegram channel Direct Action Z, which describes itself as an information resource of Eduard Limonov’s Other Russia party.

The posters accused Azerbaijan’s State Security Service of torture and President Ilham Aliyev of covering it up. They also carried the slogans “Russian blood is on your hands” and “Hands off Russian citizens”.

In a statement, the organisers portrayed the detention of eight Russian nationals in Azerbaijan, criminal proceedings against Ivan Knyazev, Semyon Uralov and Alexei Chadayev, Baku’s position on Ukraine and the deaths of Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh in 2023 as manifestations of a single “anti-Russian policy”. They also accused the Azerbaijani diaspora of running “shadow businesses”.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry described the incident as an “unacceptable provocation” and said it could be a continuation of what it alleges is a campaign against Azerbaijan by a number of Russian media outlets. Baku called on Moscow to investigate the incident and ensure the security of its diplomatic mission.

Azərbaycan Respublikasının Rusiya Federasiyasındakı Səfirliyinin qonaq evi qarşısında təxribatla bağlı açıqlama



⬇️⬇️⬇️https://t.co/YPLnFLJ4Mx



Statement on the provocation in front of the Guest House of the Embassy of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Russian Federation… pic.twitter.com/D9TwDicyqr — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 27, 2026

Same group staged protest exactly one year ago

One detail that makes it difficult to dismiss the incident as a random street protest is the date. On 27 August 2025, three members of the same movement staged a protest outside the Azerbaijani consulate in St Petersburg. They were detained by police.

The accusations made at the time differed from those voiced now. The protesters opposed Baku’s alliance with Ankara, its support for Ukraine and Azerbaijan’s competition with Russia on the energy market. In the following months, individual pickets were also held outside the consulate under the slogan “Russophobia is a disease”.

The fact that the second protest took place exactly a year later gives the impression that it may be a continuation of the earlier campaign. However, the organisers did not say whether the date had been chosen deliberately.

Close to Kremlin or opposed to it?

The Other Russia of E. V. Limonov is an unregistered political organisation founded by former members of the National Bolshevik Party, which a Russian court designated as extremist and banned in 2007. Its ideology combines Russian nationalism, “Soviet nostalgia” and imperialist ideas.

Its members support Russia’s war against Ukraine, and some have fought on the Russian side. The movement’s Interbrigades unit has operated in Donbas since 2014. In this respect, the group’s foreign policy rhetoric does not contradict the Kremlin’s broader line.

However, this does not mean the organisation is directly controlled by the Kremlin. National Bolshevik activists have also protested against the Central Bank, Roskomnadzor and other state bodies. In October 2025, four members of the movement were detained during a protest outside the Central Bank. In February 2026, activists from the organisation placed a lock on the door of Roskomnadzor’s Moscow office before leaving the scene.

On 18 August, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that statements by Knyazev, Uralov and Chadayev did not reflect Moscow’s position towards Azerbaijan. In their latest statement on Azerbaijan, the National Bolsheviks, in turn, accused the Foreign Ministry of failing to defend the three men. The group claimed that the state was putting the interests of “foreign entities” above those of Russian citizens.

In other words, the protest was directed not only against Baku but also against Moscow’s own policy, which the organisers regard as “not tough enough”.

Question of preferential treatment

National Bolshevik activists themselves are also periodically detained and given administrative jail terms. It would therefore be an oversimplification to portray them as an untouchable group carrying out the Kremlin’s orders.

On the other hand, it is clear that political protests in Russia are not treated equally. According to the latest available data from OVD-Info, more than 20,000 detentions for expressing anti-war views were recorded between February 2022 and July 2025. At the same time, groups that support the war in Ukraine but call on the authorities to take a tougher line have been able to hold public events, raise donations and operate actively on social media.

The Counter Extremism Project, which researches extremist movements, describes the relationship between the Kremlin and the National Bolsheviks as an “uneasy alliance”: the group criticises the authorities and its members are periodically detained, but its activities in Ukraine and pro-war campaigning are generally treated with considerably greater tolerance.

This pattern does not prove that the protest outside Azerbaijan’s diplomatic mission was organised at the state’s behest. However, it once again raises the question of which protests the authorities immediately suppress and which they allow to proceed without intervention.

Defending rights or exerting ethnic pressure?

The situation of the Russian nationals detained in Azerbaijan continues to raise questions that remain unanswered. In footage released after their detention, some appeared to have visible signs of violence on their faces. There have also been reports that the psychological condition of convicted Russian national Dmitry Fedorov has deteriorated and that he has stopped recognising his relatives.

However, the National Bolsheviks’ statement goes beyond defending the rights of individual detainees. It combines human rights concerns with rhetoric about “Russian blood”, criticism of Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine and accusations directed at the Azerbaijani diaspora as a whole.

World.title: India's PM Modi calls on Putin to end war in Ukraine
World.content:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has told Russian President Vladimir Putin the war in Ukraine needs to end for humanity's sake and that New Delhi would support every peace effort to stop the fighting.

Mr Modi, who made his comments at the start of talks with Mr Putin in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, called the president "my friend" and hailed growing economic ties between the two countries, which he said were guided by the need to put the interests of both nations above all else.

India, along with China, is one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil, which has helped Moscow replenish its budget since it sent tens of thousands of troops into Ukraine in 2022 and was hit with sweeping Western sanctions.

"As you are aware, India supports all peace efforts in this regard, and we shall continue to do so in the future," the prime minister told Mr Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, according to a Kremlin transcript of their exchange.

"Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, whilst every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace," he said.

The Ukraine-Russia war has been fought for more than four and a half years, since February 2022. (Reuters: Oleksandr Ratushniak)

"We need to move from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities.

"And we will need to move precisely in this direction."

Mr Putin thanked the Indian leader and said, "we are moving forward along this path".

The Kremlin — which has repeatedly said Russia is only ready to end the war on its own terms, which Ukraine has dismissed as an unacceptable demand to capitulate — said after the talks Mr Putin had briefed Mr Modi on how the special military operation, Russia's preferred description for its action in Ukraine, was progressing, the state TASS news agency reported.

US Treasury secretary says no economic relief for Russia until war ends

Meanwhile, on the sidelines of a G20 meeting in the United States, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ruled out economic relief for Russia in talks with Finance Minister Anton Siluanov.

Mr Bessent met bilaterally with Mr Siluanov at a G20 finance leaders meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, and a source familiar with the meeting said Mr Bessent said agreements on other issues were impossible unless the war in Ukraine ended.

Scott Bessent met with his Russian counterpart on the sidelines of a G20 finance ministers and central bank governors meeting in North Carolina. (Reuters: Sam Wolfe)

The meeting in North Carolina marked the Russian finance minister's first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine.

His appearance irritated European officials who are working on more sanctions against Russia.

Earlier, a US official told Reuters the focus of the meeting was US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Ukraine.

Oscar Jenkins gives first interview since conviction Oscar Jenkins has given his first interview since he was sentenced to 13 years' imprisonment by Russian authorities.

Russia's finance ministry said the two officials discussed financial cooperation within the G20 framework.

When Mr Siluanov tried to discuss areas of mutual interest, the source said Mr Bessent interrupted him and said, "nothing is possible until the war is over".

The US imposed sanctions on Russia's oil majors in October 2025, but after the US-Israeli war against Iran cut off energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, Mr Bessent issued licenses allowing the sale of seaborne Russian oil stored in tankers to ease supplies, with some of the funds going to Moscow.

Reuters

World.title: 'Canberrans suing their own government' costing ACT tens of millions
World.content:
Legal action taken against the ACT government continues to cost the territory tens of millions of dollars each year, with the price of medical negligence payouts on the rise.

Newly released answers to questions taken on notice during budget estimates reveal the ACT Insurance Authority (ACTIA) paid out $60.7 million in damages, settlements and legal costs relating to medical negligence claims last financial year.

In 2024-25, the territory paid more than $39 million for the same medical negligence-related costs, and in 2023-24 that figure was about $28.6 million.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said it was concerning that medical negligence payouts had more than doubled over a two-year period.

"Certainly, some lawsuits will not be avoidable, and we can understand as a community that our government will be exposed to some extent to liability claims," he said.

"But seeing a more than doubling of medical negligence, damages and settlements over just a two-year period is seriously concerning — both from a medical perspective, and also from a budgetary perspective.

"How many health procedures could have been provided by investing sufficiently in the health system to avoid the medical negligence claims that have been put forward?"

Thomas Emerson says the ACT government should review the impact of increasing legal bills on the territory's finances. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Footpath-related injury payouts

ACTIA also paid out nearly $2.8 million on footpath-related personal injury claims last financial year.

In 2024-25, the amount paid out for footpath-related injury claims was about $1.72 million, and in 2023-24 it was just more than $1 million.

In 2025-26, the government spent nearly $7.2 million on footpath maintenance and repairs, meaning the cost of paying out personal injury claims was 38 per cent of what the government spent on footpath maintenance.

Footpath-related personal injury claims cost the ACT government more than $2.7 million in the last financial year. (Supplied: Stuart Poole)

"This is evidence that the government is not investing upstream and actually addressing the issues that are leading to harm in our community," Mr Emerson said.

"Because of that, we as taxpayers are having to pay more downstream in legal costs and payouts because of the government having not fulfilled its duties."

Mr Emerson also noted that $3.2 million was spent settling eight of the 85 institutional abuse claims opened in the past three financial years, suggesting there may be a bill of over $30 million for the outstanding cases.

'Cost of incompetence'

Mr Emerson said the cost of "Canberrans suing their own government" was having a big budgetary impact.

"These figures show the whole-of-government cost of incompetence is massive. They're pretty shocking figures," he said.

"While not every lawsuit is avoidable, the ACT government should be closely investigating the impact of its growing legal bill on the territory's finances."

The ACT government paid out more than $60 millions in damages, settlements, and legal costs for medical negligence claims in the last financial year. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Mr Emerson said his criticism was not directed toward "Canberrans pursuing their own legal rights, but instead of the escalation in claims and damages that we're seeing".

"The scale of legal costs and payouts revealed through these questions presents a huge opportunity for the ACT government to pursue budgetary savings and reduce community harm," he said.

"It's such a cop-out for the government to complain about assembly committees criticising their fiscal performance while Canberrans are literally suing them for their failures."

'Really crude numbers'

But Health Minister Marisa Paterson said the figures did not provide the full picture, and that the government had been settling more cases in a timelier manner.

"These are really crude numbers, so they don't provide any explanation of what is actually happening," she said.

"I think the government is getting better at settling these type of matters in a timely way and managing historical matters as well.

"And also there have been a couple of large settlements too."

Marisa Paterson says the government has been settling more cases. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

She said the government had learned from the cases and was always looking to make improvements.

"Particularly in the medical negligence space, in terms of many of these issues have been inquiries and there have been recommendations," she said.

"Obviously when … anything like this happens, the government does look into what has been the cause, and it's about continuous improvement to ensure these things don't happen again."

World.title: Breaking: Jury finds ex-gang leader guilty in Tupac Shakur killing case
World.content:
A Las Vegas jury has found a former gang leader guilty of murder in a case accusing him of masterminding the drive-by killing of legendary hip-hop artist Tupac Shakur, bringing a decades-old cold case to a close.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, was charged in Nevada's Clark County with a single count of murder using a deadly weapon. He had pleaded not guilty.

Davis was accused of leading a group of men to kill Shakur, 25, who was one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, in retaliation for the beating of Davis's nephew.

The jury reached a guilty verdict after less than three hours of deliberations.

A jury has found Duane "Keffe D" Davis (centre) guilty of orchestrating the killing of rapper Tupac Shakur. (AP: Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal)

Tupac Shakur was stopped at a red light in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, when a white Cadillac pulled up beside him and shots were fired.

He died six days later from his wounds.

Police had said they long suspected Davis but did not have enough evidence to charge him until he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir. Those, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, made up the bulk of the prosecution's case.

Davis's lawyer said his client's words were mere bravado and could not be corroborated by other evidence.

Tupac mystery may soon be solved Three decades after the murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, the world may get some answers about who killed the young superstar, and why.

The trial began on August 17. Prosecutors played hours of recorded conversations in which Davis said he was enraged after Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis's nephew at a Las Vegas casino on September 7, 1996.

Davis and three other men, including his nephew, went looking for Shakur and record label executive Marion "Suge" Knight in a white Cadillac on the night of the beating, he said.

Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat, and when they found Knight and Shakur's car, one of the two men in the back opened fire.

Prosecutors have not named the shooter, and the three other men who were in the car have since died. Under Nevada law, Davis can be charged with murder even though he did not pull the trigger.

Davis was a leader of the Southside Compton Crips, a Los Angeles-area street gang that feuded with rival gang Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur and his record label Death Row Records.

Shakur's killing in 1996 became a seminal moment in rap history and heightened hip-hop culture's violent image during "gangsta" rap's heyday, an era defined by feuding between East and West Coast artists.

Reuters

World.title: Hybrid trains touted as a solution to west Melbourne's transport woes
World.content:
The Victorian Liberals are promising new hybrid trains for commuters in Melbourne's booming west, as a newly upgraded station at Melton opens today.

If elected in November, the Coalition is promising $1.7 billion for 25 new hybrid diesel-electric trains on the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines.

The lines are currently served by smaller V-Line trains, with local communities waiting for promised electrification of the line to run larger, more frequent Metro services.

The state government said it would run higher-capacity V-Line trains on the Melton line from next year, while it finishes investigating electrification.

Former premier Daniel Andrews promised to separate and electrify train lines to Wyndham Vale and Melton in 2018.

In 2018, the Victorian Labor government first promised to separate and electrify the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Shadow Transport Minister Matthew Guy said it was taking too long and that hybrid trains could already use the existing line.

"We believe hybrid suburban trains is the fastest, quickest, and cheapest way to solve the problem of getting the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines electrified," he said.

"Or at least getting suburban trains to where people need them."

Mr Guy said hybrid trains would also have even bigger capacity and the potential to travel through the City Loop.

"The nine car V-Line trains the government are announcing is just substandard surface," he said.

" They're country trains going into Australia's fastest growing growth corridor. We believe there should be suburban trains for suburban people. "

The Victorian Liberals say the new trains would also have the ability to travel along the Melbourne City Loop. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

Upgraded Melton station

The newly upgraded Melton train station opens today, but residents said more improved public transport infrastructure was needed for the area's booming population.

Melton is the fastest-growing area in Australia, with an average of 38 new residents a day over 2024-25 according to the local council.

The new elevated train station has longer platforms to allow for more V/Line carriages from next year, to accommodate more passengers.

The state government said the longer platforms would boost capacity by 50 per cent during peak services, and that more commuter car parks would open in the coming months.

Minister for Public Transport Vicki Ward said the upgrades were needed to allow for electrification along the line.

"The new Melton Station is a major investment in Melbourne's growing west, making it easier for working Victorians to get where they need to go," she said in a statement.

"Labor is continuing to deliver for Melton. We've finished the station and now we're doing the works to prepare for electrification."

The newly upgraded Melton train station has opened to the public. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mt Atkinson resident Jaksha Shah said residents have long been waiting for the line to be electrified so trains can run more often, and for new train stations to be built in growing suburbs at Mt Atkinson and Thornhill Park.

"What was the future I bought into and what is the reality I am living in?" she said.

"I bought into a future where there was going to be a Mt Atkinson Westfield mall, a train station, walking from my home because I live 700 metres from the actual train line."

Hybrid trains versus 'permanent solutions'

Infrastructure Victoria said hybrid trains were already operating in some areas of Europe, but that it would not be the best long term solution for Melbourne's west.

Government to shut down independent body Infrastructure Victoria Independent advice to help the Victorian government prioritise spending on infrastructure will be axed under the latest pivot from Premier Ben Carroll.

"Our independent advice is that in the medium to long term electrification of the line to Melton will certainly help integrate it better and run more frequent services more reliably," chief executive Jonathan Spear said.

"Trains are only part of the challenge," he said.

"We would both need to have more tracks, especially to duplicate the track between Sunshine and Melton, and we would need to build new stations.

"We would also need to invest in the fleet to run on them."

Train stations are often bustling across Melbourne's CBD and surrounding suburbs. (Supplied: Fiona York)

Dr Spear said while Infrastructure Victoria hasn't done a "head-to-head" comparison of the hybrid proposal versus the "permanent" electrification solution, there was clearly an urgent need for solutions as the western communities grew.

He said they had estimated the permanent solution would cost between $4 billion and $5 billion.

"[That's] to do the electrification to Melton, the duplication of the tracks, the new stations and the new trains," he said.

"For every dollar we would spend on that, the community would get $2 back — so that's a good investment.

"Even with the current commitment to build the Suburban Rail Loop, we think it would be affordable."

World.title: Messi's legendary run for Argentina almost never happened after heartbreak
World.content:
Lionel Messi's retirement from the Argentina national side brings down the curtain on one of world football's most storied international careers.

The records and achievements of Messi are stuff of legend, and his status in international sport is reserved for only the very greatest of their craft.

Messi was denied the perfect finish to his Argentina career in July, defeated in a thrilling FIFA World Cup final by Spain that went to extra time.

But the loss in New Jersey only denied the fairytale finish, and did not diminish the legend that Messi created for himself, or the legacy that he has left among his people.

But the love and admiration of his people, the two Copa America wins, and the 2022 FIFA World Cup triumph, which brought Argentina back to the pinnacle of world football and raised Messi to the legendary status of fellow countryman Diego Maradona, almost never happened.

Legend at Barca, struggles with Argentina

Messi has been on top of world football for two decades, winning the coveted Ballon d'Or as the world's best player a staggering eight times.

From 2004 to 2021, he won 10 La Liga titles, seven Spanish Cups, seven Spanish Super Cups, four Champions Leagues, three UEFA Super Cups and three FIFA Club World Cups with Barcelona.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

In a legendary 2012, he scored 91 goals in all competitions, a record haul for a calendar year, and slotted 50 goals in the 2011-12 La Liga season.

Trophies, accolades, love and admiration grew and grew for the Barcelona great, but success for Argentina was not forthcoming.

Coming through the ranks, Messi led Argentina to a Youth World Championship in 2005 and the Olympic medal at the Beijing Games in 2008.

But in the very big tournaments, trophies were harder to come by.

When Messi made his senior debut for Argentina in 2005 against Hungary, the South American giants had not won a trophy since the 1993 Copa America.

Messi's final tears As the champion wept on the pitch after the World Cup final defeat, Argentina may well have wondered with trepidation what life will look like in the post-Messi era.

Messi's Argentina senior debut was nothing to write home about either, sent off after less than a minute on the pitch for elbowing an opponent.

But Messi overcame that infamous beginning to establish himself as a star, and the hope of a nation that Argentina could return to the top of South America, and the world.

What followed was a string of bitter disappointments.

Argentina made the final of the Copa America in 2007, but was soundly beaten 3-0 by arch rival Brazil.

At the 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa, Messi failed to score at the tournament as Argentina exited at the quarterfinal stage.

Argentina was then knocked out again at the quarterfinal stage, this time at the 2011 Copa America, by eventual winner Uruguay.

These were bitter disappointments for Argentina and Messi, but the pain was about to increase, and it led to the great man announcing he did not want to be part of it anymore.

Three years, three finals, three painful defeats

Heading into the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, it had been 21 years since Argentina's last major trophy.

But the blue and whites marched into enemy territory intending to claim international football's greatest prize, and doing it in the backyard of their greatest rival.

Argentina won all three group games — over Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iran, and Nigeria — to top the group, beat Switzerland 1-0 in extra time, and finally won a quarterfinal by defeating Belgium 1-0.

A scoreless semifinal against the Netherlands, finalists in 2010, went to penalties, where Argentina won 4-2, including a successful spot kick from Messi.

But the joy ended there.

In a major final for the first time in seven years, Argentina faced a German side that had just humiliated Brazil 7-1 in the semifinal.

Like all of Argentina's games to that point, the game was tight and tense. It went to extra time, but the strike of German Mario Götze sealed Germany's triumph.

A photograph of Messi looking at the World Cup trophy after the defeat, captured by Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily in China, became the defining image of Messi for years.

Lionel Messi walking past the FIFA World Cup trophy after defeat in the 2014 final. (Supplied: Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily via X)

The heartbreak only continued for Messi and Argentina.

The Copa America was held in 2015 and 2016, with Argentina reaching the final both times and losing to Chile each time.

Both finals ended scoreless and went to penalties. Messi converted his penalty, the only Argentinian player to do so, in the 2015 defeat, but the great man missed his spot kick in 2016.

The pain of the 2016 final defeat was too much for Messi, who announced he was retiring from Argentina.

"For me, the national team is over," he said after the loss to Chile in 2016. "I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion."

"It's been four finals, I tried.

"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over.

"I think this is best for everyone. First of all for me, then for everyone.

"I think there's a lot of people who want this, who obviously are not satisfied, as we are not satisfied reaching a final and not winning it."

World football was that close to never seeing Messi reach the heights he would achieve.

Six-week retirement, 10 years of legacy building

When Messi announced on Sunday, June 26, 2016, that he would no longer play for Argentina, he ended what was by any other measure a magnificent international career.

He had made 113 appearances, scored 55 goals and led his country to four major finals.

But the absence of a trophy was not good enough — not for someone as great as Messi.

On July 10, the world watched Cristiano Ronaldo lift an international major trophy as Portugal won the 2016 Euros.

On August 12, Messi announced that he was back.

What followed after his six-week retirement is, on its own, one of the greatest international careers ever forged.

Messi would add another 94 caps to his name, score another 70 goals, and more importantly, end Argentina's trophy drought.

And Messi didn't just win one major trophy for Argentina; he won four.

The 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia was another familiar quarterfinal exit for Argentina, but it was the precursor to an era of success.

Argentina finally broke through to win the Copa America in 2021, and they did it against Brazil, in Brazil.

Lionel Messi was thrown into the air in celebatrion after Argentina ended a 28-year trophy drought. (Getty Images: MB Media)

With the COVID-19 pandemic keeping many fans away from the famed Maracanã Stadium in Rio, Argentina ground out a 1-0 win to claim the nation's first major trophy in 28 years.

Messi was hoisted in the air by teammates in images that went around the world.

The drought was over, and the rain was here to stay. Argentina won a second trophy in 2022 when they defeated European champions Italy in the relaunched Finalissima, but greater prizes were to come.

By this stage, Messi had surpassed everything achieved by Maradona, except one.

Maradona almost single-handedly won the World Cup for Argentina in 1986, and gave him a legendary status that was near God-like.

Now, it was Messi's time to do the same.

He did it in Qatar at the 2022 World Cup, leading the blue and whites back to the top of world football.

The final against France, the defending world champions, was anything but ordinary. Those who were accustomed to Argentina grinding out 1-0 wins got the shock of their lives when they traded blows with France in one of the greatest finals ever played.

Messi scored two goals, including in extra time, while Ángel Di María also scored for Argentina. But the South Americans met their match in France, or more specifically, Kylian Mbappé, who scored a hat-trick, including a 118th-minute penalty to send the final to spot kicks.

In the penalty shootout, Messi converted, Mbappé converted.

Argentina was perfect. France was not.

When Gonzalo Montiel's shot hit the back of the net, Argentina was world champion and Messi had reached the God-like status that had only been reserved for Maradona.

The image of Messi kissing the World Cup became the defining image of his illustrious career.

Lionel Messi finally got his hands on the FIFA World Cup trophy, which had eluded him for so long. (Getty Images: China News Service/VCG/Cui Nan)

One more trophy would follow for Argentina, another Copa America in 2024 to make it three major trophies in four years.

That trophy was icing on the cake for Messi's legacy, which by now was in uncharted territory.

Messi's international career by numbers

1

Lionel Messi led Argentina to the FIFA World Cup title in 2022. He also led his country to two more finals, 2014 and 2026, which both resulted in 1-0 defeats in extra time.

2

Lionel Messi led Argentina to two Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024. Before then, the last time Argentina was champion in the Copa America was in 1993.

6

Lionel Messi has played in a record six FIFA World Cups — 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2026. Only Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo has also managed that feat.

21

Lionel Messi scored 21 goals at the FIFA World Cup finals. He is second on the all-time list behind French star Kylian Mbappé, who has scored 22 from just three tournaments.

34

Lionel Messi holds the record for the most FIFA World Cup finals matches played. He was on the field 34 times for Argentina in a FIFA World Cup tournament. Ronaldo is second on the list with 27 appearances for Portugal.

125

Lionel Messi holds the Argentina goal-scoring record, netting 125 times for his country. That is more than double the previous record holder, Gabriel Batistuta, who scored 54 times for his country.

207

Lionel Messi made 207 appearances for Argentina, a national record. He made his debut in 2005 against Hungary, and played his final match against Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final. Ronaldo holds the world record for international appearances, playing 233 times for Portugal.

World.title: Labuschagne dropped as Australia names ODI squad for African series
World.content:
Australia has named its ODI squad for its back-to-back series in Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month, with World Cup winner Marnus Labuschagne among five players dropped.

Australia are reigning ODI world champions, after a stunning final win over India in Ahmedabad in 2023.

Labuschagne scored a half-century in that final, but his struggles since then have led to him being dropped from the ODI squad that will play in Africa, almost a year out from the next World Cup, which will be held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Labuschagne has missed five of Australia's previous 56 ODIs, but the 32-year-old has been dropped, along with Matt Short, Ben Dwarshuis, Todd Murphy and Liam Scott, from the squad picked to play in Pakistan and Bangladesh in May and June.

Pat Cummins and Mitch Starc will play in the ODIs against South Africa, while Mitch Marsh and Travis Head return after not playing in Pakistan or Bangladesh.

Emerging stars Cooper Connolly, Oliver Peake and Joel Davies have been added to the Australian ODI squad.

Australia ODI squad: Mitchell Marsh, Pat Cummins (SA only), Xavier Bartlett, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Joel Davies, Nathan Ellis, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Spencer Johnson, Oliver Peake, Matthew Renshaw, Billy Stanlake, Mitchell Starc (SA only), Adam Zampa

World.title: Illegal firewood trade harming WA forests and hurting businesses
World.content:
Residents of Western Australia's southern forests say illegal firewood gathering is harming the landscape and undercutting legitimate businesses.

Firewood removal from non-designated areas of national parks, nature reserves and conservation estates is illegal across WA, carrying penalties of up to $500,000 or 12 months' imprisonment.

A Department of Biodiversity Conservation and Attractions (DBCA) spokesperson said in the past three years there had been 116 cautions, infringements and prosecutions for unlawfully taking forest produce in the South West.

Felled trees have been increasingly seen in non-designated collection areas around Donnybrook. (Supplied: Colleen Bandy)

But locals, residents and businesses say enforcement is next to non-existent, with illegal harvesting having a significant impact on the landscape.

Habitat trees 'gone forever'

Donnybrook local Colleen Bandy said she had heard chainsaws and increasingly noticed felled trees in the bush near her home.

"We're seeing more and more people coming, and felling live Jarrah trees and taking them away for firewood, and it's not a firewood collecting area," she said.

She said she was devastated by the loss of habitat.

"I cry when I see beautiful big habitat trees that have been felled," she said.

"Mainly it's just the trunks that have been taken, the branches are left there.

"There's hollows in them that the birds and possums live in and they're just gone, gone forever."

Impacts on business

Geoff North is a farm forester in Walpole, about a 212-kilometre drive south of Donnybrook, and sells parts of his trees to firewood merchants.

He said the sale of illegal firewood was undercutting legitimate businesses.

Geoff North grows Australian native trees on his plantation in Walpole. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding )

"I'm directly competing with people who illegally source it," he said.

"Obviously, if someone's just able to go and collect it for free illegally, well, it's just got to make it hard for my customers to sell their wood at a decent return," he said.

Mr North said illegal firewood collection was a longstanding issue.

"I've known for years that it happens," he said.

" I can hear chainsaws around the bush here too. I think it's pretty common knowledge that people go and help themselves to firewood. "

Council taking action

Community leaders are now looking to take more direct action to protect local forests from illicit harvesting.

The Shire of Donnybrook Balingup unanimously supported the decision at a meeting last week, voting for its chief executive officer to deliver a report on the issue.

Councillor Anita Lindemann, who brought the issue to the council's attention, said she had seen multiple trees cut at the base in areas close to town.

The Shire of Donnybrook Balingup unanimously voted to investigate ways to protect its forests. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

Her motion also detailed reports of chainsaws heard in non-collection areas, cars making their own tracks through the bush and "little management" of the sale of wood online.

"I've been walking in these areas and running in those areas surrounding Donnybrook within a 5-kilometre radius of the township for the past 15 years," she said.

" I've observed a noticeable increase in firewood collection and the felling of old trees in these non-designated firewood collection areas. "

A DBCA spokesperson said firewood could only be collected from approved areas of state forest in the Perth Hills and the South West.

"During the autumn and winter period, DBCA undertakes targeted patrols of known illegal firewood collection hotspots," they said.

"Fallen tree limbs and other naturally occurring woody debris play an important role in the ecosystem by providing habitat, nutrients and food for a variety of wildlife."

World.title: Unification Church leader Hak Ja Han jailed for corruption
World.content:
A South Korean court has sentenced Hak Ja Han, the 83-year-old leader of the Unification Church, to two years in prison for bribing the wife of ousted conservative president Yoon Suk Yeol, and other corruption charges.

The Seoul Central District Court convicted Han, widow of church founder Sun Myung Moon, of violating the political funds act, bribery and embezzling church funds, the court said in a statement.

Han was arrested in September 2025 and later charged with colluding with church officials to give then-first lady Kim Keon Hee luxury goods when her husband was in office, in pursuit of political favours.

What is the Unification Church and why did it face dissolution in Japan? The Unification Church has had close ties to world politics for decades, but a court ruling in Japan challenged its legacy.

Han was also charged with giving politician Kweon Seong-dong, a Yoon loyalist, 100 million won ($102,000) months before Yoon's inauguration in May 2022.

Earlier this year, Kim received a four-year prison term at an appeals court for receiving a Graff diamond necklace and two Chanel bags from the Unification Church, and stock price manipulation, a charge that is unrelated to the church.

On Monday, the Seoul court sentenced a church official to six months in prison and gave two other church officials suspended terms over their involvement in Han's case.

Kweon received a two-year sentence at the Supreme Court, the top court in South Korea, in July.

Han is revered by followers as 'True Mother'

Despite Monday's verdict, Han was out of prison because the Seoul court earlier accepted her request to suspend her arrest until September 2 due to health issues.

A team of investigators led by special prosecutor Min Joong-ki earlier requested a 13-year prison term for Han.

Revered as "True Mother" by her followers, Han is the top leader of the Unification Church, which is officially called the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification.

A mass wedding organised by the Unification Church in 2013 saw some 3,500 couples matched by the church tie the knot. (AFP - Kim Jae-hwan)

In a statement on Monday, the organisation apologised for causing "big concerns and disappointment to the people".

But it said it could not accept the ruling against Han and would appeal against it.

South Korea's former first lady allegedly took bribes of handbags and art Kim Keon Hee, the wife of ex-president Yoon, is alleged to have accepted lavish bribes including fine art, jewellery and designer handbags, and to have meddled in state affairs.

The Unification Church, widely known for mass weddings, was founded in 1954 by Moon, a self-proclaimed messiah who preached new interpretations of the Bible and conservative family values.

He built the church into an international movement with extensive business interests worldwide.

Moon died in 2012 at age 92.

In a blow to the church's branch in Japan, a Tokyo court last year ordered a revocation of its legal status after the government accused it of manipulative fundraising and recruitment tactics that sowed fear among followers and harmed their families.

The order came after a man, who admitted to killing former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe in 2022, said he was motivated by a desire to expose Japanese politicians' ties to the Unification Church.

Probe of church ties began after Yoon's martial law debacle

South Korean investigations of the church-involved scandal started after Yoon was removed from office following a Constitutional Court ruling in April 2025 over his imposition of martial law that threw the nation into turmoil.

The scandalous downfall of Yoon Suk Yeol Former South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol's sentence for insurrection comes after a tumultuous era of shamanism, Chanel bags and conspiracy theories.

His successor Lee Jae Myung, a liberal, appointed three special prosecutors to investigate Yoon's martial law and other allegations during his presidency.

In February, Yoon was sentenced to life in prison for rebellion in connection with his martial law enforcement.

In December 2024, Yoon abruptly imposed martial law and sent troops and police officers to the National Assembly, saying he aimed to eliminate "anti-state forces" and "shameless North Korea sympathisers".

The martial law lasted six hours and he was forced to lift it after the assembly unanimously voted it down.

Yoon has defended his actions, calling it a desperate attempt to draw public support for his fight against the liberal opposition Democratic Party that obstructed his agenda.
