World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Charles Perrottet asked if wife Anita lied to commission as evidence continues
World.content:
Charles Perrottet is being asked to explain what he told his wife Anita about payments she received for his advice to benefit Toplace, after she told the ICAC her husband never did any work for her company.

Charles Perrottet has told the corruption inquiry that his wife’s company Macquarie Consulting received money as remuneration for advice he had given help his friend Jeremy Greenwood with his client, Jean Nassif’s Toplace.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer, SC, has asked Perrottet to explain why he never mentioned this arrangement in his private hearings, and no other people involved in the arrangement, including his wife Anita who received the money, ever mentioned this to the commission before.

Anita previously gave evidence that Charles never did any work for her business Macquarie Consulting, and was never paid. She said she nor her husband ever did any work to benefit Toplace, and that all the money she received from Greenwood’s company Beckington was solely for work she was doing for their client Greyhound Racing NSW.

“Did your wife then lie to the commission last week about the amount that was in fact covering your advice?” Dwyer asked.

World.title: Ex-gang leader found guilty of first-degree murder of Tupac Shakur
World.content:
Breaking CultureMusicPop music Ex-gang leader found guilty of first-degree murder of Tupac Shakur Jonathan Landrum Jr and Jessica Hill Updated September 1, 2026 — 10:34am ,first published September 1, 2026 — 8:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Las Vegas: A jury has found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of orchestrating the killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, marking the first conviction in a case that has gripped hip-hop fans for decades. The 63-year-old Davis was convicted Monday (Las Vegas time) of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison. The jury deliberated for three hours after a weeks-long trial in Las Vegas. Tupac Shakur in 1993, just three years before he died. AP After the verdict was read, Shakur’s sister, Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, cried and reached back to a person behind her. Also in the courtroom was Davis’ son, who covered his face with one hand. Shakur was on his way to perform at a club in Las Vegas when a Cadillac pulled up beside him and music mogul Marion “Suge” Knight. Shakur was shot multiple times and died a week later. Davis is the only person ever charged in Shakur’s death, after he previously said he was in the Cadillac when it pulled up beside Shakur and gunfire erupted. Prosecutors argue Davis orchestrated the shooting, but his attorney argues there is no physical evidence connecting his client to the crime.



Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis acquired a gun and “went hunting” for Shakur and Knight, the co-founder of Death Row Records, after they beat up Davis’ nephew earlier that night. Palal acknowledged that Davis’ accounts of the killing evolved over the years but argued those differences reflected his changing motivations and efforts to protect himself. One critical detail, he said, remained consistent: Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired. “The core facts remain. The material facts remain,” Palal said. Murder accused Duane Davis in court in Las Vegas on Monday. Steve Marcus/POOL Reuters via AP Palal told jurors that if they believe Davis’ statements, they do not have to be independently corroborated with additional evidence.



Still, Palal pointed to the rivalry between the gangs the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru, the fight with Davis’ nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, and testimony that members of Shakur’s circle identified Anderson and Davis as suspects the night of the fatal shooting. Related Article Courts After 30 years, the man accused of orchestrating Tupac’s murder is on trial. Here’s what to know “Who fired is not the question,” Palal told the jury. Prosecutors haven’t argued that Davis pulled the trigger, but instead that he was criminally responsible because he provided the gun and ordered the attack. “The shot caller doesn’t just ride along,” Palal said. The prosecutor also argued the shooting was premeditated, pointing to testimony and Davis’ accounts that the group initially searched for Shakur before later spotting him on the road and making a U-turn. “It’s a plan, not an impulse,” Palal said.



Davis, 63, faced a single count of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang in the killing of Shakur in Las Vegas nearly 30 years ago. The panel of 16 jurors, four of whom are alternates, heard testimony from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defence witnesses over nine days. The prosecution hammered home the argument that Davis called the shots for the attack on Shakur that night based on the accused man’s book and interviews. Davis’ defence attorney reiterated his claim that the prosecution’s narrative is fiction and that they failed to back up Davis’ claims with evidence. Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal points to Davis as he makes closing arguments. Steve Marcus/POOL Reuters via AP The verdict brings to a head a decades-long case that for years has drawn the eyes of hip-hop fans and true crime experts. Shakur, who was considered one of the most influential rappers of all time, was in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, and stopped at a red light when a white Cadillac pulled up beside him, and shots were fired. Knight was also wounded but survived.



For years, nobody was charged in the rapper’s death until Davis began making public statements, saying he was in the Cadillac and gave the gun to others in the back seat. Davis described the shooting as an act of retaliation after Knight and Shakur’s entourage beat up Davis’ nephew hours before the shooting. Under Nevada law, someone who helps another person commit murder can be convicted of the crime. Davis is the only person still alive who was in the Cadillac. Loading Davis’ own words used in evidence Palal held up Davis’ 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, and played an interview in which Davis encouraged people to buy it to get the “real truth”. Although the book contains a disclaimer saying some facts were changed, Palal argued that names, hotels and other details changed while the central account did not.



Palal also rejected the defence’s contention that Davis fabricated his accounts to make money. “It is an entirely different proposition to be profiting from a murder,” Palal said. “And that is what Mr Davis is doing.” Defence attorney Michael Sanft also turned to his client’s memoir during his closing argument. While reading an excerpt, he said the N-word aloud, prompting people watching in an overflow courtroom to recoil and shake their heads. In multiple interviews, Davis said he handed the gun to the back seat, but in others as well as in his book, Davis wouldn’t say who pulled the trigger. Defence attorney Michael Sanft makes his closing arguments. Steve Marcus/POOL Reuters via AP The prosecution’s witnesses included a gang expert who described Davis as the shot caller that younger gang members had to obey.



Witnesses also testified to the heated gang rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru, which were associated with duelling record companies Bad Boy Records and Death Row Records. He was just bragging, defence argues Sanft has told jurors that his client’s words were braggadocio and were meant to make Davis money, not to tell the truth. Sanft, who took on the case without pay, argues there is a lack of physical evidence tying Davis to the crime, such as phone records or bills. During the trial, investigators said a Las Vegas hotel bill was found at Davis’ residence during a police search, but it wasn’t clear when it was dated – or where that evidence is currently located.



The case is nearly 30 years old, which has affected the kind of evidence presented in court. Prosecutors warned jurors that material collected in the ’90s is different from what law enforcement collects today, including hotel surveillance video from the night of the shooting. World.title: 2GB slumps to another poor ratings result, ABC Melbourne rises
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesRadio ratings 2GB slumps to another poor ratings result, ABC Melbourne rises Calum Jaspan September 1, 2026 — 10:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Talkback station 2GB has lost further ground to Sydney’s leading radio station, SmoothFM, but it’s a different story in Melbourne, with 2GB’s sister station, 3AW, continuing to dominate the airwaves. The differing fortunes of the two networks, bought by pokies and pubs baron Arthur Laundy and his family this year, have only widened since the business was sold earlier this year. Station 2GB slumped to an 11.2 per cent share in the fifth radio ratings, down 0.5 percentage points. Breakfast show host Ben Fordham and 2GB owner Arthur Laundy: the station has lost more ground to SmoothFM in Sydney. The station is a distant second in Sydney to Lachlan Murdoch’s SmoothFM which rose 0.1 percentage points to a 13.5 per cent share. Breakfast host at 2GB, Ben Fordham, continued to lead in the breakfast slot with a 14.8 per cent share, but Mornings host Mark Levy remains in second, behind Smooth’s Ty Frost.



The result marks the sixth straight survey since 2GB was the clear number one station in Sydney. The Laundy family purchased the suite of talkback stations from Nine (the owner of this masthead) earlier this year for $56 million, creating the new radio business called Tapt Media. 3AW remained the clear number-one station in Melbourne with a 14.1 per cent share, down 0.1 percentage points. Its breakfast show hosted by Russel Howcroft and Ross Stevenson again led the slot with a 19.5 per cent share despite, dropping 0.6 percentage points. Stations 2GB and 3AW traditionally benefit from their extensive coverage of the winter sports codes in their respective markets, the NRL and AFL. Breakfast hosts at 3AW Russel Howcroft and Ross Stevenson remain on top in Melbourne. 3AW There was little movement across both markets in the survey period which spanned May 24 to June 27 and then July 12 to August 15. Of the non-talkback commercial stations in Melbourne, GoldFM led once again with an 11.4 per cent share, up 0.6 percentage points. It is likely to be a welcome result for owners ARN Media, with KIIS FM languishing in both Melbourne and Sydney while the market waits for the company to appoint permanent breakfast hosts in the wake of the exits of Kyle Sandilands and Jackie “O” Henderson.



Speculation has continued to mount that KIIS will announce Dr Chris Brown as its new Sydney breakfast host. In Sydney, the station’s breakfast show had a 6.9 per cent share while its Melbourne breakfast show had a 5.1 per cent share, the same figure as delivered by The Kyle and Jackie O Show earlier this year. Related Article Workplace Jackie O suffered PTSD after Kyle’s ‘bullying’: doctor The ABC’s local stations in both Melbourne and Sydney had minor gains. In Sydney, the station grew from 5.3 to 5.5 per cent overall, while in Melbourne, the station grew 0.5 percentage points to a 6 per cent share. Both breakfast shows also had positive results, with Craig Reucassel’s show up 0.7 percentage points to a 7.8 per cent share, while the Melbourne show hosted by Bob Murphy and Richelle Hunt grew 1.3 percentage points to a 6.6 per cent share. World.title: David Campbell on why good hearing is an artist’s ultimate instrument
World.content:
Sponsored LifestyleHealth & wellnessSpecsavers Audiology David Campbell on why good hearing is an artist’s ultimate instrument Sponsored by Specsavers Audiology September 1, 2026 — 9:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In this series, we explore why proactive hearing health is vital to staying connected to your passions and loved ones. See all stories .

Behind the heavy velvet of a closed theatre curtain, an orchestra begins to tune up. It is a flurry of strings, woodwinds and brass finding their collective pitch. For singer, actor and TV presenter David Campbell, this precise moment is pure backstage magic. “There’s really nothing like it,” David says, his face lighting up with an unmistakable performer’s grin. “You hear the orchestra tune up, and that’s when you know, OK, we’re about to start. It’s so exciting.” David has spent his entire life under stage lights, inside recording booths and hosting live television. In his world, sound isn’t just an ambient element of the job; it is his internal compass. “Sound is my rhythm,” he explains. “It’s how I cue my life. And if that sound is off, then the whole performance feels out of sync.” The finely tuned instrument



In the entertainment industry, auditory precision is non-negotiable. A professional musician would never dream of walking onto a stage with a cracked guitar, an out-of-tune piano or a microphone that keeps cutting out. David argues that we need to treat our own ears with that exact same professional respect. “In this industry, your ears are the most tuned instrument you have,” he notes. Yet, while millions of Australians diligently maintain their spectacles and dental health, many frequently treat hearing as an afterthought. Recent YouGov consumer research commissioned by Specsavers highlights a stark disconnect between our past lifestyles and our current health habits. The survey revealed that more than half of older Australians (52 per cent) frequently listened to loud or live music when they were younger. For a generation raised on pub rock, local gigs and festivals, those thumping basslines are badges of honour — but they leave a lifelong footprint on our ears. Despite this high exposure, nearly half of Australians (45 per cent) admit it has been longer than a year since their last hearing check, and one in six Australians over the age of 55 (17 per cent) have never had their hearing tested at all. The core issue isn’t a lack of access, but a lack of awareness. For those who delay booking an appointment, over half (51 per cent) say they simply don’t think they need one. There appears to be a common assumption that hearing loss is an all-or-nothing game — that unless you live in total silence, your ears are operating at 100 per cent.



“Sound is my rhythm. It’s how I cue my life. And if that sound is off, then the whole performance feels out of sync.” David Campbell The rhythm of connection For David, the true risk of letting your hearing health slide isn’t just missing a musical cue on stage; it’s the subtle, irreversible erosion of moments at home. “Even at home, it’s the pitch of my kids’ voices,” David says. “When they’re excited, when they’re upset... if you’re not hearing those nuances, you’re not in the moment. You’re just missing lines. You’re not there. You’re missing the heartbeat of connection.” Melissa Chandler, senior audiologist at Specsavers Australia says the research shows a really concerning trend for those experiencing hearing difficulties. “A staggering 61 per cent of Australians who struggle to hear in conversations find themselves resorting to passive withdrawal strategies,” she explains. “This isn’t just about missing a few words; it means 31 per cent are simply pretending to hear and nodding along, while 33 per cent are avoiding restaurants or noisy social hubs altogether. This is a quiet retreat from the social connections that matter most.”



David refuses to let himself be edited out of his family’s script. He wants to go to the movies with his kids, attend live gigs and enthusiastically watch his children put on their own living-room concerts. “That is all I want to do with my spare time,” he says. “The thought that I might miss out on something like that is horrifying to me.” Sound is ‘the heartbeat of connection’ for Campbell. Nine The family wake-up call The critical importance of proactive hearing care hits incredibly close to home for David. Watching his father — legendary Australian rock icon Jimmy Barnes — navigate his own hearing struggles later in life served as a profound turning point. “I see my dad experiencing hearing issues now, which was a real wake-up call for me,” David admits. “It showed me that you just can’t take your hearing for granted. You get to a certain age, you need to get a check-up.”



Chandler echoes this sentiment, emphasising that routine hearing checks are a vital metric for long-term cognitive wellbeing. “Hearing health plays a crucial role in overall wellbeing, social connection, and quality of life,” Chandler notes. “Good hearing can keep your brain active, enhance memory and communication, and promote healthy brain ageing.” The solution is remarkably straightforward. Early detection opens the door to tailored, affordable solutions that prevent us from drifting away from the people and passions we love. Just as you wouldn’t allow a grand piano to slip out of tune, you shouldn’t let such a vital sensory instrument degrade. Protecting your hearing ensures you stay perfectly in sync with the rhythm of your life, from the grandest stage to the quietest family moments. Your hearing is your direct connection to the world — whether it’s your favourite song, the voice of a loved one or simply knowing it’s safe to cross a busy street. Don’t wait for the music to fade before you take action. Prioritise your hearing health and book a free* 15-minute hearing check today. World.title: John Galliano withdraws from Met Museum exhibition following backlash
World.content:
LifestyleFashionMet Gala John Galliano withdraws from Met Museum exhibition following backlash Vanessa Friedman and Jacob Bernstein September 1, 2026 — 9:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Facing an intense backlash, influential fashion designer John Galliano has taken the unprecedented step of withdrawing from a planned exhibition in his honour at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. “After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano wrote in a statement posted to his Instagram page. He also expressed “profound and enduring” gratitude to the museum’s leadership, and acknowledged the pain his past words had caused. John Galliano at the Louvre in Paris last year. In 2011, a French tribunal ruled that he had made hateful remarks about Jews and Asians in two incidents at a bar near his home in Paris. Getty Images “I do not want the debate surrounding me to place the Met in a difficult position or distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute,” he wrote. “I also recognise and respect that an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some.”



In a statement Monday, Max Hollein, the director of the Met, said, “Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition.” The cancellation came at a time when a number of donors and political leaders were coming forward to express their opposition to the nine-month exhibition, which had been scheduled to begin with next year’s Met Gala. Editor's pick Opinion

Met Gala The Amazon takeover of the Met Gala signals an apocalypse for fashion Damien Woolnough Fashion editor In recent days, a furor mounted over the museum’s choice to honour Galliano, who was convicted of an antisemitic hate crime by a French court in 2011. He would have been only the third living designer to receive a solo exhibition at the Costume Institute, the Met’s fashion wing. Given that the Met Gala has traditionally served as the opening night for the Costume Institute’s spring exhibition, the plan risked placing the museum in the position of seeming to sanctify Galliano during an event that has become the Super Bowl of glamour.



Galliano’s departure became known on Monday, just as key members of the Met’s board of trustees were scheduled to gather for a morning meeting to discuss the fate of the exhibition. Museum leadership had also called a Zoom meeting of the board for Monday at 4pm to “focus on a discussion of the Costume Institute,” according to an email invitation that was shared with The New York Times. On Friday, The New York Times quoted Jewish leaders who spoke out against the planned exhibition. They included Arne Glimcher, an art world titan who threatened to cut the museum out of his will; Julie Menin, the speaker of the City Council; and Elisha Wiesel, the chair of the Elie Wiesel Foundation. The Met is one of the 39 arts institutions operating on city-owned property, and it receives millions of dollars of annual support from the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs. Its ties to the city made its decision to honour Galliano a political issue. Menin sent a letter to Met leadership late last week, becoming the first local politician to oppose the planned Galliano exhibition. In an interview Sunday, Menin, a Democrat, called the since-cancelled show “a gut punch to the Jewish community in our city, who are already reeling”. Alexis Roche, Kylie Jenner and John Galliano attended last year’s Met Gala. Getty Images



John Galliano and Kim Kardashian at the 2024 Met Gala. Getty Images for The Met Museum/Vogue In 2011, a French tribunal ruled that Galliano had made hateful remarks about Jews and Asians in two incidents at a bar near his home in Paris. At roughly the same time, a video circulated showing Galliano saying “I love Hitler” and telling appalled patrons that “your mothers, your forefathers” would all be “gassed”. He was fired from his job as the creative director of Dior, a post he had held for 15 years when the video surfaced. In 2014, after Galliano had gone through a stint in rehab and discussed Judaism and its history with rabbis and the former head of the Anti-Defamation League, he became the creative director of Maison Margiela and was reembraced by the fashion world. Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate from Brooklyn, was among the politicians who came forward in recent days to criticise the Met’s plan to honour Galliano, calling it “a bad mistake”. “This seems very straightforward to me,” Lander said on Sunday. “They should cancel the show and change the Met Gala honoree.”



Related Article Exclusive

Retail Designers ditch David Jones: Is Myer winning the department store war? Those critics were joined by Alice Tisch, a prominent donor to the museum. On Friday, as the backlash mounted, Tisch sent an email to Hollein, the museum’s director. “This exhibit bespeaks a failure of governance,” Tisch wrote. She went on to call the planned exhibition a “whitewash,” adding that “it is not in the museum’s interest to have this perception out there, and it flies in the face of your rich curatorial history and ongoing fiscal and moral leadership.” On the watch of Anna Wintour, the chief content officer of Condé Nast and a museum trustee, the Met Gala has become a star-studded benefit, with celebrities seated among billionaires at tables costing hundreds of thousands of dollars.



As Wintour’s presence at the museum has grown, so has that of Condé Nast, a regular sponsor of the Costume Institute exhibitions. Last year, the Met announced that the 11,500-square-foot space off the Great Hall would have a new name: the Condé M Nast Galleries. Anna Wintour and John Galliano at the Dior Haute Couture Spring/Summer show in Paris in 2025. WWD / Getty Images The Met was aware that a show in honour of the designer, a longtime Wintour favourite, might cause a backlash. Before committing to the exhibition, Galliano met with Jewish leaders in gatherings arranged in part by Wintour and Andrew Bolton, the curator of the Costume Institute. Most of the Jewish leaders came away satisfied that Galliano was sufficiently repentant for the hateful remarks he had made. When news of the exhibition became public, Wintour told the Times, “There is no one more deserving of an exhibition of this scale than John Galliano.” She added: “His career isn’t defined by a single moment.” But others questioned why the museum had decided to honour him at a time of rising antisemitism. Angela W Buchdahl, the senior rabbi of Central Synagogue, a reform synagogue in Manhattan, was even invited to be on the host committee of the gala by Wintour but declined.



Sam Raskin, a spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, delivered a statement on Sunday: “John Galliano’s repeated use of antisemitic language is vile. The Mamdani administration recognises that the Met’s decision to honour him has caused pain and anger among many Jewish New Yorkers. The Met is an independent institution and its decisions – and how it responds to the many Jewish New Yorkers appalled by this choice – are ultimately its own. But independence does not mean insulation from criticism.” On Monday, the Met issued a statement: “Information on a new spring Costume Institute exhibition and the 2027 Met Gala will be announced at a later date.” The New York Times Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Charles Perrottet asked if wife Anita lied to commission as evidence continues
World.content:
Charles Perrottet is being asked to explain what he told his wife Anita about payments she received for his advice to benefit Toplace, after she told the ICAC her husband never did any work for her company.

Charles Perrottet has told the corruption inquiry that his wife’s company Macquarie Consulting received money as remuneration for advice he had given help his friend Jeremy Greenwood with his client, Jean Nassif’s Toplace.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer, SC, has asked Perrottet to explain why he never mentioned this arrangement in his private hearings, and no other people involved in the arrangement, including his wife Anita who received the money, ever mentioned this to the commission before.

Anita previously gave evidence that Charles never did any work for her business Macquarie Consulting, and was never paid. She said she nor her husband ever did any work to benefit Toplace, and that all the money she received from Greenwood’s company Beckington was solely for work she was doing for their client Greyhound Racing NSW.

“Did your wife then lie to the commission last week about the amount that was in fact covering your advice?” Dwyer asked.

World.title: Ex-gang leader found guilty of first-degree murder of Tupac Shakur
World.content:
Breaking CultureMusicPop music Ex-gang leader found guilty of first-degree murder of Tupac Shakur Jonathan Landrum Jr and Jessica Hill Updated September 1, 2026 — 10:34am ,first published September 1, 2026 — 8:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Las Vegas: A jury has found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of orchestrating the killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, marking the first conviction in a case that has gripped hip-hop fans for decades. The 63-year-old Davis was convicted Monday (Las Vegas time) of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison. The jury deliberated for three hours after a weeks-long trial in Las Vegas. Tupac Shakur in 1993, just three years before he died. AP After the verdict was read, Shakur’s sister, Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, cried and reached back to a person behind her. Also in the courtroom was Davis’ son, who covered his face with one hand. Shakur was on his way to perform at a club in Las Vegas when a Cadillac pulled up beside him and music mogul Marion “Suge” Knight. Shakur was shot multiple times and died a week later. Davis is the only person ever charged in Shakur’s death, after he previously said he was in the Cadillac when it pulled up beside Shakur and gunfire erupted. Prosecutors argue Davis orchestrated the shooting, but his attorney argues there is no physical evidence connecting his client to the crime.



Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis acquired a gun and “went hunting” for Shakur and Knight, the co-founder of Death Row Records, after they beat up Davis’ nephew earlier that night. Palal acknowledged that Davis’ accounts of the killing evolved over the years but argued those differences reflected his changing motivations and efforts to protect himself. One critical detail, he said, remained consistent: Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired. “The core facts remain. The material facts remain,” Palal said. Murder accused Duane Davis in court in Las Vegas on Monday. Steve Marcus/POOL Reuters via AP Palal told jurors that if they believe Davis’ statements, they do not have to be independently corroborated with additional evidence.



Still, Palal pointed to the rivalry between the gangs the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru, the fight with Davis’ nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, and testimony that members of Shakur’s circle identified Anderson and Davis as suspects the night of the fatal shooting. Related Article Courts After 30 years, the man accused of orchestrating Tupac’s murder is on trial. Here’s what to know “Who fired is not the question,” Palal told the jury. Prosecutors haven’t argued that Davis pulled the trigger, but instead that he was criminally responsible because he provided the gun and ordered the attack. “The shot caller doesn’t just ride along,” Palal said. The prosecutor also argued the shooting was premeditated, pointing to testimony and Davis’ accounts that the group initially searched for Shakur before later spotting him on the road and making a U-turn. “It’s a plan, not an impulse,” Palal said.



Davis, 63, faced a single count of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang in the killing of Shakur in Las Vegas nearly 30 years ago. The panel of 16 jurors, four of whom are alternates, heard testimony from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defence witnesses over nine days. The prosecution hammered home the argument that Davis called the shots for the attack on Shakur that night based on the accused man’s book and interviews. Davis’ defence attorney reiterated his claim that the prosecution’s narrative is fiction and that they failed to back up Davis’ claims with evidence. Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal points to Davis as he makes closing arguments. Steve Marcus/POOL Reuters via AP The verdict brings to a head a decades-long case that for years has drawn the eyes of hip-hop fans and true crime experts. Shakur, who was considered one of the most influential rappers of all time, was in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, and stopped at a red light when a white Cadillac pulled up beside him, and shots were fired. Knight was also wounded but survived.



For years, nobody was charged in the rapper’s death until Davis began making public statements, saying he was in the Cadillac and gave the gun to others in the back seat. Davis described the shooting as an act of retaliation after Knight and Shakur’s entourage beat up Davis’ nephew hours before the shooting. Under Nevada law, someone who helps another person commit murder can be convicted of the crime. Davis is the only person still alive who was in the Cadillac. Loading Davis’ own words used in evidence Palal held up Davis’ 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, and played an interview in which Davis encouraged people to buy it to get the “real truth”. Although the book contains a disclaimer saying some facts were changed, Palal argued that names, hotels and other details changed while the central account did not.



Palal also rejected the defence’s contention that Davis fabricated his accounts to make money. “It is an entirely different proposition to be profiting from a murder,” Palal said. “And that is what Mr Davis is doing.” Defence attorney Michael Sanft also turned to his client’s memoir during his closing argument. While reading an excerpt, he said the N-word aloud, prompting people watching in an overflow courtroom to recoil and shake their heads. In multiple interviews, Davis said he handed the gun to the back seat, but in others as well as in his book, Davis wouldn’t say who pulled the trigger. Defence attorney Michael Sanft makes his closing arguments. Steve Marcus/POOL Reuters via AP The prosecution’s witnesses included a gang expert who described Davis as the shot caller that younger gang members had to obey.



Witnesses also testified to the heated gang rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru, which were associated with duelling record companies Bad Boy Records and Death Row Records. He was just bragging, defence argues Sanft has told jurors that his client’s words were braggadocio and were meant to make Davis money, not to tell the truth. Sanft, who took on the case without pay, argues there is a lack of physical evidence tying Davis to the crime, such as phone records or bills. During the trial, investigators said a Las Vegas hotel bill was found at Davis’ residence during a police search, but it wasn’t clear when it was dated – or where that evidence is currently located.



The case is nearly 30 years old, which has affected the kind of evidence presented in court. Prosecutors warned jurors that material collected in the ’90s is different from what law enforcement collects today, including hotel surveillance video from the night of the shooting. World.title: 2GB slumps to another poor ratings result, ABC Melbourne rises
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesRadio ratings 2GB slumps to another poor ratings result, ABC Melbourne rises Calum Jaspan September 1, 2026 — 10:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Talkback station 2GB has lost further ground to Sydney’s leading radio station, SmoothFM, but it’s a different story in Melbourne, with 2GB’s sister station, 3AW, continuing to dominate the airwaves. The differing fortunes of the two networks, bought by pokies and pubs baron Arthur Laundy and his family this year, have only widened since the business was sold earlier this year. Station 2GB slumped to an 11.2 per cent share in the fifth radio ratings, down 0.5 percentage points. Breakfast show host Ben Fordham and 2GB owner Arthur Laundy: the station has lost more ground to SmoothFM in Sydney. The station is a distant second in Sydney to Lachlan Murdoch’s SmoothFM which rose 0.1 percentage points to a 13.5 per cent share. Breakfast host at 2GB, Ben Fordham, continued to lead in the breakfast slot with a 14.8 per cent share, but Mornings host Mark Levy remains in second, behind Smooth’s Ty Frost.



The result marks the sixth straight survey since 2GB was the clear number one station in Sydney. The Laundy family purchased the suite of talkback stations from Nine (the owner of this masthead) earlier this year for $56 million, creating the new radio business called Tapt Media. 3AW remained the clear number-one station in Melbourne with a 14.1 per cent share, down 0.1 percentage points. Its breakfast show hosted by Russel Howcroft and Ross Stevenson again led the slot with a 19.5 per cent share despite, dropping 0.6 percentage points. Stations 2GB and 3AW traditionally benefit from their extensive coverage of the winter sports codes in their respective markets, the NRL and AFL. Breakfast hosts at 3AW Russel Howcroft and Ross Stevenson remain on top in Melbourne. 3AW There was little movement across both markets in the survey period which spanned May 24 to June 27 and then July 12 to August 15. Of the non-talkback commercial stations in Melbourne, GoldFM led once again with an 11.4 per cent share, up 0.6 percentage points. It is likely to be a welcome result for owners ARN Media, with KIIS FM languishing in both Melbourne and Sydney while the market waits for the company to appoint permanent breakfast hosts in the wake of the exits of Kyle Sandilands and Jackie “O” Henderson.



Speculation has continued to mount that KIIS will announce Dr Chris Brown as its new Sydney breakfast host. In Sydney, the station’s breakfast show had a 6.9 per cent share while its Melbourne breakfast show had a 5.1 per cent share, the same figure as delivered by The Kyle and Jackie O Show earlier this year. Related Article Workplace Jackie O suffered PTSD after Kyle’s ‘bullying’: doctor The ABC’s local stations in both Melbourne and Sydney had minor gains. In Sydney, the station grew from 5.3 to 5.5 per cent overall, while in Melbourne, the station grew 0.5 percentage points to a 6 per cent share. Both breakfast shows also had positive results, with Craig Reucassel’s show up 0.7 percentage points to a 7.8 per cent share, while the Melbourne show hosted by Bob Murphy and Richelle Hunt grew 1.3 percentage points to a 6.6 per cent share. World.content:
Two homes in two separate suburbs have been ravaged by fire overnight, leaving one person with burns and suspicions one property was deliberately torched.

The fire at the Baldivis home on Monday. 9 News Perth

A family-of-six is reeling after their home on Hillsborough Avenue in Baldivis was destroyed by fire around 5pm yesterday, with a fundraising page stating the family “lost everything in a matter of moments”.

“Unfortunately due to the cost of living their insurance has lapsed and they literally only have the clothes on their back,” the page read.

One person was rushed to Fiona Stanley Hospital suffering burns.

World.title: Nick Kyrgios’ cocaine suspension was ‘pretty much expected’, says Tsitsipas
World.content:
SportDrugs in sport Nick Kyrgios’ cocaine suspension was ‘pretty much expected’, says Tsitsipas Brian Mahoney September 1, 2026 — 9:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stefanos Tsitsipas was not surprised that Nick Kyrgios was suspended from tennis for drugs. “Pretty much expected, to be honest,” Tsitsipas said. “I am surprised it came so late, though.” Nick Kyrgios and Stefanos Tsitsipas played doubles together in Washington in 2019. Getty Kyrgios was banned in August after he revealed he tested positive for cocaine in June when he was in Spain to play at an event. The Australian could be suspended for four years, though a lighter punishment is expected. Tsitsipas was asked about Kyrgios on Monday after upsetting No. 10-seeded Arthur Fils in the first round of the US Open.



“I mean, to be entirely honest with you, I knew about this before the announcement. Myself, I knew about it,” Tsitsipas said. “So what can I tell you? I will just tell you the truth. I knew about all of this before any announcement was made, and when I saw it on social media, I was, like, ‘Here we go.’ I kind of expected it, to be honest.” View post on X Tsitsipas and Kyrgios played a fiery match at Wimbledon in 2022, when Kyrgios reached his only Grand Slam final. Tsitsipas blasted a couple shots directly at Kyrgios, intentionally hit a ball into the crowd, and afterward called Kyrgios a “bully.” Kyrgios has largely battled injuries since and said when he was suspended that he had felt “helpless and alone,” though added that “none of that excuses what I did.”



Nor did it come as a shock to Tsitsipas. Related Article Updated

Drugs in sport ‘I’m sorry to the kids who follow me’: Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis “I knew that those were things that were happening away from the tennis courts. I will tell you that,” he said. “I’m not going to try and cover up someone that I know the truth for. I’ll consider myself a nice person with everyone, but these were behaviors that I personally heard on the tour and heard other people in that same environment saying those sort of things to me.“ AP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

Sam Raskin, a spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, delivered a statement on Sunday: “John Galliano’s repeated use of antisemitic language is vile. The Mamdani administration recognises that the Met’s decision to honour him has caused pain and anger among many Jewish New Yorkers. The Met is an independent institution and its decisions – and how it responds to the many Jewish New Yorkers appalled by this choice – are ultimately its own. But independence does not mean insulation from criticism.” On Monday, the Met issued a statement: “Information on a new spring Costume Institute exhibition and the 2027 Met Gala will be announced at a later date.” The New York Times Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: ‘My heart is aching’: Wall of the missing lays bare desperate race to find Nepal victims
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods ‘My heart is aching’: Wall of the missing lays bare desperate race to find Nepal victims Samaan Lateef and Jorg Luyken September 1, 2026 — 8:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kathmandu: A wall in Nepal’s largest hospital has been covered with photographs as relatives try to track down their loved ones. Each day, visitors put pictures of the missing up at Tribhuvan Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, in the hope that staff or passers-by will recognise the face and say they are alive. A woman helps a boy put up a photograph of his missing relative on a wall at the Tribhuvan Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu. AP Photo/Dar Yasin Almost 4000 people, ranging from toddlers to the elderly, remain missing in Nepal after a flood swept down the country’s border with Tibet last week. Among them is 31-year-old Bishal Nepali, whose sister, Sunita, broke down in tears as she added his photograph to the crowded rows.



“Urgent request for search and rescue. Our family is worried. After flooding we have no contact with him,” read the note attached to the poster. Nepali’s wife, 26-year-old Monita Nepali, said he had often crossed the Chinese border. A man looks at photos of people reported missing. Getty Images Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday that the death toll from the flash flooding had climbed to 939, with 3925 reported missing. Getty Images Bishal and Monita Nepali last spoke at 7am on Wednesday, about two hours before the flood, when he went out for a morning walk in the border region. His phone has been off ever since.



“My heart is aching and my hope is fading. I feel he will come back but with each passing day I lose hope of his return,” Monita Nepali said. Over the weekend, the Nepalese authorities began to use mass burial sites after morgues ran out of room to store the decomposing bodies. A boy examines the list of missing flood victims outside the emergency ward. Getty Images Visitors scan the pictures and lists of the missing. Getty Images With morgues full and humid temperatures speeding up decomposition, authorities said they had no choice but to bury bodies before they had been identified.



“We have decided to bury the unidentified bodies because we don’t have the capacity to preserve all the bodies recovered from the flood-affected areas,” said Rajendra Prasad Dhamala, a Nepalese government spokesman. In Bharatpur, three hospital morgues had reached capacity, forcing authorities to establish makeshift facilities. Nepalese military personnel carry a body to a burial site in Chitwan on Monday. AP Photo/Dar Yasin Numbered identification tags placed inside pots mark the graves, AP Photo/Dar Yasin Some 200 unidentified bodies were buried in a nearby forest, beneath numbered metal markers in concrete pots.



At the burial site, security workers in protective gear carried the bodies, one by one, on stretchers as cameras recorded the process. Related Article Graphic content

Floods NSW hiker first Australian declared dead in Nepal flood disaster “Most of the bodies have already started decomposing after being stuck in mud and to prevent further decomposition we have kept them in plastic airtight bags before burying them 1.5 metres underground,” Dhamala said. Of more than 900 bodies recovered in Nepal so far, only 20 have been identified. After days under mud and floodwater, many have become disfigured, making them harder to identify.



In Pokhara, two families claimed the same body, forcing police to turn to DNA testing. Fingerprints and dental records have also been used. Family members from abroad are also arriving in Nepal to search for loved ones. To help families, photos are displayed on small television screens at morgues. Loading Loading The London Telegraph spoke to many families during the past week who said several relatives had died, but their names had not appeared on the official missing list, which suggests the death toll could rise further.



On Monday, Nepal once again raised the number of people confirmed as missing, with the total close to 4000, with a further 900 on the Chinese side of the border. Of that total, 600 are foreign nationals. Related Article Floods ‘Survived by just 10 seconds’: How teacher’s quick decision saved 900 children Rescuers in Nepal are racing against the clock to reach an estimated 900 hydropower workers trapped in tunnels submerged by a wave of mud that cascaded down the valley when the glacier collapsed. The Nepalese army said search-and-rescue teams were using controlled explosions, excavators and searchlights to clear water and mud and reach the trapped workers. Amid the devastation, stories of heroism have begun to emerge.

World.title: Man charged over alleged double murder in Auckland's Wattle Downs
World.content:
A 30-year-old man is facing two charges of murder, following the discovery of two bodies in Auckland's Wattle Downs last week, but police say it's possible more than one person is involved.

Emergency services were called to a house on Gambare Place at 1.45pm on Thursday last week after a report of person armed with a handgun at the property and a woman injured.

When police arrived two people were found dead due to gunshots.

Detective Inspector Tofilau Faamanuia Va'aelua said a police investigation was ongoing to figure out if more than one person was involved.

"We are pleased to have been able to charge this man in relation to this tragic incident, however the investigation remains ongoing and we are not ruling out any further arrests."

World.title: What does future look like for petrol prices now?
World.content:
A government decision to delay fuel tax increases will mean some short-term relief, but motorists shouldn't be hanging out for fuel prices to return to where they were before conflict broke out in the Middle East, economists say.

It was announced on Monday that, rather than increasing by 12 cents in January and then 6c and 5c a year into 2029, tax will rise 5c every six months beginning in 2028.

Data from fuel price monitoring site Gaspy shows that 91 petrol has dropped in price by 1.6 percent over the past 28 days, and is now an average $3 nationwide.

Diesel is down 0.62 percent and 95 1.4 percent over the same period.

The cheapest petrol on Tuesday was at Pak 'n Save Tauranga, at $2.676.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

ASB senior economist Mark Smith said petrol prices were lower than they might be expected to be, given what was happening internationally.

"It's been very surprising, I think, for a lot of people given the Strait of Hormuz is functionally closed, the US and Iran are in a pretty heated conflict. It's been surprising how benign fuel prices are, just over $3 a litre for unleaded. That's certainly surprising compared to what we would have thought a couple of months ago."

He said the experience had shown that people were managing to divert fuel supplies.

"There is quite a lot of fuel still going through the Strait of Hormuz, through those dark channels. They've managed to divert production from other means via pipelines.

"The US has also stepped up product, so those things have certainly been helpful."

He said fuel spreads has increased from about $20 a barrel to about $70. "That's going to add to the prices."

Smith said it was hard to know what prices would do through the rest of the year and into 2027.

"It's a pretty fast-moving sort of conflict and we have been encouraged by how people have changed behaviour.

"People are probably driving a bit less than they were six months or so ago. We've seen the supplier response take effect, that's encouraging.

"This sort of conflict adds a bit of a risk premium. If you think of oil prices going forward, while we do expect oil prices to come back down it's likely to be quite a bit higher than it was pre-conflict. Similarly with refining spreads as well.

"The expectation hat we're going to return to February levels for fuel prices looks pretty ambitious at the moment."

Mike Jones, chief economist at BNZ, agreed prices were likely to stay higher.

"A lot can happen and quickly, as we saw in June when the Strait of Hormuz reopened for a time and crude oil prices briefly returned to pre-conflict levels," he said.

"I think it is worth recalling that, before the conflict, the global oil market was generally regarded as being in a state of oversupply. That should help prices correct lower if there is a durable resolution and oil can move through the Strait more freely.

"The complication is that global oil inventories have been drawn down significantly this year. Those stocks will take time to rebuild, which could slow the pace at which oil and fuel prices return to more normal levels. Our assumption is that fuel prices ease towards the end of this year but remain above pre-conflict levels in the near term."

World.title: Hipkins leaves door open on borrowing for fuel tax freeze
World.content:
Chris Hipkins won't rule out borrowing more to pay for the shortfall in the country's land transport fund after Labour announced it would freeze fuel tax increases for the next three years.

The Labour leader was firm on Thursday when he announced the policy that it would have to "scale" investments under the National Land Transport Fund to make sure any projects fitted within the funding that was available.

"That happens every three years when the when the new GPS (Government Policy Statement) on land transport is set out," he said last week.

"This is a government that's telling councils they've got to scale their ambitions to fit within a rates cap, that every other government agency has to scale to fit within it, so will the National Land Transport Fund."

By Monday Hipkins wouldn't rule out needing to borrow more to fill the shortfall in the transport fund as a result of halting any increases to fuel tax.

Asked multiple times by RNZ if he would commit to not borrowing more to top up the transport fund, Hipkins repeated he wasn't announcing the party's fiscal policy.

"We'll set out in our own fiscal plan different spending choices to the current government. So I'm not going to set out our fiscal plan today."

On Tuesday morning Hipkins was again questioned on his way into caucus about how Labour would deal with the shortfall, and what would be cut to pay for it.

He confirmed he wouldn't be reversing "the top-ups that the government announced yesterday", which was roughly $1.5 billion worth.

Fuel excise taxes were due to be increased by 12 cents from 1 January 2027, then increase annually by 6 cents and 4 cents heading into 2029 - a total increase of 22 cents.

Instead, the tax will go up by 5 cents every six months, beginning in 2028 through the end of 2029 - a total increase of 20 cents, which the prime minister announced on Monday.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop confirmed of the $1.5b needed to keep up with the required work, half a million dollars of that would come from the rainy day fund previously set aside in this year's Budget for the fuel crisis.

The other $1b would be outlined once the government had seen the pre-election fiscal update from Treasury, he said.

Bishop says the shortfall for Labour is much larger, however, and put a price tag of $4.6b on the cost of not doing any fuel tax increases for three years.

Hipkins disagrees it would be that much and while he says he has an idea of what it might be, he wasn't prepared to share it.

He told RNZ on Tuesday he would look very closely at whether he needed to find any other funding streams, outside of the government's top-up and the scaling back of investments in the transport fund, to pay for the shortfall.

"There are some things that we won't do. You know, we won't be shovelling money into a gondola that the current government can't answer questions about.

"We won't be spending $300 million on roads of national significance that then get cancelled," he said.

"Every government should prioritise within the National Land Transport Fund - that is what we will do."

World.title: 'They should be at work': Christopher Luxon on 10,000 striking public servants
World.content:
Public Service Minister Paul Goldsmith has criticised public servants planning to strike next week, saying the industrial action is part of a "broader political campaign" to change the government.

About 10,000 members of the Public Service Association (PSA) are set to strike on the afternoon of Wednesday, 9 September following prolonged pay negotiations.

Affected agencies included the Ministry of Social Development (MSD), the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) and the Ministry for Ethnic Communities (MEC).

Speaking to reporters at Parliament on Tuesday, Goldsmith said the action looked politically motivated.

"They've got little pamphlets out there saying 'change the government'," he said. "The people of New Zealand will be inconvenienced out of what could be seen as a broader political campaign."

Goldsmith said public servants received "very significant" pay bumps under the Labour government and had continued to be offered modest increases.

"They've got a right to strike, but I think it's poor form."

Public Service Minister Paul Goldsmith RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Speaking separately, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he'd prefer the public servants to be "actually working" instead of striking.

"They should be at work or they should be around the table negotiating," he said. "But that's up to the agencies that deal with."

In a statement, the PSA said the government should focus on settling collective bargaining rather than attacking the union.

"Workers have a fundamental right to strike, and the government should respect that and focus on settling this dispute," national secretary Duane Leo said.

Need to see improved offer - union

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons earlier told RNZ employers needed to come back to the table with an improved offer.

She denied Goldsmith's claim that the strike was politically motivated and said ministers should focus on settling the dispute rather than attacking the union.

"Union members have endorsed the strike action because the offers in bargaining are not there. We need to see an improved offer from the employers, and the government should support them to do that.

PSA national secretary said public servants should get pay increases consistent with the increased cost of living. Supplied

"We need to see public servants getting pay increases that are consistent with the increased cost of living."

Ministers punt major ministry merger plan into next term

In May, the government announced plans to cut a further 8700 public service roles over the next three years.

It also promised to streamline and merge the roughly 40 government departments, but further details have yet to be revealed.

A newly released document, reported on Tuesday, revealed Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche last year advocated to reduce the number of government agencies down to between 15 and 20.

In his letter to then-minister Judith Collins, Roche said the consolidation would take three to five years and be driven by common technology and "a lot more AI".

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche last year advocated reducing the number of government agencies. RNZ / REECE BAKER

"This is not making more MBIEs - in fact we will be shrinking MBIE," he said.

"This is what you have asked me to do. I will front it and I will defend it, because I think it is the right thing to do."

Goldsmith said no decisions had been made on the final make-up of the public service: "That's something that the next government will consider."

Asked what had taken so long, Goldsmith said the programme was a "reasonably complex exercise".

He said National would take a public service policy into the election, but would not say whether it would identify a desired number of government departments.

Luxon said his government would pursue "major reform" in its second term.

World.title: 'The smell of death': Son tells trial how he found his father dead and mother missing at Ellerslie home
World.content:
It was the smell of death that made Chi-Ho Ricky Kwok suspect his father was dead.

His next question was where was his mum.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li was on trial for the murders of Fuk Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong in their home in Auckland's Ellerslie in 2023.

He's also charged with conspiring to murder someone else, who cannot be named.

A jury in the High Court at Auckland heard harrowing evidence about the night Ricky Kwok went to check on his parents, and found his dad dead and his mum missing.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li is on trial. Nick Monro

Kwok, an only child, told the court his parents would come to Hamilton where he lived on a regular basis.

The Kwok's were meant to visit their son for Joseph's birthday, shortly before a trip to Hong Kong, but never arrived.

Just after 1pm, Kwok grew nervous, calling them to no avail.

Kwok, who followed his theatre nurse father and midwife mother into a career as a vascular surgeon, said it was "extraordinary unusual" for his mother not to pick up.

"I was very concerned," he said.

Kwok alerted the police and asked for a welfare check.

He was worried his parents had been involved in a car crash on their way to Hamilton, after WhatsApp messages weren't able to reach his parents phones.

He made the decision to drive to Auckland to check himself.

The home cordoned off in 2023. (File photo) RNZ / Nick Monro

Arriving in Auckland, Kwok saw his parents car was missing from their driveway when he arrived.

Inside the Celtic Crescent house, Kwok found a body - his father.

It was then his medical training kicked in.

"As I approached towards that area, which was technically the area just beside the dining table, there was this smell," Kwok told the court.

"Medically, I would describe it as melena, essentially the smell of rotting blood, fermented blood."

Kwok knew not to touch the body, something he'd also learned from his medical training and watching "too much CSI dramas".

He did however check for a pulse, which he could not find.

"On top of that, the reason why I suspected that he was dead was because he had that smell of death that, again, working in the profession, you know when someone's been dead for at least a couple of hours," Kwok said.

"There's a certain rotting smell associated with that."

It was then, Kwok's mind shifted.

"My first fear was, dad's gone, but where's mum?" he said.

"Especially because there was no reply when I was calling out for her."

Kwok searched the house but could not find his mother.

"My medical instinct was that he was dead already but mum was missing and she was hopefully still alive but perhaps unconscious for whatever reason," he said.

"You can't save the dead, but you can save the living."

When he couldn't find his mother, he called the ambulance and police.

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and Mei Han Chong with their son. Supplied / NZ police

The operator asked if he needed an ambulance, and it was then Kwok checked for the signs of death.

He had already checked for a pulse, and could not see signs of breathing, but had not checked his father's pupils.

Kwok lifted a jacket and bloody towel that had been covering his father's face.

He was asked by Crown prosecutor Alysha McClintock if he could recognise his father.

"Battered, bruised, bloated," Kwok said.

Soon after, he went to the front neighbour's property to see if they had heard anything.

They invited him inside, and made him a hot chocolate as he waited for police to arrive.

World.title: US pushes critical minerals agenda in Cook Islands with new Penrhyn port
World.content:
RNZ's Teuila Fuatai in Koror, Palau

The United States and New Zealand will co-fund a new "lifeline" port with the Cook Islands on Penrhyn atoll - a former US military base.

The US says it will commit $50 million USD, while New Zealand will contribute $10 million USD.

The US Deputy State Secretary Christopher Landau said it builds on the Critical Minerals Framework that the Cooks signed with the US in February, which advances the keen interest from Washington in deep sea mineral resources in the Cook Islands.

"This project underscores the United States' strong commitment to our partners in the Pacific," Landau said, noting that U.S. personnel constructed Penrhyn's port and airstrip over 80 years ago.

"Through transformational infrastructure initiatives such as this, we are making the United States and our partners safer, stronger, and more prosperous."

New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters, the Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown and the US Deputy State Secretary Christopher Landau come together in Palau to announce a new upgrade of the port on Penrhyn atoll in the Cooks, 1 September 2026. Teuila Fuatai

Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown called the port a "lifeline" for the Pa Enua, adding capacity for domestic shipping and inter-island travel.

"We thank the United States and New Zealand for partnering with us to deliver on a priority our people have themselves identified," Brown said.

Landau, Brown and New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters made the announcement at the Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting in Palau this morning.

The February agreement between the US and the Cooks committed them to "responsible investment aligned with high environmental, social and governance standards," and "the development of secure, diversified and resilient critical minerals supply chains."

World.title: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis found guilty of orchestrating Tupac's murder
World.content:
CNN reports that prosecutors didn’t allege Davis fired the shots that killed Tupac Shakur but accused him of orchestrating the killing.



Davis briefly raised his fist, looking into the audience, as he exited the courtroom after being found guilty.



Family members appeared emotional as the guilty verdict was read.



There were no audible reactions in the courtroom, but Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur – the rapper’s sister – appeared to cry quietly.



Judge Carli Kierny scheduled sentencing for October 13 shortly after prosecutors announced they were dropping their pursuit of a “gang enhancement” due to witness logistics.

World.title: Louise Upston refuses to apologise after benefits wrongly suspended in second MSD error
World.content:
Social Development Minister Louise Upston is refusing to apologise after some people's benefits were wrongly suspended.

Upston says she's awaiting the outcome of a review into the matter, and she's already said sorry for another problem caused by the same law change.

The benefit payments were incorrectly stopped following a law change that was rushed through Parliament last year.

The new law requires some beneficiaries to re-confirm their circumstances at least once every 52 weeks, to check whether they are still eligible.

The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) said processing delays caused by a high volume of people confirming their circumstances meant some of their paperwork was not checked in time, so their benefit payments stopped.

It could not say how many people had been affected, but confirmed they had all been paid back.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon apologised on Friday, a week after he and Upston said sorry for another related but separate problem which saw thousands of pensioners miss out on their Winter Energy Payment.

Upston on Tuesday was asked whether she would also apologise for the wrongly suspended benefit payments.

"I've already done that," she said.

It was put to Upston that she had apologised for the first problem, but not the second.

"As I said, I've got a report that I'm expecting on the 10th of September [from MSD].

"When I have all the detail, I promise you, I will come back to you with exactly the extent of who was affected, how and why, and what the actions are."

Upston said she was frustrated by the problems.

"Clearly, with the Winter Energy Payment and others, there were people who didn't receive payments that should of, and that is challenging for those individuals."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Social Development Minister Louise Upston apologised on Friday for another related but separate problem. Kim Baker Wilson / RNZ

Questions remain over comments in the House

MSD said it informed Upston of both problems on 13 August.

On 18 August, Upston was asked in Parliament whether beneficiaries had missed payments due to processing delays.

She said "no", but after multiple further questions, said "possibly".

RNZ asked Upston to clarify her comments.

She said she was informed of the Winter Energy Payment problem on Thursday [13 August] and it was resolved by Saturday morning.

"There are other challenges related to delays in processing, and so by the 10th of September, I will have a report that goes into any issue that has been identified that relates to the [Confirm] Your Circumstances, and that's what I'm waiting on information for."

Upston was also asked whether she had misled Parliament, but she did not respond.

Labour urges Upston to take responsibility

Labour's social development spokesperson Willow-Jean Prime said Upston should correct the record in the House, given her first answer said the problem had not occurred.

Prime said Upston was throwing officials under the bus when the problem was caused by "rushed lawmaking".

It did not wash that MSD and the Minister could not say how many beneficiaries were affected by the second problem, but could say how many missed out on the Winter Energy Payment, said Prime.

"If they have been able to confirm that they have repaid all of that money to those people who have missed out on their payments due to their errors, then they know how many people there are," she said.

World.title: Former rival says Nick Kyrgios's drug ban 'pretty much expected'
World.content:
Stefanos Tsitsipas says he was not surprised when Nick Kyrgios was suspended from tennis for drug use.

Kyrgios was banned earlier this month after he revealed he tested positive for cocaine in June when he was in Spain to play at an event.

The Australian could be suspended for four years, though a lighter punishment is expected.

Tsitsipas was asked about Kyrgios on Monday after upsetting 10th-seeded Arthur Fils in the first round of the US Open.

The former world number three, who had a famously contentious relationship with Kyrgios, said he was surprised the suspension did not come sooner.

"I mean, to be entirely honest with you, I knew about this before the announcement. Myself, I knew about it," Tsitsipas said.

"So what can I tell you? I will just tell you the truth. I knew about all of this before any announcement was made, and when I saw it on social media, I was, like, 'Here we go.' I kind of expected it, to be honest."

Tsitsipas and Kyrgios played a fiery match at Wimbledon in 2022 , when Kyrgios reached his only Grand Slam final. Tsitsipas blasted a couple of shots directly at Kyrgios, intentionally hit a ball into the crowd, and afterward called Kyrgios a "bully".

Kyrgios has largely battled injuries since and said when he was suspended that he had felt "helpless and alone", though added that "none of that excuses what I did".

Nor did it come as a shock to Tsitsipas.

"I knew that those were things that were happening away from the tennis courts. I will tell you that," he said.

"I'm not going to try and cover up someone that I know the truth for. I'll consider myself a nice person with everyone, but these were behaviours that I personally heard on the tour and heard other people in that same environment saying those sort of things to me.

"So when I saw it it I was like, 'well, pretty much expected, to be honest'. I am surprised it came so late, though."
